The committee said the investigations would proceed alongside its legislative and oversight activities aimed at strengthening transparency, accountability and efficiency in Nigeria’s petroleum industry.

World.title: Anambra Police: Presence at Ibezim’s service to maintain peace
World.content:
By Vincent Ujumadu

The Anambra State Police Command has explained that the heavy security presence at St. Faith’s Anglican Cathedral, Awka, during a church service conducted by the suspended Archbishop Alexander Ibezim on Sunday was to maintain law and order and prevent a breakdown of peace.

Ibezim, the Anglican Archbishop on the Niger and Bishop of Awka Diocese, was suspended by the Primate of the Church of Nigeria (Anglican Communion), Most Rev. Henry Ndukuba, who directed him to proceed on a six-month leave with immediate effect.

The suspension was announced pending investigations into allegations against Ibezim and recent developments in the diocese.

The Primate also barred Ibezim from officiating at any activity of the Church of Nigeria (Anglican Communion), the Province of the Niger or the Anglican Diocese of Awka during the period of his leave.

The Bishop of Aguata Diocese, Rt. Rev. Samuel Ezeofor, was subsequently directed to oversee the Diocese of Awka and the Archdiocese on the Niger.

However, the Board of the Diocese of Awka has rejected the suspension, threatening to leave the Church of Nigeria and join the Church of England if the Primate insists on enforcing the decision.

Against this backdrop, police operatives were heavily deployed at St. Faith’s Anglican Cathedral, Awka, on Sunday as Ibezim conducted the service.

Reacting to reports about the police presence, the Police Public Relations Officer in Anambra State, SP Tochukwu Ikenga, described some accounts of the deployment as misleading.

Ikenga cautioned against what he called the misrepresentation of security interventions in ways that could heighten tensions surrounding the ecclesiastical dispute.

“The Command wishes to clarify that the deployment of police personnel to any location is guided by the need to maintain law and order, prevent a breakdown of peace, protect lives and property, and ensure the safety of all concerned, irrespective of their affiliations or positions in the dispute,” he said.

He stressed that the police presence should not be interpreted as an endorsement of any party or position in the church disagreement.

“The Nigeria Police Force remains a neutral institution committed to enforcing the law, safeguarding citizens’ rights, and preventing disputes from escalating into threats to public peace and security,” Ikenga added.

The police spokesman urged members of the public to refrain from circulating narratives capable of inflaming tensions or deepening divisions within the religious community.

He assured that the command would continue to discharge its constitutional responsibilities professionally and impartially, without fear or favour.

Ikenga added that the police would not allow any disagreement, whether religious or otherwise, to degenerate into a breach of public peace and security.

World.title: N4,000/$ Exchange Rate: NDC asks why refineries are not working
World.content:
By Henry Umoru

ABUJA — The Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) has faulted the Federal Government’s warning that a return to petrol subsidy could push the naira to between N3,000 and N4,000 per dollar, demanding explanations for the failure of the country’s refineries to operate effectively.

The party also questioned why Nigeria had mortgaged a sizeable portion of its crude oil to secure foreign loans, alleging that the arrangement had affected the country’s ability to supply the Dangote Refinery with sufficient crude oil to meet domestic demand.

The NDC’s National Publicity Secretary, Osa Director, made the remarks while reacting to comments by the Minister of Finance and Coordinating Minister of the Economy, Taiwo Oyedele, who warned against a return to petrol subsidy.

Oyedele had said reinstating the subsidy could trigger capital flight, undermine investor confidence and weaken the naira to N3,000, N3,500 or even N4,000 to the dollar.

In response, Director said the government should address the underlying problems in the petroleum sector rather than focus solely on the potential consequences of restoring the subsidy.

“The most important aspect of the subsidy conversation is not yet addressed. Why are our refineries not working? Why did the APC government mortgage a sizeable portion of our crude oil to take foreign loans to the extent that we are unable to supply Dangote Refinery the needed crude oil to satisfy domestic consumption and demand?” he asked.

He argued that addressing the challenges affecting domestic refining and what he described as criminality in the subsidy regime would make the minister’s warning unnecessary.

“If all these and the criminality in the subsidy regime are addressed, the doomsday prediction of the Minister of Finance would not be necessary,” Director said.

Oyedele had issued the warning during a press briefing at the International Monetary Fund and World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, on Monday.

The minister said investors had repeatedly questioned whether the Federal Government would abandon its economic reforms ahead of the next election cycle.

He added that President Bola Tinubu had maintained that the national budget had made no provision for petrol subsidy since June 2023, insisting that the subsidy had therefore been removed.

World.title: At 50: Brand refresh raises questions about heritage, consumer loyalty
World.content:
By Chioma Obinna

As competition in Nigeria’s non-alcoholic beverage market continues to evolve, Maltina, one of the country’s longstanding malt drink brands, has unveiled a refreshed visual identity to mark its 50th anniversary, retaining its familiar taste while introducing redesigned packaging across its product range.

The new identity, unveiled by Nigerian Breweries Plc last week, features updated designs across glass bottles, cans and PET bottles, with enhanced gold elements and a stronger orange colour scheme aimed at giving the brand a more contemporary appearance.

The redesign highlights a broader challenge facing established consumer brands: how to modernise their appearance to appeal to changing consumer preferences without losing the familiarity and trust built over decades.

For Maltina, which has been part of Nigeria’s beverage market since 1976, the anniversary presents an opportunity to reinforce its heritage while repositioning the brand for a new generation of consumers.

However, beyond the visual changes, the success of the refresh will depend on how consumers respond to the new packaging and whether the brand can sustain its relevance in an increasingly competitive market.

Other features of the refreshed identity include a gold crown cork, brighter sunrays, a more prominent golden barley icon, a bolder calcium coin and a “Since 1976” heritage mark, underscoring the brand’s five-decade history in Nigeria.

Despite the packaging changes, Nigerian Breweries said Maltina’s familiar taste and nutritional composition remain unchanged.

The company said the drink is fortified with calcium, with one 33cl bottle providing the equivalent of half a glass of milk. The brand is also endorsed by the Nutrition Society of Nigeria as a non-alcoholic drink rich in Vitamin A.

Speaking on the refreshed identity, the Marketing Director of Nigerian Breweries Plc, Sarah Agha, said the redesign was intended to keep the brand relevant to contemporary consumers while preserving its heritage.

“For 50 years, Maltina has grown alongside generations of Nigerians. This refreshed identity is an evolution of a much-loved brand, designed to keep Maltina fresh, relevant and connected to today’s consumers while preserving the nourishing taste they know and trust,” Agha said.

Her remarks reflect the company’s effort to balance continuity with change, maintaining the product attributes familiar to existing consumers while introducing a new visual experience that could attract younger buyers.

For established brands, packaging plays an important role in consumer recognition, influencing how products stand out on retail shelves and how customers relate to them. A redesign, therefore, must do more than create a different appearance; it must preserve the identity that consumers associate with the product.

Maltina’s decision to retain its taste and nutritional composition while updating its packaging suggests that the company is seeking to refresh its market appeal without altering the product experience on which its reputation has been built.

As part of the relaunch, Nigerian Breweries is introducing a consumer engagement campaign tagged “What’s Your Word?”, inviting Nigerians to describe their first impressions of the new packaging in one word.

According to Agha, the campaign is intended to involve consumers in shaping the brand’s next chapter by encouraging them to share their reactions to the refreshed identity.

“This relaunch is about more than a new pack. It is an invitation for Nigerians to help shape the next chapter of a brand that has been part of their lives for five decades. We look forward to hearing the words the new Maltina inspires,” she added.

World.title: Catholic bishops declare nationwide fasting, prayer
World.content:
The Catholic Bishops Conference of Nigeria, CBCN, has declared a nationwide prayer and fasting programme to promote free, fair, credible and peaceful elections in 2027.

The programme, themed ‘Let Justice and Peace Flow’, is drawn from Amos 5:24.

The bishops announced the initiative in a statement signed by their President, Archbishop Matthew Ndagoso, and Secretary, Bishop Peter Odetoyinbo, yesterday in Abuja.

They said the programme was necessary as Nigeria approached the 2027 general elections amid recurring challenges of electoral violence, rigging, vote-buying and ethno-religious divisions.

The bishops urged dioceses, parishes, church societies, prayer groups, families and individuals to participate actively in the spiritual exercise.

They said the initiative was aimed at seeking God’s guidance for electoral officials and security personnel to discharge their responsibilities faithfully, while inspiring citizens to vote conscientiously and discouraging electoral malpractice and violence.

According to the statement, all parishes would observe October 31 and November 28 as days of prayer and fasting for Nigeria.

Activities would include fasting, the Rosary procession, Holy Mass and the recitation of the CBCN prayer for the 2027 elections.

The bishops also designated December 8, the Solemnity of the Immaculate Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary, as a nationwide diocesan day of prayer.

The programme would begin with Holy Mass at 3 p.m., presided over by the diocesan bishop, during which a pastoral letter titled “2027 Elections: Call to Responsible Choice and Action” would be read.

The Mass would be followed by a Rosary procession to the cathedral at 4:30 p.m. and conclude with Eucharistic Benediction.

The statement further declared January 15, 2027, the eve of the general elections, a nationwide parish day of prayer and fasting.

The bishops urged Nigerians to reject tribalism, corruption, bribery and voter apathy, while encouraging citizens to vote and protect their votes peacefully.

They called for a credible electoral process free from rancour and bloodshed.

World.title: Jigawa NUJ secures release of six inmates
World.content:
By Muhammad Inuwa, Dutse

The Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ), Jigawa State Council, has secured the release of six inmates from the Gumel Correctional Centre by paying fines imposed on them by the courts.

The intervention was part of activities marking the council’s maiden Press Week, aimed at promoting humanitarian services and supporting vulnerable members of society.

This was disclosed in a statement jointly signed by the NUJ State Chairman, Comrade Isma’il Ibrahim Dutse, and the Council Secretary, Comrade Aminu Umar Shuwajo.

According to the statement, the six beneficiaries had remained in custody because they could not afford to pay the fines imposed on them as alternatives to imprisonment.

They were identified as Musa Ilu, popularly known as Gwaska; Umar Sani; Inusa Lawan; Hassan Shu’aibu; Nuhu Hassan; and Suraja Tahir, also known as Chanko.

The union said the intervention reflected its commitment to giving back to society and supporting people facing difficult circumstances.

In a related development, the NUJ delegation visited the Dutse Correctional Centre, where it donated essential items to improve the welfare of inmates.

The items included cartons of Maggi Star seasoning, May soap, Klin detergent and sanitary pads.

Presenting the items, Dutse said the visit was part of activities lined up to mark the council’s maiden Press Week.

Receiving the donations, the Officer-in-Charge of the centre, CSC Muhammad Nazir, commended the union for the humanitarian gesture.

Nazir described the intervention as the first of its kind by journalists in the state and acknowledged the media’s role as a partner in societal development.

He assured the union of continued cordial relations with the correctional service and urged other unions and organisations in the state to emulate the gesture.

World.title: Tinubu extends tenures of Immigration, Correctional Service Chiefs
World.content:
By Johnbosco Agbakwuru

ABUJA — President Bola Tinubu has approved 18-month tenure extensions for Sylvester Ndidi Nwakuche, Controller-General of the Nigerian Correctional Service, and Kemi Nanna Nandap, Comptroller-General of the Nigeria Immigration Service.

Following the approval, Nwakuche’s tenure will now end on May 26, 2028, while Nandap’s will end on June 30, 2028.

The approval, which followed a recommendation by the Minister of Interior, Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo, is aimed at addressing succession gaps in both services and giving their respective boards sufficient time to appoint successors.

President Tinubu commended Nwakuche and Nandap for the reforms achieved under their leadership and charged them to consolidate the gains.

Tinubu nominated Nwakuche as Controller-General of the Nigerian Correctional Service in December 2024. The Senate confirmed his appointment in March 2025.

The President nominated Kemi Nanna Nandap as Comptroller-General of the Nigeria Immigration Service on February 21, 2024. The Senate confirmed her appointment on March 1, 2024.

World.title: THE MATH OF INDEPENDENCE
World.content:
DAMILOLA BAKARE argues against the overwhelming vestiges of colonialism

On October 1st, 2026, Nigeria turns 66.

Sixty-six years of owning a flag, a constitution, and a seat at the UN. Yet as a single, amalgamated British territory, Nigeria existed for only 46 years (1914–1960).

How does 46 years of colonial setup continue to outlive 66 years of self-rule?

Nigeria inherited a 46-year-old colonial system, but we have also had six and a half decades to modify it, replace it, or build something entirely different. That is the real paradox. The flag came down, but the wiring remained. The ideas, incentives and hierarchies did not leave with the British. A mindset does not leave because those who installed it left, it must be deliberately replaced, and no one did that for us in 1960.

Colonialism was not just about the District Officers and administrative boundaries, it was also about creating a hierarchy of knowledge, authority, language, culture and values. It taught people, over generations, what should be considered sophisticated and local; what was legitimate and what was informal; what was polished and what was not; what counted as knowledge and what was superstition. Those ideas did not require British officials to remain in Nigeria to survive, they were reproduced by Nigerians themselves.

That is what makes the idea of mental colonialism worth examining as Nigeria marks 66 years of independence. We see it every day in the courtroom, where lawyers still wear 17th-century British horsehair wigs and black gowns in 35-degree heat to appear learned. You see it in the civil service, where a three-piece suit in 38-degree Abuja remains the uniform of seriousness, while Kaftan or Isiagu is “casual.” Local entrepreneurs struggle to gain legitimacy in their own market, while imported brands are automatically associated with quality and prestige. The message is consistent: authority must look foreign to be real. To be fair, none of this is explained by colonialism alone, globalisation, class, economic incentives and modern media all play their part. But colonial history helped build the hierarchies through which we still assign value.

We devalue what makes us, us. Consider beauty.

Skin bleaching is widespread across Africa, with Nigeria recording some of the highest reported rates. The exact figures vary, but the pattern is undeniable.

Why does lighter skin command such a premium in a society whose overwhelming majority is Black? The answer is not colonialism alone. Colourism, class, gender expectations, advertising, and modern beauty culture all play a role, but colonialism built the framework for these to grow.

We see the same pattern in the world of work. Skilled trades are often viewed as backup plan by graduates rather than professions requiring expertise, certification, and entrepreneurship. Yes, higher pay and growth opportunities sometimes explain these preferences, but do they explain why certain forms of work are considered inherently more prestigious even when they pay less than skilled trades?

The problem is not aspiration. It is the hierarchy of aspiration.

Colonial influence did not survive through one channel, several factors; some created during colonial rule and others expanded after independence account for this phenomenon.

Colonial education was closely connected to the administrative and economic needs of the colonial system. It was built to produce clerks not creators. Overtime, the Nigerian elite learned to equate intelligence with fluency in English, not competence in solving Nigerian problems. We inherited that meanwhile; the objective of education should be to produce Nigerians capable of understanding the world and solving Nigerian problems.

Indirect rule preserved chiefs but reduced their legitimacy. They became accountable upward to the Crown, not downward to the people. At independence, we inherited that extractive architecture where a state designed to control territory and collect revenue, not to serve citizens. And that is one of the deepest questions of post-colonial Nigeria.

The 1914 amalgamation was for British balance sheets, not Nigerian cohesion. We kept the structure, changed the flag, and wondered why it still extracts rather than serves.

After Britain left, the cultural centre of gravity did not automatically return to Nigeria. American and European media, fashion, advertising became the standard. So, colonialism evolved into globalization and now, the real question is whether Nigeria will remain a consumer of global culture or become a major exporter of it.

The success of Afrobeats and Nollywood shows what is possible. Nigerian culture is already shaping global tastes, but largely through the drive of exceptional individuals rather than deliberate national strategy. Like South Korea with K-pop and K-dramas, Nigeria should create the incentives, policies, and institutions needed to export its culture at scale. Cultural influence should not depend solely on talent. It should be supported by strategy.

One, de-Lugardize Education. If the problem is partly the hierarchy through which we value knowledge, the solution cannot be to replace one hierarchy with another. Rather, we must build an education system that treats Nigerian knowledge, experience, and realities with equal seriousness.

An agriculture student should learn both global agricultural science and the realities of farming in Nigeria. An engineering student should be trained to design for the infrastructure challenges they are likely to encounter at home. A public policy student should study ideas from Britain and the United States but also be challenged to develop solutions for problems in Kano, Lagos, Bayelsa, Enugu, or Yobe.

Our universities should reward practical problem-solving. Government funding should prioritise research that addresses local challenges and produces solutions with direct social and economic impact. Education should prepare Nigerians not only to understand the world, but also to improve the country they live in.

Two, Make Nigerian-ness Profitable. Promote the use of Nigerian fabrics even in corporate settings. Rwanda did it with Made-in-Rwanda. It kills the colonial idea that “corporate” means suit and tie in 38-degree heat. Then tax bleaching creams like tobacco and use the revenue to run campaigns and sensitisation schemes that restore pride in being dark-skinned and natural-haired.

Three, Kill the Colonial Economy. The economy created in 1914 was designed to export raw materials and import finished goods. More than a century later, we still follow that model. True economic independence requires policies that promote value addition at home, creating jobs, skills, and wealth before goods leave our shores.

We must also rebrand work. Nigeria should establish national guilds for skilled trades such as welding, tailoring, and farming, with recognised certification, pensions, and professional status comparable to ICAN or the NBA. Countries such as Germany have shown that vocational excellence can be a source of prestige and national strength.

Colonialism is no longer an excuse 66 years later. But it remains an explanation for how certain hierarchies were built. We have had time to dismantle them. The question is not whether 46 still shapes us. It does. The question is what we have done with 66.

Bakare is Development Communications Expert and Founder, Full Life Creed

World.title: NAFDAC, REGULATORY FAILURE AND POISON IN THE MARKETPLACE
World.content:
KALU OKORONKWO urges the regulatory agency to consistently protect the lives of Nigerians

The National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC) was established in 1993 in the aftermath of Nigeria’s devastating 1990 paracetamol syrup poisoning disaster, which was associated with at least 109 child deaths linked to diethylene glycol contamination. Its creation represented a critical institutional intervention intended to strengthen public protection against unsafe medicines and other hazardous consumer products.

More than three decades after its establishment under Decree No. 15 of 1993 and subsequent amendments, the existence of NAFDAC has not eliminated the threat of substandard and falsified medicines, adulterated foods and potentially hazardous beverages.

This contradiction raises a fundamental question that goes beyond the existence of regulatory laws or the visibility of enforcement operations. How effectively has NAFDAC translated its statutory mandate into tangible protection for human life? The persistence of unsafe products in the marketplace demands an incisive examination of regulatory oversight, enforcement capacity, institutional accountability and the gap between the promise of public protection and the realities confronting Nigerian consumers.

NAFDAC’s establishment was an important response to the need for effective regulation of medicines, foods, beverages and other products within its statutory mandate. But creating an agency, however necessary, is not the same as eliminating the problem it was designed to address. Legislation can confer authority, institutions can establish procedures, and regulators can recruit inspectors and acquire laboratory equipment. The ultimate test is whether these mechanisms consistently protect the public.

That distinction became painfully clear during the My Pikin teething medicine disaster of 2008–2009. A joint investigation involving Nigerian public-health authorities and international experts identified 57 poisoning cases, with 54 dead, among children aged between one to three years. Investigators detected diethylene glycol contamination in samples of the implicated medicine recovered from patients’ homes and in batches associated with its manufacturer. NAFDAC initiated a recall, and the manufacturing facility was shut down.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) described the incident as Nigeria’s second and largest diethylene glycol-associated poisoning outbreak since 1990. The tragedy remains especially disturbing because the victims were young children whose caregivers had reason to believe they were administering medicine to relieve discomfort. The product was not merely defective merchandise; it was a substance entrusted with a therapeutic purpose that instead became associated with fatal poisoning.

In recent years, concerns about falsified medicines, unwholesome foods and unsafe beverages have continued to expose weaknesses in Nigeria’s product safety environment. Reports of enforcement operations and product seizures point to the scale of the challenge. But the discovery of unsafe products does not, by itself, establish how many people have been harmed or does it prove regulatory negligence in every case.

In Lagos, Onitsha, Port Harcourt, Aba, Kano and other commercial cities, the circulation of unwholesome products raises questions about the effectiveness of inspection, surveillance, distribution controls and the enforcement of existing standards. According to figures attributed to NAFDAC’s enforcement operations, products valued at approximately ₦22.73 billion were destroyed between January and August 2026.

During the same eight-month period, the agency reportedly recorded 5,542 enforcement activities, conducted 213 raids, documented 821 product-seizure entries, closed or sealed 179 premises and made 52 arrests. It also handled 474 new cases, concluded 295 cases and carried out 22 destruction exercises.

These figures suggest considerable enforcement activities, but their public health significance depends on what they reveal about the effectiveness of regulation. How many dangerous products were intercepted before reaching the markets and to the consumers? How many investigations resulted in successful prosecutions? And how effectively were the supply chains behind the offences dismantled? Such questions are essential because the number of raids conducted or the value of goods destroyed cannot, on their own, establish that the public is safer.

The My Pikin investigation offers a sobering illustration of the limits of reactive enforcement. The CDC report found that 28 per cent of the affected children had received the implicated medicine after the recall had been announced. This finding underscores the importance of rapid public communication, effective product tracing and the timely removal of dangerous products from circulation. A recall is indispensable, but its success depends on whether the warning reaches consumers and whether the affected product can be withdrawn before further exposure occurs.

When a product itself becomes the source of danger, consumers may have little means of protecting themselves. They depend on regulators, manufacturers, distributors and retailers to ensure that what reaches the market is safe.

Consider the case of a young man who reportedly developed complications and died after taking antimalarial medication purchased from a pharmaceutical outlet. Without verified details, the cause of his death cannot responsibly be attributed to a falsified or contaminated medicine. Nevertheless, such an account raises an important question: what safeguards can consumers rely on when a product purchased for treatment may itself pose a risk?

The same concern extends beyond medicines. Imagine a family buying palm oil to prepare a favourite meal, unaware that the product may have been adulterated. Consider parents purchasing fruit for their children without knowing whether it was handled or stored safely before reaching the market. For millions of Nigerians, these concerns reflect a wider anxiety about the safety and authenticity of products consumed daily in homes, workplaces, markets and healthcare facilities.

Recent enforcement operations have brought these risks into sharper focus, including investigations into suspected illegal production and repackaging of alcoholic and energy drinks using materials bearing the names of established brands.

At Zamfara Plaza, within the BBA Trade Fair Complex along the Badagry Expressway in Ojo, Lagos State, NAFDAC operatives reportedly uncovered a suspected illicit production or repackaging facility housed in a two-storey building. The operation followed intelligence gathering and surveillance concerning suspected counterfeiters operating within the Trade Fair International Market.

Two suspects, identified in reports as Chibuzor Okafor and William John, were arrested. Officials reportedly recovered drums, filters, packaging materials, a heating device and other equipment suspected to have been used in the operation. According to NAFDAC, some of the suspects were caught in the act.

Speaking during the raid, the Assistant Director of the agency’s Investigation and Enforcement Directorate, Mr Kunle Ojo, expressed concern about the scale of the discovery. “What we have discovered today is a lot, and it’s mind-boggling. We are here to protect the lives of many Nigerians,” he said. One of the most troubling aspects of the operation emerged from an explanation reportedly offered by one of the suspects.

Okafor, who identified himself as a drinks dealer, told Saturday Vanguard that he changed the bottles in which drinks were contained. “I deal on drinks. I change the bottle of the drink. It’s not that the bottle is not good. It’s the drink in there, because the other one is already damaged. So that’s why we are putting it to the next bottle,” he said.

The account raises a fundamental question for consumers: what exactly was inside those bottles, and could buyers establish whether the contents were genuine, properly manufactured and safe to consume? The answer depends on evidence from the investigation and, where necessary, laboratory analysis. The broader concern, however, is clear: packaging can create an impression of authenticity that the contents may not justify.

In Ondo State, many families are still grieving following the loss of loved ones after drinking contaminated local brew. No fewer than 49 people died with 182 hospitalized, after consuming Monkey Tail, a very popular local brew suspected to have been caused by methanol poisoning, highlighting the dangers posed by unregulated alcoholic drinks in the market.

A serious discussion of medicine safety must distinguish between falsified medicines, substandard medicines and contaminated medicines. Although these categories can overlap, they describe different problems and may require different regulatory responses. Falsified medicines involve deliberate deception about a product’s identity, composition or source. A criminal operator may imitate the packaging of a reputable brand, manufacture a product under a false identity or misrepresent its ingredients. Patients may believe they are purchasing a genuine medicine when the contents do not match what the label claims.

The danger is that a falsified product may contain the wrong ingredient, an incorrect quantity of the active ingredient, no active ingredient at all or a harmful substance. A patient receiving a falsified antibiotic, for example, may fail to obtain effective treatment. Someone relying on medication for a chronic or life-threatening condition may experience complications because the product does not deliver the expected therapeutic benefit.

Substandard medicines, by contrast, are authorised medical products that fail to meet applicable quality specifications or standards. The failure may result from manufacturing defects, inadequate quality control, degradation during storage or transportation, or other departures from required specifications. Unlike falsification, substandard quality does not necessarily imply deliberate fraud.

This distinction matters because the appropriate response must address the actual cause. A manufacturing defect calls for an investigation of quality systems and corrective action. Deliberate falsification requires investigators to trace the criminal supply chain and pursue appropriate enforcement. Both can endanger patients, but their causes and accountability pathways differ.

Contaminated medicines contain unwanted or harmful substances introduced during manufacturing, handling, storage or another stage of the supply chain. Contamination may occur accidentally because of inadequate quality control or results from deliberate adulteration. The My Pikin tragedy illustrates the devastating consequences when a toxic chemical enters a medicine intended for children.

These categories are not mutually exclusive. A falsified medicine may also be contaminated, while a substandard product may contain an unintended impurity. The concerns are: what the evidence establishes about the product, what hazard it presents and what failure allowed it to reach patients.

The consequences range from treatment failure and avoidable complications to poisoning and death. In some cases, the danger cannot be detected without laboratory testing. A medicine may have convincing packaging, an intact seal and an apparently legitimate registration number while its contents remain unsafe. Consumers cannot reasonably be expected to verify pharmaceutical composition by sight, smell or taste.

Food adulteration may involve the substitution of ingredients, concealment of defects, misleading labelling or the use of prohibited substances. Contamination may arise from unsafe raw materials, polluted water, inadequate sanitation, poor storage or failures in production hygiene. Similar weaknesses can compromise packaged water, soft drinks and alcoholic beverages.

A bottle of water may appear clean while containing a microbial hazard. A processed food may look wholesome while containing an undeclared or unsafe ingredient. A beverage may be sold under a familiar brand identity without having been manufactured by the legitimate producer.

These are different risks, but they share a common feature which consumers often lack the information or technical capacity to identify. Product safety therefore cannot rest primarily on the vigilance of individual buyers. It requires effective regulation, responsible manufacturing, reliable distribution systems and consequences for deliberate violations.

Successive NAFDAC administrations have contributed to the development of Nigeria’s regulatory framework. From Professor Gabriel Ediale Osuide, the agency’s pioneer Director-General, through the tenure of the late Professor Dora Akunyili, the technological modernisation associated with Dr Paul Orhii, the transitional leadership of Mrs Yetunde Oni and the regulatory reforms pursued under Professor Mojisola Christianah Adeyeye. Each administration has left its mark on the institution.

Akunyili became particularly associated with the high-profile campaign against counterfeit medicines. Orhii’s tenure was associated with efforts to introduce technology into product authentication and regulatory processes. Later administrations continued efforts to strengthen regulatory systems and improve institutional capacity. These contributions deserve recognition. However, institutional history must be assessed alongside present-day performance. The relevant question is whether successive reforms have produced consistent and measurable improvements in the safety of products available to ordinary Nigerians.

The challenge is not simply whether NAFDAC conducts raids, seizes goods or destroys products. It is whether enforcement disrupts the networks responsible for placing dangerous products on the market. When investigations end with the removal of goods from a warehouse, without adequately tracing their origin or identifying the people who financed, manufactured or distributed them, the underlying commercial network may survive. Effective enforcement must follow the product through the supply chain, establish how it entered circulation, identify responsible parties and pursue prosecution where the evidence warrants it.

Where a genuine manufacturing defect is involved, regulators must investigate the process that caused the failure and determine whether other batches are affected. Where falsification is established, investigators must trace the supply chain and gather evidence against those responsible. In both cases, recalls and public warnings must be timely, accessible and sufficiently specific to help consumers identify affected products.

The same principle applies to food and beverages. Factory inspections must go beyond paperwork to examine production hygiene, ingredients, water quality where relevant, packaging, storage and the systems used to maintain consistent safety. Registration should not be treated as a permanent guarantee that a product will remain compliant regardless of how it is manufactured, transported or distributed.

These responsibilities are complicated by informal supply chains, counterfeit branding, cross-border trade, limited consumer information and the commercial incentives that encourage some operators to cut corners. Such difficulties are reasons to strengthen surveillance, improve coordination and direct resources towards high-risk products and supply routes—not reasons to lower expectations of regulatory performance.

Where credible evidence establishes negligence, misconduct or corruption by public officials, accountability must extend to those responsible. At the same time, allegations must be investigated fairly, and arrests must not be presented as convictions. Regulatory credibility depends on both the willingness to act and the integrity of the process.

Unsafe products do not respect income, education or geography. A falsified medicine can enter an urban distribution network; contaminated food can reach a major retail outlet; and an adulterated beverage can be sold to consumers who have no reason to suspect wrongdoing. The economic consequences also extend beyond the immediate health risks. Families may face additional treatment costs, loss of income and prolonged care for affected relatives. Public hospitals may have to manage preventable complications, while legitimate manufacturers and traders can suffer reputational damage when counterfeiters imitate their products. Trust in the market and in regulatory institutions is weakened when consumers cannot confidently distinguish genuine goods from unsafe substitutes. These wider costs reinforce the need to treat product safety as a central public-health and governance concern, rather than merely an enforcement issue.

NAFDAC’s reported enforcement activities in 2026 demonstrate continued intervention against unsafe and non-compliant products. The volume of operations and the value of goods destroyed are important indicators of activity, but they do not, on their own, establish how much the risk to consumers has declined.

A credible assessment requires a broader set of performance measures. These should include the speed with which safety alerts are issued, the proportion of recalled products successfully removed from circulation, the time taken to investigate reported hazards, the outcomes of prosecutions, the recurrence of violations and the agency’s ability to identify dangerous products before they cause widespread harm.

A country’s public-health system is judged not only by the medicines it approves, the factories it inspects or the products it destroys. It is also judged by whether parents can reasonably trust the medicine they give their children, whether families can purchase food without undue fear of hidden hazards, and whether consumers can rely on the institutions responsible for product safety.

NAFDAC must therefore be judged by a demanding but fair standard: its ability to prevent harm, detect danger, respond promptly, enforce the law and demonstrate measurable improvements in public protection. No regulatory system can eliminate every risk. The question is whether Nigeria can make dangerous products harder to produce and distribute, identify hazards before they cause widespread harm, and ensure that those responsible face meaningful consequences.

The ultimate measure of NAFDAC’s success is not simply the monetary value of products destroyed or the number of raids conducted. It is the effectiveness of its vigilance, independence and enforcement in keeping unsafe products out of Nigerian homes and the consistency with which it protects the lives it was established to serve.

Okoronkwo is a communications strategist, a leadership and good governance advocate

World.title: ECONOMIC HARDSHIP AND THE 2027 ELECTIONS
World.content:
As the 2027 general election draws nearer, Nigeria’s persistent economic hardship, compounded by rising costs of petrol (PMS) and cooking gas, presents a significant challenge for President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and the All Progressives Congress (APC). While the administration may point to its economic reforms and other achievements, it must not underestimate how the daily struggles of ordinary Nigerians could influence the outcome of the election.

President Tinubu assumed office in May 2023 at a time when Nigeria faced considerable economic challenges. His administration introduced major reforms, including the removal of the petrol subsidy and changes to the foreign exchange system, arguing that these measures were necessary to address structural weaknesses and establish a more sustainable economy. These reforms have had important fiscal and market implications, but their immediate costs have placed considerable pressure on households and businesses.

As the cost of living continues to concern Nigerians, increases in petrol and cooking gas prices threaten to intensify the burden. Higher fuel prices affect transportation, food distribution, production and the cost of providing essential services. Cooking gas price increases also place additional pressure on households already struggling to meet basic needs. The effects are interconnected: when transportation and production costs rise, the prices of goods and services often follow.

Although international developments, including tensions arising from the conflict involving the United States and Iran, can influence global energy markets, domestic policies and market conditions also determine how these pressures affect Nigerian consumers. The government should therefore consider temporary, targeted interventions to cushion the impact of external shocks without undermining the broader objectives of economic reform.

History offers important lessons about the relationship between public hardship and electoral outcomes. In the United States, economic concerns, particularly the cost of living, contributed to Donald Trump’s return to the presidency in 2024. Although immigration, political identity and other issues also influenced voters, dissatisfaction with the economy featured prominently in the election.

Nigeria’s experience is equally instructive. In 2015, President Goodluck Jonathan lost his re-election bid amid widespread concerns about insecurity and the management of national affairs. While these factors did not operate in isolation, the election demonstrated how a government’s perceived inability to address citizens’ most pressing concerns can weaken its electoral support.

The lesson is that citizens experiencing prolonged hardship may become receptive to alternative leadership, regardless of the explanations offered by the incumbent government. This can produce what is commonly described as a protest vote: a decision by voters to reject the ruling party to express dissatisfaction with their circumstances or the government’s performance.

For the APC, the danger is not necessarily that the opposition may have a superior campaign strategy, but that widespread frustration could become a political force in its own right. Party structures, political alliances and campaign promises matter, but they may prove insufficient if voters believe their living conditions have deteriorated without adequate relief.

Ultimately, if the 2027 election will be determined by the free and fair expression of Nigerians’ choices, as promised by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) it is responsibility of the APC is to earn public confidence through results, not assume that political loyalty will guarantee electoral success. Economic hardship may yet prove more formidable than any opposition campaign. The time to respond is now. Listening to Nigerians, easing avoidable suffering and demonstrating measurable progress would serve both the public interest and the government’s political future.

Kenechukwu Aguolu, Kenerek1@gmail.com

World.title: PUBLIC PROCUREMENT AND INDUSTRIAL DEVELOPMENT
World.content:
Uba Sani pushes for government patronage of Made-in-Nigeria Vehicles, writes KABIR DANJUMA

When Governor Uba Sani unveiled the 2026 Peugeot 5008 at the Dangote Peugeot Automobile Nigeria (D-PAN) Limited factory in Kaduna, the event represented more than the introduction of a new vehicle model. It offered an opportunity to renew an important conversation about Nigeria’s industrial future: how government patronage can help sustain local manufacturing, create jobs and turn domestic production into a driver of economic growth.

The governor’s message was direct. Nigerian governments should do more than celebrate locally manufactured products; they should create practical demand for them. By pledging to make a strong presentation to the National Economic Council (NEC) on the need for federal and state ministries, departments and agencies (MDAs) to patronise D-PAN vehicles, Sani placed public procurement at the centre of the debate on industrial development.

He also pledged that Kaduna State would order some of the vehicles, declaring that his administration intended to lead by example. The proposal raises a fundamental question for Nigeria’s manufacturing sector: what happens when the government becomes an active customer of the industries it hopes to grow?

The Peugeot 5008 unveiling provided a platform for the governor to underscore the economic importance of the automobile assembly plant to Kaduna State. Sani commended Alhaji Aliko Dangote for what he described as patriotism through sustained investment in Nigeria. He noted that D-PAN had created jobs, helped address skills gaps and stimulated economic activity within its immediate environment and across the state.

These contributions illustrate why manufacturing matters beyond the factory floor. An operating industrial plant creates demand for workers, technical expertise, logistics, maintenance, supplies and other supporting services. Its economic influence can extend into surrounding communities, where businesses and households benefit from the spending generated by industrial activity.

For Kaduna, strengthening such an enterprise offers an opportunity to deepen the state’s industrial base while creating pathways for residents to participate in productive economic activity.

But industrial investment also requires a dependable market. A factory may possess the equipment, workforce and capacity to assemble vehicles, yet its long-term sustainability depends on customers willing and able to purchase its products. This is where Sani’s call for government patronage becomes particularly significant.

Government procurement can be an important instrument of industrial policy. Federal and state institutions require vehicles for official duties, field operations, inspections and administrative responsibilities. Where locally manufactured products meet the necessary requirements, directing a portion of that demand towards domestic producers can support industrial activity.

Sani’s proposed engagement with the NEC seeks to extend this argument beyond Kaduna State. His objective is to encourage governments at both federal and state levels to consider D-PAN vehicles when making procurement decisions.

His pledge that Kaduna State would place an order is equally important because it gives practical expression to the message he wants other governments to embrace. However, sustainable patronage must be built on more than declarations. Public procurement should consider price, quality, safety, durability, after-sales support, maintenance costs and value for money. Transparent purchasing processes and clear standards would help ensure that patronage supports local industry without compromising public accountability.

For D-PAN and other Nigerian manufacturers, the opportunity is to demonstrate that locally produced vehicles can meet the operational requirements of institutional buyers while offering dependable service throughout their working life.

If that confidence is established, government demand could become one component of a broader market that includes private businesses, corporate fleets and individual consumers. Sani’s emphasis on D-PAN’s contribution to employment and economic activity reflects a wider challenge facing Nigeria: converting investment into sustainable livelihoods.

Manufacturing creates opportunities for workers with different levels of technical expertise, from production and assembly to administration, engineering and maintenance. It can also stimulate demand for transport, catering, equipment servicing and other support services.

The governor’s argument is that supporting the factory helps sustain an economic ecosystem rather than merely promoting a particular vehicle.

For host communities, the presence of an industrial enterprise can bring employment opportunities and additional commercial activity. For the state, it offers a chance to strengthen productive capacity and expand the economic base beyond reliance on traditional sources of revenue.

Yet the benefits are not automatic. They depend on the plant’s ability to sustain production, compete effectively and build relationships with local suppliers and skilled workers. Strong connections between industry and local businesses can deepen the economic impact of an investment by keeping more value within the domestic economy.

This makes the governor’s appeal for government patronage part of a larger conversation about how Nigeria can support businesses that invest, employ people and contribute to local production.

One of the most forward-looking aspects of the governor’s remarks was his call for D-PAN to consider graduates of the Kaduna State Institute of Vocational and Skills Development. According to Sani, the graduates had completed intensive training in partnership with the National Board for Technical Education (NBTE). He urged the company to explore opportunities to engage them.

The appeal highlights the relationship between vocational education and industrial growth. Training programmes become more valuable when graduates can apply their skills in real workplaces, gain experience and develop pathways towards sustainable employment.

For an automobile assembly plant, relevant technical skills can support production, equipment maintenance, quality control and other operational functions. Industry participation in training can also help ensure that the skills being taught reflect practical workplace needs.

A stronger partnership between D-PAN, vocational institutions and technical education authorities could therefore create benefits on both sides. Young people would gain opportunities to apply their training, while the company could access a pool of locally trained talent.

The next step is to translate the governor’s appeal into practical arrangements, whether through recruitment, internships, apprenticeships or further technical training. Such opportunities would help connect education with employment and give skills development a clearer economic purpose.

Sani also praised D-PAN’s corporate social responsibility initiatives in communities around its operations, while encouraging the company to do more.

He noted that the factory and its host community were coexisting peacefully, describing continued support for the community as essential to maintaining that relationship.

The point is important because industrial development is not sustained by investment and production alone. Businesses operate within communities whose residents have legitimate interests in employment, infrastructure, environmental responsibility and social wellbeing.

Constructive relationships can build trust, reduce tensions and create an environment in which businesses and communities benefit from one another. Corporate social responsibility is most effective when it responds to clearly identified local needs and complements, rather than replaces, the obligations of government.

For D-PAN, deeper community engagement could reinforce its place in Kaduna’s economic landscape. For the state government, supporting a productive relationship between the company and its host community forms part of creating conditions for sustainable industrial activity.

The unveiling of the 2026 Peugeot 5008 has placed the question of local automobile production and government procurement back in focus. Sani’s proposed presentation to the NEC offers a route towards broader discussions on how public institutions can support domestic manufacturers.

The real test, however, will be implementation: whether Kaduna State follows through on its proposed purchase, whether other governments assess the opportunity on transparent value-for-money grounds, and whether D-PAN can sustain the quality, service and production standards needed to build customer confidence.

The governor’s call also points to a wider responsibility for manufacturers. Government patronage can provide demand, but long-term industrial competitiveness requires innovation, efficient operations, reliable products and sustained investment in people and technology.

Nigeria’s industrial future will depend partly on whether it can create a stronger connection between investment, skills, public procurement and local production. D-PAN’s role in Kaduna provides one setting in which that relationship can be tested and strengthened.

Ultimately, the significance of Sani’s intervention goes beyond a single vehicle unveiling. It is a call to treat local manufacturing as an economic asset whose success can support employment, technical development and wider commercial activity.

If the proposed patronage translates into transparent procurement, sustained production and meaningful employment opportunities, the benefits could extend well beyond the factory gates. That is the promise behind the governor’s appeal: turning government purchasing power into practical support for Nigerian industry, while ensuring that public investment delivers value to the people it serves.

Danjuma writes from Kaduna State

World.title: Again, Egypt to Host CAF Women’s Champions League Final
World.content:
The Confédération Africaine de Football (CAF) has confirmed that Egypt will host CAF Women’s Champions League Final Competition for the second successive years.

Egypt have now hosted the event three times – having hosted the inaugural event in 2021.

Eight Clubs, Zonal Winners in their respective CAF Zones, from across the continent will gather from November 1 to 15 2026 to compete for the Continental Title.

Several clubs have already secured their qualification through regional tournaments:

Mamelodi Sundowns, the two-time champions from from South Africa (representing COSAFA), Uganda’s Kawempe Muslim (representing CECAFA), Cameroon’s Lekie FF (representing UNIFFAC), and Mali’s USFAS (representing WAFU – A).

Morocco will be represented by Fath Union Sport (FUS) Rabat, which qualified via the UNAF qualifiers and also the defending champions, AS FAR Rabat.

The final two spots will go to the representative from the WAFU Zone B region (yet to be determined) and the club representing the Host Nation, Egypt.

The CAF Women’s Champions League has firmly established itself as a prominent event on the African women’s football calendar. The 2026 edition will offer the qualified clubs another opportunity to compete at the highest continental level and contribute to the development of women’s football across the continent.

World.title: AKPABIO AND THE SUICIDE BILL
World.content:
Mental illness is a medical condition which is treatable

The opposition of the Senate President, Godswill Akpabio, to the move to decriminalise attempted suicide is quite unfortunate. Although the Senate passed the Suicide Prevention Bill 2026, sponsored by Senator Asuquo Ekpenyong, for a second reading, Akpabio insisted that survivors should be jailed. The bill seeks to decriminalise attempted suicide and provide survivors with medical treatment, rehabilitation, and psychological support. “As far as we are concerned, we are saying that suicide is a crime for now,” Akpabio said at plenary. “Therefore, if you attempt it, you better succeed. If you don’t succeed, we will send you to prison.”

Following Akpabio’s remark, the Association of Psychiatrists in Nigeria (APN) warned that threatening suicide attempt survivors with imprisonment could deepen stigma and discourage people experiencing mental health crises from seeking help. According to the APN, a person who survives a suicide attempt should be treated as someone experiencing severe psychological distress and requiring urgent medical attention, not punishment. “The appropriate response is urgent medical care, compassionate assessment, treatment, safety planning and follow-up—not a threat of imprisonment,” the APN said.

The Ekpenyong bill proposes crisis helplines, public awareness programmes, training for police officers, teachers and health workers, and a national data system to strengthen suicide prevention. It also seeks to address what its sponsor described as inconsistencies between the National Mental Health Act, which recognises attempted suicide as a psychiatric emergency requiring intervention, and provisions of the Criminal Code and Penal Code that criminalise the act. After scaling a second reading last Tuesday, it was referred to the Senate Committees on Judiciary and Health for further legislative action, including a public hearing. Although Akpabio has said his position does not necessarily represent that of the Senate, it is still nonetheless unfortunate.

Since depression, according to experts, is one of the commonest reasons why people commit suicide, we should not criminalise what is no more than a medical condition. Indeed, changing the narrative on suicide, according to the World Health Organisation (WHO), “is about transforming how we perceive this complex issue and shifting from a culture of silence and stigma to one of openness, understanding, and support.”

Instructively, only two months ago in August, the Federal Executive Council (FEC) approved a proposal to amend the National Mental Health Act with the aim of removing criminal penalties for attempted suicide, officially shifting Nigeria’s legal framework from punishment to care and psychological support. Currently, both Section 327 of the Criminal Code Act (Southern Nigeria) and Section 231 of the Penal Code (Northern Nigeria) criminalise suicide attempts. Medical practitioners under the aegis of the Society of Family Physicians of Nigeria, (SOFPON) have for years been raising concerns about the growing number of Nigerians living with depression, a major risk factor for suicide. Besides, the nation’s present socio-economic environment has been a predisposing factor to depression and perhaps suicide. Therefore, to successfully deal with this problem of suicides, there is an urgent need to address the issue of stigma. On that score, we endorse the Ekpenyong bill and urge the National Assembly to expedite action on its passage.

Mental illness is nothing to be ashamed of. Like diabetes and heart disease, it is a medical condition which is treatable. Many people with mental health illness return to a productive and fulfilling life after promptly seeking help. But the country is not doing enough to tackle this public health emergency, and it is responsible for the growing cases of suicides. Stemming the tide requires a multi-sectoral and multi-disciplinary approach involving various government ministries, agencies, and departments (MDAs), especially that of health, labour and employment, and social services. But it must begin with an amendment to the existing laws still in operation in Nigeria that criminalise a serious health challenge.

World.title: Grange School, St Saviour’s Dominate 2nd Pan African School Games
World.content:
Grange School, Ikeja, emerged as the overall winner in the Under 13 and Under 15 categories at the second Pan African School Games, while St Saviour’s School, Ikoyi, claimed the overall title in the Under 11 category of the three-day tournament held at James Hopes College, Lekki.

Grange School received a new bus sponsored by Mikano Changan Motors after securing the highest number of points in the Under 13 and Under 15 categories. St Saviour’s School dominated the Under 11 category, winning the overall title.

The three-day event, held at James Hope College, Lekki, brought together more than 400 students from 11 schools. Organised by Seun Akinbohun, Busola Tejumola and Aderoju Ope Ajayi, the Games give children opportunities to compete, develop their sporting abilities and build friendships with students from other schools.

This year’s edition attracted strong support from leading corporate organisations, including Prime Atlantic, Zenith Bank, Plumtre Advisory, Mikano Changan Motors, UAC Foods, Nigerian Exchange Group (NGX), Team 33 Productions, Flytime, What Media, Kantar, Logic City and Flutterwave. The Lagos State Government and the Lagos State Sports Commission also partnered with the organisers in support of the initiative.

In the Under 11 category, St Saviour’s School, Ikoyi, won swimming and athletics, while St Saviour’s School and Lagos Preparatory & Secondary School shared the football title. St Saviour’s School secured the overall title in the age group. Grange School won swimming and athletics in both the Under 13 and Under 15 categories, while Riverbank School won football in both age groups. Grange School’s combined results placed it first in the overall standings for the Under 13 and Under 15 categories.

Speaking at the event, the Director of Sports at the Lagos State Sports Commission, Travih Nunayon, commended the organisers and said the commission had deployed talent scouts to identify promising athletes during the Games.

Nunayon, who represented the commission’s Director General, Lekan Fatodu, said the event provided an opportunity to discover young athletes and support their development. He added that discussions had begun with the organisers on sustaining the initiative.

According to him, athletes identified during the competition could be considered for events such as the National Youth Games and the National Intermediate Games, with the commission continuing to monitor their progress.

Co-founder Aderoju Ope Ajayi said the Games were established to help children develop their potential in sports alongside their education. She explained that the founders, who are also sports parents, understood the opportunities that participation in sport could offer, including scholarships.

“We want children to look back and say this is where I was discovered, this is where I got a scholarship opportunity and this is where I had my opportunities,” she said.

Ope Ajayi, who also serves as Chairman of the Lagos State Aquatics Association, welcomed the support from participating schools, families and partners.

Participants and coaches commended the organisers and expressed hope that future editions would bring more schools together, giving more children the chance to compete, learn and enjoy school sports.

World.title: NPFL Boss, Abdulrahman, Talks up Rangers for CAF Champions League Ticket
World.content:
Rangers International have been congratulated for the CAF Champions League first leg win against Algeria’s MC Alger in Abeokuta and charged the Flying Antelopes to seal the qualification ticket to the group stage on Friday.

The Flying Antelopes are scheduled to fly out of Lagos today ahead of the crucial reverse fixture in Algeria.

Dr Ayo Abdulrahman, the Chief Operating Officer of the EuroMatchNPFL, gave the charge in a message to the league champions shortly after the match, which he was in attendance to lend support to the country’s flag bearers.

“Rangers players showed determination to win even when they were one player down, and winning by two goals was a befitting reward for the hardworking players and managers of the team,” Abdulrahman stated.

Rangers ran out 2-0 in the very tough first leg fixture, and they go into the second leg hoping to make the advantage count.

The team is departing for the fixture today, seeking to get a good feel of the usually hostile Algerian clubs’ fans.

But Abdulrahman stressed that Rangers players must be psychologically prepared to absorb all the antics their opponents and their fans will throw at them.

“It’s not going to be a tea party, don’t expect them to offer you flowers. Stay focused, take the fight to them, and respond to the dictates of the game, especially when you have to defend, ” the NPFL Chief admonished.

Rangers are hoping to qualify for the group stage of the financially rewarding CAF Champions League and ensure that Nigeria retains the continental four slots. The match comes up at 8 pm on Friday in Algeria with a temperature forecast predicting 26 degrees.

World.title: CAS reveals date to rule on legitimate AFCON 2025 winners
World.content:
Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has revealed a date to rule on who the legitimate winners of the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON).

In January 2026, Senegal were crowned AFCON champions after beating Morocco 1-0 in a final filled with controversies.

On the night, a number of Senegal players walked out of the pitch in protest for a dubious penalty which was awarded to Morocco.



They then returned to pitch after the game had stopped for almost 15 minutes, and Edouard Andy denied Brahim Diaz from the spot.

Pape Gueye then scored the winner for Senegal, much to the delight of many African football fans.

Morocco lost the game but they later protested the result with CAF who ruled in their favour, and Senegal appealed the ruling with CAS.



Now, in a statement released on Monday, CAS revealed that its panel has begun its work and continues to deliberate on the matter.

CAS said the final ruling on who the legitimate AFCON 2025 winners will be released at the end of November 2026.

CAS TO DETERMINE LEGITIMATE AFCON 2025 WINNERS IN NOVEMBER

“This is a procedural update regarding the decision for the appeal by the Senegalese Football Federation (FSF, in French) against the Confederation of African Football (CAF) and the Royal Moroccan Football Federation (FRMF, in French),” reads the statement.



“The hearing took place behind closed doors at CAS headquarters, in Lausanne, on Thursday 8 October 2026.”

“The Panel have begun and continue their deliberations.”

“The CAS arbitrators have decided to issue a complete ruling which includes legal grounds, known as a CAS Award. This process will require several weeks, with the CAS Award expected at the end of November 2026.”



“Only information provided through CAS channels is considered official and any announcement concerning this case will be published on the CAS website,” concluded the statement.

World.title: Jerry Sikhosana feels sidelined and neglected by Orlando Pirates
World.content:
Legendary striker Jerry Sikhosana has expressed his frustrations at how his former club Orlando Pirates treat him.

Sikhosana cemented his legendary status in the mid-1990s, and helped Pirates win the CAF Champions League in 1995.

The now 57-year-old scored the only goal of the game in the second leg of that final against ASEC Mimosas in Abidjan.



Sikhosana was signed by Pirates from Witbank Aces in 1993, and he left the Soweto giants in 1998.

However, he returned for a second stint between 2000 and 2001.

At the time he left, Sikhosana had scored 44 goals in 125 official games for the Sea Robbers, and he’s never been part of the club’s setup in any capacity.



Now, speaking on Chillers Punch podcast, Sikhosana expressed how painful it has been for him to not even be treated as a legend he is by Pirates.

He recalled how he once had to queue for a match ticket with the rest of the fans, and also being given a VIP ticket by Kaizer Chiefs Marketing Director Jessica Motaung.

JERRY SIKHOSANA FEELS UNWANTED BY ORLANDO PIRATES

“You look at the Pirates jersey with a star, and the first impression should be, ‘thank you Jerry Sikhosana, you gave us a star’,” said Sikhosana.



“But you’d go to the stadium, fold my arms and queue with the supporters to go and buy a match ticket. I swear to God that’s what is happening.

“I was once in Durban with Brian (Baloyi). We moved to a suite, I bumped into Thandi (Merafe), and she looked down.

“I then saw Eddie (Edward Motale) and Lucky (Lekgwathi), and they wearing these new Pirates tracksuits, and you could see that these are the two legends that were picked for that game.



“And they were like, ‘and what about the uniform?’, and asked them ‘what uniform? I’m not a Pirates legend. I’m just wearing my clothes’.

“Chiefs legends wore their own uniform. I wouldn’t wear the Pirates merchandise. All I wanted there was to ask for a ticket as a Pirates legend but I was deprived and Chiefs gave me.”

World.title: Stellenbosch University’s Huis Marais sorry after male students’ streaking incident
World.content:
Huis Marais has apologised for a streaking incident that took place last week. Images via X

Huis Marais, the men-only official residence of Stellenbosch University, has apologised to the public after a streaking incident upset the local community.

HUIS MARAIS SORRY FOR STREAKING INCIDENT

On its social media platforms, Huis Marais issued a statement apologising to the public.

This is related to an incident last week where a group of nine male students and residents stripped off their clothes and ran around the residence and the Huis Visser building.



According to the statement, the incident resulted from a lost bet among the quad cricket-playing pals.

“Huis Marais does not condone this behaviour. We understand the impact this has on the residence, the Validus Cluster, and the Stellenbosch University community.

“We acknowledge the role that incidents like this play in the perpetuation of GBV culture, particularly in the current climate of the country” 

Huis Marais apologised to those who had witnessed the streaking as well as the repercussions the incident had on its reputation.

It revealed that an internal disciplinary meeting resulted in sanctions being imposed and a deduction from the honoraria of the house committee members.

The statement continued: “We feel it is important to state that all the residents turned themselves in immediately after the incident was reported. They too, acknowledge the recklessness of their actions and the negative impact they have had on the people affected by the incident. 

“However, we want to make it clear to those affected that the initial intent behind their actions was not to harm, harass or offend anybody. This is not who we are and does not align with our values.

CONTROVERSIAL INCIDENTS OVER THE YEARS

Huis Marais, a men’s residence at Stellenbosch University, has faced several controversies over the years, including allegations of initiation abuse, debates over gender transformation, and the 2022 incident in which a student urinated on a fellow student’s belongings.



Student Theuns Do Toit made deadlines when he was filmed entering the room of black student Babalo Ndwayana, whilst intoxicated, and urinating on his belongings, including his laptop and textbooks. A video of the incident went viral, triggering widespread outrage and allegations of racism.

Not long after, Du Toit was expelled by Stellenbosch University following a disciplinary hearing. The committee also criticised Huis Marais’s leadership, particularly its excessive drinking amongst students.

A criminal case against Du Toit was heard at the Stellenbosch Magistrates’ Court last year; however, he was found not guilty of crimen injuria and malicious damage to property.
