World.title: Canadian who stole a Las Vegas flamingo after drinking '30 to 40' beers convicted of animal cruelty
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

What happens in Vegas stays in Vegas. Unless you drink "30 to 40 beers" and steal a flamingo — because that will make international news.

A Las Vegas court convicted an Ontario man of animal cruelty charges Monday for snatching a flamingo named Peachy from its habitat at an iconic Las Vegas hotel in what prosecutors called a drunken and malicious act.

Mitchell Fairbarn was accused of "willfully, unlawfully, maliciously and feloniously" injuring the flamingo in the early morning hours on March 3, according to the indictment viewed by CBC News. He pled not guilty and his trial started last week.

After jurors returned convictions on felony and misdemeanor animal cruelty counts, Fairbarn remained in custody pending a Dec. 1 sentencing hearing. He faces up to four years in prison for the felony conviction, plus six months of jail time for the misdemeanor conviction.

"I thought it was something that we could joke about for the rest of our lives," Fairbarn, described by various Las Vegas media outlets as a contractor from rural Ontario, said in court Friday.

The façade of the Flamingo hotel in Las Vegas is seen at night on Las Vegas Boulevard in this file photo. (Pascal Le Segretain/Getty Images)

Fairbarn told the court that on the day of the incident, he drank "30 to 40" beers over the course of 24 hours while he was in Las Vegas for a construction expo, he said in video footage of the trial posted by multiple media outlets.

Fairbarn entered the flamingo habitat at the Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino around 5 a.m. on March 3, according to the Las Vegas Review-Journal, and took the bird because he thought it would be a "silly joke" with his friends.

"I thought it would be, at the time, funny," Fairbarn said.

The Flamingo's wildlife habitat, which the hotel says spans four acres and is certified by the National Wildlife Federation, is home to the resort's namesake Chilean flamingos, among other birds, turtles and fish.

Peachy was shaking, bleeding: witness

Video played at the trial showed Fairbarn holding the flamingo by the neck in an elevator and carrying it down a hotel hallway. He spent about 15 minutes with the bird, and two-to-three minutes with it in his room, reported 8NewsNow, citing police evidence heard in court.

Two of Fairbarn's friends testified earlier this week that they had been out drinking, then woke up in their hotel room to find the flamingo there before moving it to the hallway, notes Fox 5 Las Vegas.

A hotel facilities engineer searching for Peachy eventually corralled the bird into a corner with a towel, and told the court Peachy was shaking and bleeding.

The flamingo was injured during the incident, suffering seven to eight missing feathers, broken feather shafts and blood loss consistent with trauma, the bird's treating veterinarian testified in court, according to Fox5 Las Vegas.

Peachy, who is 27 years old, needed antibiotics, anti-inflammatories and weeks of pain medication, the news outlet reported.

CBC News has reached out to the Las Vegas Justice Court for access to court filings and has not yet received them. But multiple local media outlets present in court have aired footage from court where Fairbarn doesn't deny his actions — just his intent.

His lawyer Joshua Tomsheck said Monday it was a drunken act and no harm was intended. When Tomsheck asked Fairbairn Friday if he had any malicious intent "in your mind or your heart when you picked up that bird," Fairbarn shook his head and answered, "no."

CBC News has reached out to Tomsheck, but has not yet received a response.

Fairbarn testifies during his trial at the Regional Justice Center on Friday in Las Vegas. He says he didn't intend to hurt the flamingo he took up to his hotel room in March. (Benjamin Hager/Las Vegas Review-Journal/The Associated Press)

Justice delivered: animal rights advocate

Prosecutors said Fairbarn willfully caused the bird physical pain, noting feathers were found on the hotel floor and video showed the bird squawking while Fairbarn handled it. But Tomsheck said his client regrets his actions while intoxicated and never meant to harm the bird, a key element in the felony charge.

"He should not have done that, should not have gone into the habitat, shouldn't have touched a bird, shouldn't have taken Peachy inside," Tomsheck said in court Monday.

"The truth is, Mitch was drunk. Mitch was stupid. He made bad decisions."

Fairbarn told the court Friday that he has remained under house arrest in Nevada since the incident. Court records viewed by CBC News show he had to surrender his passport as one of his bail conditions.

Jurors began deliberations after both sides presented closing arguments Monday morning.

Nevada animal rights advocate John Waudby, who recently helped strengthen the state's animal cruelty laws, told The Associated Press he believes justice was delivered on Peachy's behalf.

"I hope this sends a message to anybody else that wants to mess with our animals, that you're not going to do it in Nevada," he said outside the courtroom after Monday's verdict.

The Flamingo Las Vegas Hotel and Casino is home to the resort's namesake Chilean flamingos, which reside at the hotel's wildlife habitat. (Ceasars Entertainment)

Peachy has since recovered, according to Fox 5 Las Vegas. But the flamingo is just one of several recent cases involving animal cruelty at Las Vegas casinos, reports the Las Vegas Review-Journal.

In June, a woman was charged after allegedly jumping into the fountain at The Venetian and grabbing a duckling named Daffy. In May, a teen girl was arrested and accused of stabbing three horses the the South Point Arena & Equestrian Center so they couldn't compete in a barrel race.

World.title: 'Not out of the woods': Family rallies around soldier badly burned in CFB Wainwright fire
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Before he was airlifted to hospital and intubated, Cpl. Sean Hiatt — the second-youngest in a family of 12 — managed to call his mom and tell her he'd been injured in a training accident at CFB Wainwright.

The 24-year-old was coherent at the time, according to his sister, and it gave the family hope.

Now they're focused on his immediate care, and taking things 12 hours at a time.

On Saturday afternoon, Hiatt suffered burns to about half of his body when wind gusts of up to 90 km/h pushed a grass fire one kilometre in less than a minute and onto a group of soldiers doing live-fire training.

Four soldiers were killed and 39 were injured. Hospitals across the province took in the wounded, including University of Alberta Hospital in Edmonton where Hiatt’s medevac landed.

“He was, and still is, sedated and intubated, he was completely wrapped up, they didn’t know the degree at that point because they had to get him stable,” Hiatt’s sister Kelly Patterson said in an interview with CBC News.

“It is really rough…. It was a shock to see him like that.”

Of the injured, 19 are in critical condition, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said at a news conference on Sunday.

One of those is Hiatt, from Edson, Alta., about 200 kilometres west of Edmonton.

One by one, family members began showing up at Hiatt’s bedside — brothers, a nephew, sisters and parents — to be with the guy they describe as “happy going”and “cheerful.”

'He's a fighter'

Patterson says her brother “perked up” with every visit, breathing a little bit better and “looking a little brighter."

The road ahead is going to be long and Patterson says Hiatt is “not out of the woods.”

Doctors are still concerned about lung damage and have yet to begin skin grafts. He faces weeks in the ICU and months longer in hospital.

The family is leaning on prayer and the knowledge that Hiatt is "a fighter.”

“He got out of there so he’s going to make it,” said Patterson.

'The whole community is feeling this'

Meanwhile, 200 kilometres from Hiatt’s hospital bed, he and the other injured and fallen soldiers are on the minds of folks in Wainwright, a town deeply connected to its base.

“Everyone’s really connected, everyone really cares for each other,” said Grade 12 student Rylan Pow. “It really was heartbreaking honestly.”

Grade 12 students showed up Monday morning with bouquets of flowers to pay their respects to those who were injured and killed in Saturday's fire at CFB Wainwright. (Gilbert Rowan/CBC)

On Monday morning, with their principal’s blessing, Pow and his entire class from Blessed Sacrament School showed up with their teacher to lay flowers at the town’s memorial clock cenotaph.

Teacher Janae Wildboer said she was in a panic when she learned of the fatal fire and wondered what she could do to help.

“Our school just wanted to do something to honour those who have lost their lives,” said Wildboer. “The whole community is feeling this; it's heavy and we're just now supporting where we can.”

'Still kind of in shock'

Down the street, outside of the Royal Canadian Legion Branch 29, which was set up Monday as a referendum polling station, David Campbell finished voting and then turned his mind back to the tragedy.

"Everyone's still kind of in shock,” said Campbell, who has lived in the area for more than 40 years.

“The base is very important, a lot of people work here. We’re farmers and we have cattle in the community pasture, we work with the military all the time, they live in town here, a lot of them.

“They’re part of the community, we know so many of them. Their kids are in hockey, my grandkids are playing hockey with a lot of the kids. It's very devastating.”

Smoke in the air

As the winds changed direction Sunday night and into Monday, the smell of smoke drifted in and out of the community. Fire Chief Aime Smyl warned that could continue in the days ahead.

The fire is still burning but considered contained, said Smyl in his social media post Monday afternoon. It’s not expected to breach the fire guard.

Local MP and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre attended the Wainwright cenotaph with flowers Monday morning. (Josh McLean/CBC News)

Smyl also thanked the seven other fire services that stepped up to help with Saturday’s grassfire response.

“I am also humbled by the number of departments that reached out to help,” he wrote.

By Monday morning, some of Smyl’s firefighters had been awake for three days, according to Local MP and Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre, who showed up at the cenotaph with flowers after a meeting with the fire chief.

Poilievre thanked the first responders, “who ran towards and not away from the fire” to help.

“It has been a phenomenal show of the best of Canada here in Wainwright.”

World.title: Quebec's reserves of maple syrup almost depleted, says new report
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The head of Quebec's maple syrup producers' association says the province's strategic syrup reserve has run dry amid high demand for the product.

Québec Maple Syrup Producers president Luc Goulet says government support will be needed to ensure the industry doesn't miss out on opportunities to grow the sector.

Maple syrup yields depend on weather conditions. As a result, the producers' association has established a strategic reserve to ensure prices and supply remain relatively stable.

Last year, U.S. commercial customers stocked up, fearing that U.S. President Donald Trump would carry out his threat to impose tariffs.

Goulet says the buffer has been exhausted as sales continue to rise.

"Our strategic reserve has been reduced to zero," Goulet said in an interview at the release of a report on the industry's economic benefits.

That means the industry could lose customers if weather conditions are less favourable for maple sap flow, he said.

Goulet cites the stock shortages in 2007 and 2008 as an example.

"We lost some markets because the product wasn’t available," Goulet said. "Then, consumers very quickly turn to another sweet product. And once that happens, those consumption habits are established."

Quebec maple syrup is gaining market share abroad, according to the president of the Maple Industry Council, which represents authorized buyers.

Louis Turenne notes that exports increased by 9.34 per cent in 2024 compared to the previous year. The pace accelerated in 2025 with a 15.8 per cent increase as the threat of new tariffs loomed over the industry.

In 2026, exports rose at a slower rate — 2.48 per cent from January through August compared to the same period the previous year.

"It's always hard to beat an exceptional year," Turenne said.

Currently, nearly 65 per cent of maple syrup exports go to the United States. (Christinne Muschi/The Canadian Press)

Goulet acknowledges that satisfying the demand of eager consumers is a nice problem to have.

However, he believes the industry can still grow. "There is still a great deal of untapped potential in Quebec’s maple groves," he said.

Investments from Quebec City "are too low for our liking," says Goulet, who hopes to have the ear of the newly elected Parti Québécois government.

"When we’re told that we have an industry that's thriving, that we’re growing, and that we don’t need support — well, I no longer accept that line of reasoning at the government level," he said.

For his part, Turenne believes that Quebec could encourage increased production by providing financial support to producers, and helping processors in their search for new markets abroad.

Currently, nearly 65 per cent of maple syrup exports go to the United States.

"We’ve made significant progress in diversifying our markets in recent years. Twenty years ago, that figure was 80 per cent," Turenne said.

“But we need to accelerate the opening and development of European, Australian, and Asian markets to become less dependent on the U.S. market,” he said.

Industry concentrated in Quebec

While the maple leaf graces the Canadian flag, the syrup industry is heavily concentrated in Quebec.

More than 70 per cent of North American production is in the province, according to the industry group's report, released Thursday.

When production, processing, and specialized equipment manufacturers are included, the maple syrup industry contributed $1.21 billion to the gross domestic product in 2025, the report said.

In total, the sector employs more than 10,000 full-time equivalent workers and generated $285 million in tax revenue, excluding municipal taxes and fees for the lease of public lands.

This figure does not include the sugar shacks that many Quebecers visit in the spring.

"Sugar shack operations are more akin to the restaurant industry," Turenne said.

The maple syrup producers' group used the recent election campaign to highlight the industry's importance as an employer and economic driver, and Goulet says the candidates were often surprised by the important role it played.

In some municipalities, "if you take away maple syrup production, you might as well shut down the villages," Goulet said.

World.title: Findings from fatal CFB Wainwright fire investigation will be made public, top commander says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's top military commander committed on Monday to publicly releasing the findings of the investigation into the fire at the training range in Wainwright, Alta., which claimed the lives of four soldiers and left dozens of others injured.

There are three separate parallel investigations underway — two military and one civilian, said Gen. Jennie Carignan, the chief of the defence staff, in her first interview since a sudden brush fire swept through an exercise area at the sprawling military base.

Speaking on CBC's Power & Politics, Carignan said the military's investigative service is on the scene and there will be a board of inquiry (BOI), a technical investigation into the circumstances, as well as a civilian coroner's investigation by the province of Alberta.

The military is under no obligation to proactively release its findings. Normally, the board reports to the defence chief and the minister. In fact, it took public pressure for the board of inquiry investigation into the 2004 fatal fire aboard HMCS Chicoutimi to be made public.

Carignan said she was drafting the terms of reference, which set out the scope of the inquiry, for the board, but she couldn't commit on Monday to saying when the review panel will convene.

"We want to make sure that the board of inquiry starts on firm ground," Carignan told host David Cochrane, referring to the instructions she is preparing.

"I want to make sure that we also make the findings public once the board of inquiry is completed."

WATCH | Carignan speaks about training near brush fires: 'Normal' for Armed Forces to conduct training near fires: top military commander | Duration closed caption 0:59 Chief of the Defence Staff Gen. Jennie Carignan says that Canadian Forces personnel on the ground determine whether or not to continue training. She spoke with Power & Politics following the deadly fire on Saturday at CFB Wainwright.

Separately, Carignan said the Canadian Forces fire marshal is reviewing what happened. The RCMP have been asked to assist Alberta's medical examiner.

There were tributes in the House of Commons on Monday to the soldiers killed in what military officials describe as a swift-moving brush fire that overwhelmed members of C Company 3rd Battalion Princess Patricia's Canadian Light Infantry who were using the Wainwright training range to prepare for deployment to Latvia.

The military said the brush fire was already burning when a sudden change in the wind drove it toward roughly 84 troops who were practising hand grenade throwing and small group attacks at one portion of the exercise field.

Sgt. Morgan Wong, Pte. Shaun Farrell, Pte. Aidan Goulding and Pte. Hayden Lykkemark all died in the fire. Another 39 troops were injured, 19 of them critically.

Carignan said it's normal for troops to continue training even if there's a brush fire nearby because it adds to the realistic conditions they'd face in combat. There are however, she said, limits and safety is paramount.

"The folks on the ground make a determination on how this could affect training, and mitigation measures are put in place," Carignan said. "To address this, we also have firefighting equipment or support on site to respond to potential fires, of course, depending on the magnitude."

Military regulations dictate the range safety officer makes the call on whether an exercise can continue and under what circumstances.

Retired colonel Rory Fowler, a former military lawyer now in private practice, suggested the public should temper its expectations about what it will see in the board of inquiry report, particularly if there is blame to be had.

"BOIs are not supposed to investigate wrongdoing," Fowler said. "In fact, a little over 10 years ago, [the regulation] was amended to remove an article that directed that a BOI was to identify if anyone was at fault."

Fowler said if there is blame, it might be handled through the military justice system — or disciplinary system.

PHOTOS | The aftermath of the fire:

"Unlike a coroner's inquest, the underlying purpose of a BOI is not to serve a public purpose other than the governance of the Canadian Armed Forces," Fowler said.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, after paying tribute to the fallen soldiers, said he has confidence in the system.

"The military wants to get to the bottom of what exactly happened," Carney said. "There's a few processes that we'll go through here and we will get the answers to what caused this terrible tragedy as expeditiously and transparently as necessary."

In his House of Commons remarks, Carney committed to giving the military "all the resources that they need" to investigate.

WATCH | Carney on the military investigation: Carney says military 'aided by' feds and RCMP to investigate CFB Wainwright fire | Duration closed caption 0:39 Prime Minister Mark Carney says the Canadian military has 'started a comprehensive investigation' into what caused the deadly fire at CFB Wainwright to get answers 'as expeditiously and transparently as possible.'

Military law expert and retired colonel Michel Drapeau said Carignan's commitment to releasing the findings is important, but only "a first step."

Drapeau, who has represented families at a number of boards of inquiry over the past 20 years, said there needs to be more transparency as the process unfolds.

He'd like to see a commitment to proceedings being held in public where the families can attend.

"National security is not at stake here," Drapeau said. "The family has a right to know, and the Canadian public has a right to know."

Drapeau has long advocated for an independent body — such as an inspector general — that would conduct arm's-length investigations.

"There is merit to the argument that the Canadian Forces should have in place a mechanism for true public inquiry," Fowler said.

World.title: Curling controversy: Unusual finish generates boos, ruffles feathers at Slam event
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Grand Slam of Curling's competition committee plans to meet this week to discuss an unusual finish at the Co-op Invitational that sent two Canadian teams into the playoffs and led to pointed words from an American rink left outside the cutline.

Boos were heard throughout Victoria's Save-On-Foods Memorial Centre when teams skipped by Matt Dunstone and Brendan Bottcher were not aggressive in the final end of their round-robin finale Friday night.

Both teams deliberately threw stones through the house early in the end before Bottcher scored one for a tie that forced a shootout. That gave both sides enough points to advance and eliminated Danny Casper's rink from playoff contention.

"They're on ESPN in the U.S. and [Sportsnet] in Canada, thousands of people are watching it, I'm sure, and it looks horrible," Team Casper second Ben Richardson said from Victoria over the weekend. "It definitely leaves a bitter taste in my mouth.

"I can't speak [for] all the people that watched it, but it's definitely not a good look for our sport.”

Normally, a one-point game would lead to a tense eighth and final end. But with the stakes clear — reach the shootout and you're guaranteed a playoff spot — both rinks chose a passive style down the stretch.

When it became obvious both teams were comfortable with a tied score, many spectators voiced their displeasure that any late-game excitement had been scuttled.

"Don't be upset with the players, be upset with the format," said Dunstone, who earned two points for the 6-5 shootout victory.

Bottcher picked up one point for the shootout loss, giving him seven points overall and the final berth. Casper, who would have played a tiebreaker if the game was decided in regulation, missed the cut with six points.

"I understand why both of them would want a shootout," Richardson said. "I don't understand why both of them would not try to win in the last end. I completely disagree with that."

At issue for many were the early shots in the eighth end.

WATCH | Schwaller beats Ramsfjell in men's final: World No. 1 Schwaller beats Norway's Ramsfjell in Co-op Invitational men's final | Duration closed caption 2:09 Switzerland's Yannick Schwaller earns the second Grand Slam of Curling title of his career with a 7-3 victory over Norway's Magnus Ramsfjell in the men's final at the Grand Slam of Curling's Co-op Invitational in Victoria

Walker miss raised eyebrows

Team Dunstone lead Ryan Harnden drew the button, and Team Bottcher lead Geoff Walker flashed his first rock. The Walker miss raised the eyebrows of Team Casper third Luc Violette.

"You would always see a team throw a corner guard in that situation if they were trying to maximize their odds of winning the game outright," he said.

Harnden's second shot stopped at the top of the four-foot ring. Walker then made a double-takeout and his shooter rolled out.

Violette said the flash improved Dunstone's chances to steal. He would have expected Harnden to follow with a tight centre guard in that situation.

"Instead, they lobbed one right on top of it to leave an easy double," he said.

For second stones, Team Dunstone's Mark Nichols deliberately threw his first rock through the house, and Team Bottcher's Tanner Horgan did the same thing.

That sparked boos and jeers throughout the venue. Some spectators shouted "Borrrrr-ing!" while others yelled out "Shame! Shame!"

The broadcast team also sensed what was happening.

"Both of these teams, if this game goes to a shootout, will get into the playoffs," said on-air host John Cullen. "This looks like maybe a bit of a handshake agreement that both teams are saying, 'Let's do it."'

"I doubt that there's any agreement," analyst Brent Laing replied. "I think they're both just smart enough to know there's no need [to] take on any risk, and the other guy thinks the same thing."

After exchanging hits, Dunstone's final rock settled on the 12-foot ring and Bottcher drew the button for one point. Both skips said there was no agreement in place to play for the draw.

WATCH | Weekend recap: Grand Slam of Curling's Victoria stop: That Curling Show returns with a weekend recap of GSOC Victoria | Duration 29:28 The beloved That Curling Show returns with Devin Heroux accompanied by Canadian curling legends, Joanne Courtney and Brad Gushue as they recap the first stop in the Grand Slam of Curling in Victoria BC.

'How the scoreboard played out'

"In eight, they threw a rock in the house and Geoff's first rock picked," Bottcher said in a text message. "That said, our team knew we needed a point to qualify given the format."

Dunstone, reached on the phone from Victoria, said: "there was no conversation whatsoever."

"It was just how the scoreboard played out," he said.

Nic Sulsky, CEO of GSOC owner The Curling Group, said while he likes the 3-2-1-0 scoring system that's in its second season of use on the circuit, he wasn't impressed with what transpired.

"It was a little too obvious, it was a little too raw," he said. "And I feel for the Casper boys. But at the end of the day, fans are in the stands watching rocks being thrown through the house.

"I'm not a supporter of [that] in a situation like [Friday] night."

The seven-member competition committee was expected to meet Thursday or Friday, Sulsky said.

Dunstone went on to lose his quarterfinal to eventual champion Yannick Schwaller of Switzerland while Bottcher dropped his playoff opener to Canada's Brad Jacobs.

"This isn't why we didn't win this weekend," said Violette. "But at the same time, if this were another sport, I do think there would be some sort of sanction or something that happens as a result of a scenario like we saw play out."

"I feel like this was, I guess, a step back in us feeling confident in the integrity among teams at our highest level," he added.

The next stop on the circuit is the Nov. 3-8 GSOC Masters in Medicine Hat, Alta.

The referendum, which includes one question on proposed separation and another nine on various other constitutional matters, is expected to draw record numbers to the ballot box. World.title: Scott Stinson: Ontario’s electricity-import deal with U.S. undercuts Doug Ford’s energy tough talk
World.content:
Article content

The new deal to import electricity to Ontario would seem to undermine any future sabre-rattling that Ford might do on the energy file, although there are several caveats to be noted here. The Independent Electricity System Operator (IESO) is, as the name suggests, not making decisions at Ford’s behest. And its contract with Alpha Generation is a short-term arrangement to provide electricity in case Ontario needs it during the cold winter months and while the Pickering nuclear plant is undergoing a refurbishment. In the days since the Alpha contract was announced, the IESO said that Ontario will still be a net exporter of electricity to the United States and that it exported seven times as much as it imported last year. The new contract is about increasing the flexibility of the provincial power grid during the high-peak demand of the winter months.
