This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Why Tanzania Wants Nuclear Power

Tanzania nuclear power plans start from a grid with 4,646 megawatts of capacity, against a peak demand of about 2,271 megawatts. The surplus follows the opening on Saturday 22 August of the 2,115 megawatt Julius Nyerere hydropower plant on the Rufiji River.

The plant cost about 7.452 trillion Tanzanian shillings (about US$2.8 billion at 2,640 shillings to the dollar), according to the Ministry of Energy. The Daily News put hydropower at more than 60 per cent of capacity and called it vulnerable to drought.

The Uranium Behind the Plan

Mantra Tanzania, a subsidiary of Rosatom, is developing the Mkuju River project in Ruvuma region in the south of the country. President Samia Suluhu Hassan opened a pilot processing plant there on 30 July 2025.

The full complex is planned to produce up to 3,000 tonnes of uranium a year, with commissioning scheduled for 2029. Rosatom puts the investment at about US$1 billion and expects more than 4,000 jobs.

Tanzania says the site holds about 58,500 tonnes of uranium. In the first years, mined uranium will go to Russia for processing and the fuel will return, the commission said on 5 July.

The Road Map to the First Reactor

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), the UN nuclear watchdog, requires 19 steps in three phases before a country can start a plant. Tanzania has finished early preparations but has not formally entered phase one, the commission said on 5 July.

Tanzania has invited IAEA experts to judge whether its nuclear power plans are ready, and phase one covers laws and an independent safety regulator. If the review is positive, the country can move on, aiming for nuclear electricity within about seven years.

President Samia Suluhu Hassan held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin at the Kremlin in early June, with nuclear energy on the agenda. At the St Petersburg International Economic Forum that month, she said Tanzania is interested in small nuclear plants that Rosatom is discussing with it.

In the 2030s, Tanzania could consider a one or two unit plant, said Alexey Likhachev, who leads Rosatom. Floating units suit its coast, islands and rivers, he added.

The Nuclear Forum on Thursday 22 October

A one-day forum, Dialogue of Continents, takes place on Thursday 22 October at the Crowne Plaza hotel in Dar es Salaam. Women in Nuclear Tanzania and the Association of Women in Nuclear Russia organise it under the theme Nuclear Energy for the Future.

The atomic energy commission, Rosatom and the African network of Women in Nuclear back the event. Speakers will discuss careers, nuclear medicine, mining and training for young scientists.

What It Means for US Readers

Rosatom is the main foreign player in Tanzania’s uranium, so any deal on Tanzania nuclear power would deepen Russia’s footprint in East Africa. The US has banned imports of Russian-produced enriched uranium since 12 August 2024, with waivers possible only until 2028.

Tanzania’s top energy civil servant named the United States among possible nuclear partners in June 2025, alongside France, South Korea, Russia and China. He said the state would lead the project and pick partners after meeting international conditions.

The Rio Times set out Tanzania’s ties with the US, China and the Gulf in its Tanzania geopolitics explainer. It also covered the grid link that would carry Tanzanian power north and south in its report on the Tanzania Zambia power line.

What Is Not Known

No site, reactor design, financing or investment decision has been announced for Tanzania nuclear power. The result of the IAEA readiness review has not been made public.

Officials have given different demand forecasts for 2030 and 2050, so how much new power nuclear must supply is open. It is also unclear whether Tanzanian uranium processed in Russia would count as Russian-produced under US import rules.

More: Tanzania news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Tanzania have a nuclear power plant?

No. Tanzania has no nuclear power plant, and the country has not yet formally entered the first phase of the IAEA road map. Tanzania nuclear power is targeted within about seven years.

Where is Tanzania’s uranium?

The main deposit is the Mkuju River project in Ruvuma region, in the south of the country. Mantra Tanzania, a Rosatom subsidiary, is developing it, with commissioning scheduled for 2029.

Who is Rosatom?

Rosatom is Russia’s state nuclear corporation, which mines uranium, builds reactors and sells nuclear fuel. In Tanzania it runs the Mkuju River project and is discussing small reactors with the government.

Why does Tanzania want nuclear power when it has spare capacity?

Tanzania has 4,646 megawatts of capacity against a peak demand of 2,271 megawatts. Officials say Tanzania nuclear power would give steady supply for industry as demand grows and droughts threaten hydropower.

What does this mean for the United States?

Rosatom’s role links the project to US limits on Russian uranium, and the energy ministry has named the US among possible partners. No reactor deal with any country has been announced.

UGANDA · SECURITY

Key Facts — The country Uganda is a landlocked East African state of about 46 million people. It borders Rwanda, Kenya, Tanzania, DR Congo and South Sudan.

— What happened Police registered a murder case after villagers found the headless body of Robert Kabera, a 50-year-old Rwandan exile, in Mpigi district on Saturday 17 October.

— The victim Kabera was a Rwandan army sergeant major and musician. He fled to Uganda in November 2020, saying people wanted him dead.

— The police account Spokesman Kituuma Rusoke said on Monday 19 October that the head had not been recovered and that no motive had been established.

— The setting Rwanda and Uganda are neighbours. The United States is pressing Rwanda over its troops in eastern DR Congo.

— Still open No suspect has been named, no arrest has been reported and Rwanda’s government has made no public statement.

Police in Uganda are investigating the beheading of Robert Kabera, a 50-year-old Rwandan exile and former soldier. His headless body was found on Saturday 17 October in Mpigi district, near Kampala, the capital.

Police spokesman Kituuma Rusoke confirmed the murder case on Monday 19 October, according to Nile Post, a Ugandan news site. For American readers it touches the safety of exiles and the peace deal Washington brokered between Rwanda and DR Congo.

What Ugandan Police Said on Monday

Rusoke told journalists on Monday 19 October that a murder case had been registered, Nile Post reported. “We recovered the body minus the head,” he said, adding that relatives had identified the dead man as Robert Kabera.

Villagers found the remains on Saturday morning in Luwala village, in Kammengo sub-county, Mpigi district, and alerted officers. Police believe the killing took place on the night of Friday 16 October or in the early hours of Saturday 17 October.

The body was taken to the Mulago City Mortuary in Kampala, and the head has not been found. Rusoke said detectives are examining the killing and “any other details relevant to the murder,” including how Kabera lived.

Who Robert Kabera Was

Kabera, 50, was a sergeant major in the Rwanda Defence Forces, the national army. The Daily Monitor reported in 2020 that he was an army instructor, a member of the military band and a musician.

The Nile Post and the Daily Monitor, both Ugandan outlets, call the Rwandan exile a critic of President Paul Kagame. Kagame has led Rwanda since 2000, and the Monitor adds that the killing has alarmed several Rwandan refugees in Uganda.

Why He Left Rwanda in 2020

Kabera told the Daily Monitor in an interview published on Wednesday 25 November 2020 that he had crossed into Uganda on 19 November. “I am in Uganda seeking refuge from those who are after my life,” he said.

He said his troubles began with his friendship with the late gospel singer Kizito Mihigo, who died in a Rwandan police cell in February 2020. He also said he is related to the family of Fred Rwigema, the first commander of the Rwandan Patriotic Front, which now governs Rwanda.

Uganda and Rwanda, Two Neighbours With History

Uganda and Rwanda share a border and sit together in the East African Community, a regional trade bloc. The two governments have a long and sometimes tense relationship, and Uganda’s neighbours shape its trade, politics and security.

Uganda hosts many refugees, including Rwandans who say they cannot return home. Police and refugee communities will now watch whether the inquiry points to a personal, criminal or political motive.

What It Means for US Readers

Washington is closely involved in Rwanda’s ties with its neighbours. President Donald Trump hosted the signing of the Washington Accords between Rwanda and DR Congo on 4 December 2025.

Washington has backed Congo’s call for Rwandan troops to withdraw from the east of the country. Any government link to this killing would add strain, but police have named no suspect or motive.

What Is Not Known

Police have not said who killed the Rwandan exile, why, or whether the killing is linked to his criticism of the Rwandan president. No arrests have been announced, and the head has not been recovered.

Rwanda’s government has made no public statement on the case. It is also unclear whether Ugandan police will seek help from other countries or whether the family will receive protection.

More: Uganda news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who was Robert Kabera?

Robert Kabera, 50, was a Rwandan exile, a sergeant major in the Rwanda Defence Forces and a musician. He fled to Uganda in November 2020 and told the Daily Monitor he feared for his life.

Where and when was the body found?

Villagers found the headless body on Saturday morning, 17 October, in Luwala village, Kammengo sub-county, Mpigi district. Police believe he was killed on the night of 16 October or in the early hours of 17 October.

What have Ugandan police said about the motive?

Police spokesman Kituuma Rusoke said on Monday 19 October that a murder case is open and detectives are examining all relevant details. Police have not named a motive or a suspect.

Has Rwanda commented on the killing?

No Rwandan government statement has been reported in the Ugandan coverage of the case. The Nile Post describes Kabera as a critic of President Paul Kagame’s leadership.

Why does the case matter to the United States?

The United States brokered the Washington Accords between Rwanda and DR Congo and backs Congo’s call for Rwandan troops to leave. A case that strains Rwanda’s relations in the region could complicate that diplomacy.

World.title: Paraguay Signs 2 Security Deals With US
World.content:
The National Pantheon of the Heroes in Asunción, lit up for an outdoor film screening. Paraguayan outlets list a floral offering here among the planned stops of the US Deputy Secretary of State. File photo from 2012, cropped: Leandro Neumann Ciuffo, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

PARAGUAY · US POLICY · SECURITY

Key Facts — The country Paraguay is a landlocked country bordering Brazil, Argentina and Bolivia, led by President Santiago Peña of the Colorado Party. It is the only South American nation among Taiwan’s 12 diplomatic allies and a close US partner.

— Why it matters US goods exports to Paraguay reached US$4.4 billion in 2025, up 39.9% from 2024, and Washington now wants US companies to invest there.

— Why now US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau is in Paraguay from Monday 19 October on a trip that runs to 26 October and also takes in Argentina.

— What happened On Monday 19 October Landau met President Peña in Asunción, then signed two security documents with Foreign Minister Rubén Ramírez Lezcano.

— The deals One covers cooperation on intercepting suspect civil aircraft, with shared radar data and intelligence. The other is a memorandum of intent to give Paraguay a US border-screening system called PISCES.

— Power Index Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 in Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 36.0 points (October 2026 edition).

— Still open The full texts could not be found, no company has been named and no investment figure has been announced.

Paraguay and the United States signed two security deals in Asunción on Monday 19 October, during a visit by US Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau. One sets up cooperation on intercepting suspect civil aircraft, and the other brings a US border-screening system known as PISCES to Paraguay’s entry points.

For US readers, the deals show Washington building its drug-flight and migration agenda into a partnership with one of its closest friends in South America. Landau is also leading a delegation of US companies, so the security and business tracks run side by side.

This follows our earlier report on the start of the trip, US No. 2 Diplomat Tours Brazil’s Neighbours, which looked at the timing against Brazil’s runoff. It adds what happened in Asunción on the first day.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Paraguay ranks 10th of 14 with 36.0 points. Strongest pillar: state capacity & security (55); weakest: future resources (13). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

What Happened in Asunción

President Santiago Peña received Landau at the Palacio de López, the seat of government, on Monday, with Vice President Pedro Alliana, Foreign Minister Rubén Ramírez Lezcano and some cabinet members present, La Nación reported. Landau, who lived in Asunción as a boy when his father, George Landau, was US ambassador from 1972 to 1977, then made a statement to the press without taking questions, ABC Color and EFE reported.

“We have never seen these levels of cooperation that suit both countries,” Landau told reporters, in words translated from the Spanish that La Nación and ABC Color published. He said Paraguay “plays a very key role” in Washington’s renewed attention to the Western Hemisphere, and that investors will find “many win-win situations” there.

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

The Two Agreements

Later on Monday, at the Foreign Ministry, Landau and Ramírez Lezcano signed two documents, according to the ministry’s statement as published by La Nación and ABC Color. The first is an exchange of notes on cooperation in aerial interceptions of civil aircraft, meant to set a framework for interception procedures under each country’s laws and international law.

Under it, the statement says, surveillance of Paraguay’s airspace will be strengthened through an exchange of information, radar data, intelligence and technical assistance, as part of the fight against drug trafficking and other illicit activity. The US Embassy in Asunción, on X, called it an Air Interception Assistance Agreement that “will strengthen Paraguay’s capacity to monitor and protect its sovereignty against suspicious flights”.

The second document is a memorandum of intent on border security, under which the United States will provide the Personal Identification Secure Comparison and Evaluation System, or PISCES, with training for Paraguayan staff. EFE describes it as a tool that matches fingerprints and facial recognition with biographical data in real time, and the ministry says it is meant to tighten migration checks and track passenger movements.

Why the Air Agreement Matters

Paraguay’s 2022 airspace law, Law 6980, lets the Air Force commander authorise interception of suspected drug flights, first by ordering them to land and then by firing tracer rounds as warning shots. It bars officials from destroying a civil aircraft in service except in self-defence, though it does not bar lethal force when they face armed resistance from a crew, and EFE recalled that in 2023 Interior Minister Enrique Riera admitted a 90,000-hectare “black hole” in the Chaco with no air surveillance.

A proposal to add an explicit shoot-down power was raised in Congress in July 2025, and the executive opposed it, ABC Color reported at the time. On Monday ABC Color added that Washington also opposes such a law as a breach of international law, but the Rio Times found no US statement saying so, and nothing in the published descriptions of the new agreement mentions shooting down aircraft.

The Business Track and the Rest of the Visit

Landau travels with Juan Pablo Segura, the Assistant Secretary of State for Western Hemisphere Affairs, who was sworn in on 14 August 2026 after serving as Virginia’s secretary of commerce and trade. The State Department’s media note of 16 October says Landau will lead a trade delegation of US companies to explore investment opportunities in Paraguay, but the department has not named a single company.

Paraguayan outlets list a floral offering at the National Pantheon of the Heroes, working tables with local business groups and a technical visit to the Itaipú Binacional hydroelectric plant, which Paraguay shares with Brazil, among the planned stops. Peña said he would accompany much of the programme from Monday to Wednesday, and Hoy reports that Landau stays until Wednesday 21 October before going on to Buenos Aires.

The Trade Behind the Talks

The US Trade Representative’s office puts US goods exports to Paraguay at US$4.4 billion in 2025, up 39.9% from 2024, against US$558.8 million of imports, a goods surplus of US$3.9 billion. Counting services, two-way trade reached an estimated US$5.7 billion, up 35.5%, under a trade and investment framework agreement that took effect in 2021.

A Run of US Agreements

Monday’s signings extend a run of US-Paraguay agreements, including the Status of Forces Agreement on joint military training, which EFE dates to December while ABC Color reported Peña signing it with Landau in Chile on 11 March 2026, a day after the lower house completed its approval. Ramírez Lezcano also went to the State Department on 14 August 2025 to sign a Safe Third Country Agreement, hosted by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, that lets asylum seekers in the United States pursue claims in Paraguay, and he and Rubio signed a civil nuclear memorandum in early August 2026.

Taiwan’s foreign ministry lists Paraguay as the only South American country among its 12 diplomatic allies, and on 12 October Beijing announced sanctions on Paraguay’s technology minister, Gustavo Villate, and on Belize’s foreign minister, as our earlier report covered. No Paraguayan or US statement the Rio Times found links Landau’s visit to that dispute.

What It Means for You

For US companies, the State Department is sending a trade delegation to explore investment in Paraguay, but no deal, company name or dollar figure has been announced, so the only hard numbers so far are trade statistics. The delegation’s makeup is the first thing to watch, because it will show which sectors are interested.

For readers following US counter-drug and migration policy, the air and PISCES agreements tie Paraguay more closely to US surveillance and border screening. How much data flows to US agencies is not stated in any published description.

What Is Not Known

The Rio Times could not find the texts of the exchange of notes or the memorandum, so their terms, funding, duration and any limits on US personnel or data access are unknown. It is also not known who will operate PISCES in Paraguay, what it will cost or how soon it will be installed.

The State Department has not named the US companies in the delegation or said whether an investment announcement is planned. Landau wrote that he would spend three days in Paraguay and only two in Argentina, La Nación quoted him as saying, which leaves part of the 19 to 26 October window unaccounted for, and outlets differ on whether he landed on Sunday or early Monday.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Christopher Landau?

Christopher Landau is the US Deputy Secretary of State, the second-ranking official at the State Department, and a former US ambassador to Mexico. He lived in Asunción from 1972 to 1977, when his father was US ambassador to Paraguay.

What did Paraguay and the US sign on 19 October?

They signed an exchange of notes on cooperation in aerial interceptions of civil aircraft and a memorandum of intent on border security. The second brings the US PISCES screening system to Paraguay’s entry points, with training.

What is PISCES?

PISCES stands for Personal Identification Secure Comparison and Evaluation System, a US-provided tool for checking travellers at borders. EFE describes it as matching fingerprints and facial recognition with biographical data in real time.

Does the air agreement allow Paraguay to shoot down planes?

No published description of the agreement mentions shooting down aircraft, and the Rio Times could not find the texts. Paraguay’s 2022 airspace law bars destroying a civil aircraft in service except in self-defence, though it does not bar lethal force against armed resistance from a crew.

How much does the US trade with Paraguay?

The US Trade Representative’s office estimates two-way trade in goods and services at US$5.7 billion in 2025, up 35.5% from 2024. US goods exports were US$4.4 billion and imports were US$558.8 million.

Where does Landau go next?

After Paraguay he travels to Buenos Aires, Argentina, and the State Department says the whole trip runs from 19 to 26 October. The department has not published the date of each stop.

World.title: Glencore Funds US$40M South Africa Mine
World.content:
RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only — every claim links to its source article. Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesCost of living, safety, visas across Latin America › RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. × Best for expats Cost of living Safest places Easy visas Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

SOUTH AFRICA · COPPER AND ZINC

Key Facts — The country South Africa is Africa’s most industrialised economy and a major miner of platinum, gold, coal and manganese.

— What happened US$40 million of Glencore funding for Orion Minerals’ Prieska copper and zinc mine became unconditional on Monday 19 October 2026.

— The money The US$40 million is the first of two tranches, and the second tranche of US$210 million is still conditional on funding the deeper mine.

— The timing The first payment is expected by the end of October 2026, and first copper and zinc output is targeted for the end of 2027.

— The sales deal Glencore will buy all concentrate from the first section for five years, and from the deeper section for at least 10.

— What it means for you The South Africa mine adds a new, if small, source of copper and zinc, both on the US critical minerals list.

— Still open How Orion will raise the money for the deeper mine, and when the second tranche could be released.

Glencore’s US$40 million funding became unconditional on Monday 19 October 2026, clearing the way to restart a South Africa mine for copper and zinc. Orion Minerals, listed in Melbourne and Johannesburg, said in its stock-exchange filing that the first payment is due by the end of October.

For US readers, the South Africa mine adds a small new source of copper and zinc, both on the US critical minerals list. Glencore, the Swiss-based miner and metals trader listed in London, will buy its output.

What Orion and Glencore Agreed

Orion’s local subsidiary signed the final contract to sell Glencore the mine’s concentrate, the metal-rich powder left after ore is processed. It also signed an agreement between the mine’s financiers, which cleared the last conditions on the first US$40 million, called Tranche A.

Moneyweb, the South African financial news site, put the sum at R658 million (about US$40 million). Glencore’s Toby Spittle said the company was pleased to help bring Prieska back to life and make Orion South Africa’s next copper producer.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Africa Critical Minerals Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

How the Glencore Prepayment Works

The money is a prepayment, meaning Glencore pays up front and is repaid in copper and zinc concentrate rather than in cash. Orion can settle the facility at any time without a penalty.

Glencore earns a market-related return, which steps down once commercial production is declared. The return is added to the balance until about 18 months after first production from the first mine section.

Orion guarantees the obligations of its Prieska subsidiary under the facility. Triple Flag Precious Metals, a royalty and streaming company, holds security that ranks equally with Glencore’s.

What the First Tranche Pays For

Tranche A pays for the Uppers, the shallower first stage of the South Africa mine, targeted to start producing by the end of 2027. Orion has chosen Torque Africa for drilling and ENPROTEC to build and run a concentrator rated at 20,000 tonnes a month.

The money also lets construction of an accommodation village for workers begin at the site. Orion says it is mobilising construction crews and equipment while it keeps looking for funds for the deeper section.

Why Prieska Is Being Revived

Prieska produced copper and zinc from the 1970s to the 1990s, according to Orion’s project page. Over those years it yielded more than 430,000 tonnes of copper and 1 million tonnes of zinc.

The site lies near the village of Copperton in the Northern Cape, about 270 kilometres south-west of Kimberley. Miningmx reported that the South Africa mine is scoped for 22,000 tonnes of copper and 65,000 tonnes of zinc a year.

The Second Tranche and the Deeper Mine

The US$210 million Tranche B depends on, among other things, full funding for the Deeps and extra outside money for Glencore’s prepayments. Up to US$50 million of it may be drawn early for early works on the Deeps if conditions are met.

Orion says it is talking to existing and new funding partners about the rest of the money. Miningmx reported that the Deeps still needs about R2 billion (about US$122 million) from other sources.

How the Deal Got Here

Orion and Glencore announced the financing on Monday 9 February 2026. Business Day reported on Thursday 17 September that the South African Reserve Bank, the central bank and foreign-exchange regulator, had approved the foreign funding.

Miningmx reported a year earlier that Orion hoped for first copper by December 2026, so the target has since moved back by about a year. Orion’s shares rose about 3% in Johannesburg on Monday, the outlet said.

What It Means for US Readers

The US Geological Survey, the federal science agency, published a 60-entry critical minerals list on 6 November 2025. Copper was one of 10 minerals added, and zinc is on the list too.

Glencore sells metal worldwide, and the Orion contract gives it flexibility to deliver anywhere, so American buyers could eventually receive some of the output. The South Africa mine is small next to the big producers, so the deal matters more for supply diversification than for the price of copper.

Investors can follow Orion through its listings in Melbourne and Johannesburg, while Glencore shares trade in London. For more on the province, read Ramaphosa Backs Zinc Smelter on 16 October, and for the sector’s slump, South African Mining Falls 12.7% in August.

What Is Not Known

How Orion will raise the money for the Deeps is open, and Tranche B cannot move until it does. No date has been set for the second tranche.

The filing gives no total build cost for the whole mine and no jobs figure. It also does not say what return rate Glencore will earn on the prepayment.

More: South Africa news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Orion Minerals?

Orion Minerals is a copper and zinc developer with its head office in Melbourne and shares listed in Melbourne and Johannesburg. Its main project is the Prieska Copper Zinc Mine in South Africa’s Northern Cape.

What did Glencore agree to provide?

Glencore will provide a US$40 million prepayment now and up to US$210 million more if conditions are met. In return it will buy the mine’s concentrates under long-term contracts.

When will the Prieska mine produce copper?

Orion targets first production from the Uppers by the end of 2027. The first US$40 million payment is expected by the end of October 2026.

Is the full US$250 million secured?

No, only the first US$40 million is unconditional. The other US$210 million depends on the Deeps being fully funded and on Glencore raising outside money.

Why does the South Africa mine matter to Americans?

Copper and zinc are both on the US critical minerals list, and the South Africa mine adds a new supply project outside the biggest producers. The volumes are small, so the effect is on supply diversification more than on prices.

World.title: Guyana Gold Exports Hit US$826 Million
World.content:
Gold-mining pits and ponds in the rainforest near Mahdia, Guyana, seen from the air on 8 April 2011. File photo, not a mine named in the reports. Photo: Marco Farouk Basir, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

GUYANA · MINING

Key Facts — The country Guyana is the English-speaking country on South America’s Caribbean coast whose economy now runs on offshore oil, with gold as its largest export after oil.

— Why it matters Gold is priced in US dollars on the same market American investors trade, so what Guyana earns from it moves with the gold price.

— Why now The full January to June count is dated late August 2026, and gold has since fallen from its January peak.

— What happened Gold export receipts reached US$826.2 million in the first half of 2026, up US$269.8 million, or 48.5 percent, from US$556.3 million a year earlier.

— The numbers The average price per ounce exported rose 59.1 percent to US$4,528.20, while the ounces shipped fell 6.7 percent to 182,451.

— Prediction markets Polymarket traders put the chance that front-month gold futures settle at or above US$5,000 by the end of December at about 10.5 percent, as of 10:00 p.m. ET on Monday, 19 October.

— What it means for you Guyana’s gold income follows the gold price, not the tonnage mined, so a falling price cuts it quickly. The US Treasury sanctioned one of Guyana’s largest gold exporters in June 2024, which makes provenance checks matter for American buyers.

— Still open It is not explained why exports fell while declared mining output rose 11.3 percent, and where the gold was sold is not stated.

Guyana earned US$826.2 million from gold exports in the first six months of 2026, up US$269.8 million, or 48.5 percent, on the same period of 2025. The Bank of Guyana, the central bank, says the whole gain came from price, because the country shipped fewer ounces than a year earlier.

That matters to American readers because gold is the biggest thing Guyana sells after oil, and it is priced in US dollars on the same market US investors trade. The numbers come from two official reports dated 27 and 28 August 2026, and Kaieteur News, a Georgetown daily, brought them back into view on Monday, 19 October.

What the Figures Show

Gold brought in US$826.2 million in the half, against US$556.3 million in 2025 and US$408.9 million in 2024, so receipts have roughly doubled in two years. Crude oil earned US$15,053.7 million and made up 92.9 percent of all exports, while gold made up 5.1 percent.

Among exports other than oil, gold was worth about 72 percent of the US$1,146 million total, which was itself up 24.6 percent. Rice came next at US$97.8 million, down from US$123.1 million a year earlier.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Latin America Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Price Did All the Work

The central bank puts the average price Guyana received at US$4,528.20 per ounce, up 59.1 percent from US$2,845.95 a year earlier. The volume exported fell 6.7 percent, or 13,035 ounces, to 182,451 ounces.

Gold set a record in January, and the central bank puts the settlement high at about US$5,318.40 per ounce on Thursday, 29 January. It then slid, and the bank says gold closed June at about US$4,007.69, which is 24.6 percent below that peak.

Guyana’s finance ministry puts the first-half average market price at US$4,694.2 per ounce, up 52.5 percent on a year earlier. It calls the rise an upside risk for non-oil exports, the trade balance and royalties, and it warns that a price fall would reduce those benefits.

Mining Output Is Rising Too

Declared gold output rose 11.3 percent to 232,287 troy ounces in the half, from 208,757 a year earlier. A troy ounce is the standard unit for gold and weighs about 31.1 grams.

Small and medium miners lifted their declarations 18.0 percent, from 137,441 to 162,182 ounces. The one large operator, Aurora Gold Mine Inc., part of Zijin Mining Group of China, declared 70,105 ounces, down 1.7 percent from 71,316.

Exports and declarations are separate counts, and this half they moved in opposite directions. The central bank blames the lower export volume on “lower declarations”, although its own mining table shows declarations up, and neither report reconciles the two.

Where the Gold Goes and Who Watches It

The US Treasury said in June 2024 that Guyanese gold is sold on international markets including the United States, Canada, the United Arab Emirates and the European Union. Neither the central bank nor the finance ministry publishes a country-by-country breakdown for the first half of 2026.

On Tuesday, 11 June 2024, the Treasury sanctioned Nazar Mohamed, his son Azruddin Mohamed and their company, Mohamed’s Enterprise, which it described as one of Guyana’s largest gold exporters. It alleged that the company left more than 10,000 kilograms of gold out of import and export declarations between 2019 and 2023 and avoided more than US$50 million in duty taxes.

The State Department’s March 2025 narcotics report added that gold smuggling in Guyana often facilitates money laundering, as criminals use illegal gold sales to disguise illicit funds. Guyana’s law requires all gold produced in the country to be sold to the Guyana Gold Board, a state body set up in 1982, or to a licensed dealer.

The central bank’s accounts show it bought US$314.7 million of foreign currency from the Guyana Gold Board in the half. The report does not say how that sum relates to the US$826.2 million of export receipts.

What the Ministry Expects for the Full Year

The ministry now projects gold export receipts of US$2,307.0 million for all of 2026, against US$1,754.4 million in the budget and US$1,617.9 million in 2025. That would be 42.6 percent above last year and leaves US$1,480.8 million to come in the second half.

Its forecast for gold mining growth stays at 5.4 percent, so almost all of the projected gain would have to come from price. The ministry’s forecast is an average of US$4,700 per ounce for the year, while spot gold closed at US$4,164.64 on Friday, 16 October, about 11 percent below it.

What Prediction Markets Say

Traders on Polymarket, a prediction market, put the chance that front-month gold futures settle at or above US$5,000 on any trading day by the end of December at about 10.5 percent at 10:00 p.m. ET on Monday, 19 October. About US$135,700 had been traded on that line, and the whole gold market had drawn about US$2.06 million.

The line for US$6,000 stood at about 4.5 percent on roughly US$1.31 million of volume, and a dip to US$3,500 was priced at about 10 percent. These are bets by traders, not forecasts by the ministry, and the contracts settle on official CME futures prices rather than the spot price used elsewhere in this article.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

What It Means for You

For investors, Guyana is a case where a gold rally lifted export income by almost half while the ounces shipped fell, so earnings follow the gold price and not the output. A drop in gold would cut those receipts quickly, and the finance ministry itself lists a falling price as a risk.

For US companies that buy or finance Guyanese gold, the Treasury’s 2024 sanctions and the State Department’s 2025 warning make origin, declaration and payment records the central checks. For Guyana, the metal matters because oil is 92.9 percent of exports and gold is the largest of everything else, and newcomers can start with this explainer on Guyana’s role in Latin America.

What Is Not Known

The reports do not say where the gold was sold, so the US share of the US$826.2 million is not public. They also do not explain why exported ounces fell 6.7 percent while declared ounces rose 11.3 percent.

Neither report says how much of the US$826.2 million reached the state as gold royalties. Nor is it known whether gold will hold near the ministry’s US$4,700 forecast, which decides whether the second-half projection of US$1,480.8 million is reached.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much gold did Guyana export in the first half of 2026?

Guyana earned US$826.2 million from gold exports between January and June 2026, up 48.5 percent from US$556.3 million a year earlier. The figures come from the Bank of Guyana and the Ministry of Finance.

Why did export earnings jump if less gold was shipped?

The average export price rose 59.1 percent to US$4,528.20 per ounce, while the volume fell 6.7 percent to 182,451 ounces. Higher prices therefore more than made up for the lower volume.

Who produces Guyana’s gold?

Small and medium miners declared 162,182 troy ounces in the half, and the single large operator, Aurora Gold Mine Inc., declared 70,105. Total declarations came to 232,287 ounces.

Does Guyana sell gold to the United States?

The US Treasury said in June 2024 that Guyanese gold is sold on markets including the United States, Canada, the United Arab Emirates and the European Union. Guyana’s official reports do not break the 2026 exports down by country.

How much gold will Guyana export in 2026?

The finance ministry projects US$2,307.0 million for the full year, up from US$1,617.9 million in 2025. Its price forecast is US$4,700 per ounce, compared with a close of US$4,164.64 on Friday, 16 October.

World.title: Mexico to File Complaint on 17 Oct ICE Death
World.content:
The National Palace in Mexico City, where President Claudia Sheinbaum holds her morning news conferences. File photo of 16 October 2013. Photo: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

MEXICO · MIGRATION

Key Facts — The country Mexico is the United States’ southern neighbour, and about 14,000 of its citizens were in US immigration detention in June. The two governments work together on trade, security and migration, which turns every death in custody into a diplomatic matter.

— Power Index Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 71.4 points (October 2026 edition).

— Why it matters A 56-year-old Mexican man who held a US green card died on Saturday 17 October in a federal immigration detention centre in Laredo, Texas. He is counted as the 18th Mexican to die in US custody or during immigration operations since 20 January 2025.

— What happened The Mexican foreign ministry announced on Sunday 18 October a complaint to the prosecutor of Webb County, Texas, which includes Laredo, and President Claudia Sheinbaum confirmed it on Monday 19 October. The ministry also announced a request that Mexican consuls be allowed into US detention centres to check on detainees’ health.

— The numbers The man had been held for 113 days, since 26 June. His is the seventh death in ICE detention in Texas in 2026 and the second at a Laredo facility.

— What it means for you A green-card holder returning from Mexico was detained at a Laredo port of entry and held for months while his case went to an immigration judge. Deaths in ICE custody go to Congress, and ICE must make its death report public within 90 days.

— Still open The official cause of death has not been published. How he was treated in detention is disputed between ICE and his family.

Mexico will file a complaint with the Webb County prosecutor in Texas over the death of a Mexican man in federal immigration detention in Laredo, its foreign ministry announced on Sunday 18 October and President Claudia Sheinbaum confirmed on Monday 19 October. ICE, the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, says the man was 56, held a green card and had been in its custody since 26 June, and Mexico counts him as the 18th Mexican to die in US custody or during immigration operations since 20 January 2025.

For US readers the case raises three live questions: how ICE cares for the people it detains, what Congress can learn about deaths in custody, and how far a green card protects a traveller coming home from abroad. It also renews a request Mexico has pressed since April, when Sheinbaum ordered daily consular visits to ICE centres: that its consuls be let into US detention centres to check on detainees’ health, which the foreign ministry says it will raise through its embassy in Washington.

What Happened in Laredo

ICE says staff found the man unresponsive in his bed at 9:48 a.m. local time on Saturday 17 October at the Rio Grande Processing Center, began life-saving measures and called the Laredo Fire Department’s paramedics. He was declared dead at 10:10 a.m., according to ICE’s statement as quoted by KGNS, the Laredo television station.

Latin America Power Index · October 2026 edition Mexico ranks 2nd of 14 with 71.4 points. Strongest pillar: economic relationships (90); weakest: state capacity & security (46). Alignment group: Hedging. Watch21 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.7 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

ICE confirmed the death of Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias to KGNS, and Congressman Henry Cuellar, a Democrat who represents Laredo, had confirmed it to the Texas Tribune. Mexico’s foreign ministry, known as the SRE, did not publish his name.

The Rio Grande Processing Center stands at 1001 San Rio Boulevard in Laredo and is listed by ICE under its Harlingen field office. The GEO Group, the company that operates it, referred the Texas Tribune’s questions to ICE.

His daughter, Estefani Andrade, a US citizen, told the Texas Tribune that her father had lived in Dallas for decades, worked as a contractor painting apartments, and had a heart condition, diabetes and high blood pressure. She said staff at the centre would not give him his medications, and that when he reported a cough and chest tightness he told her “they would just ignore him.”

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, The LatAm Brief. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

What Mexico Says and Will Do

At her morning news conference at the National Palace, Sheinbaum said another Mexican had died in a detention centre and that Mexico would file a complaint in the United States because human rights must be protected. She said the man was detained in June, that his family had told Mexican officials he had diabetes and high blood pressure, and that he probably did not have all his medication.

The SRE issued its own statement on Sunday 18 October, demanding a prompt, thorough and transparent investigation. It said ICE’s local office had told Mexico’s consulate general in Laredo of the death and that the complaint would go to the Webb County prosecutor.

The ministry added that it has sent diplomatic notes to the US State Department, filed other complaints and arranged legal help for families. Through Mexico’s embassy in Washington it will ask US immigration authorities to guarantee consuls access to detention centres, so they can demand proper health care for detained Mexicans.

Laredo is not Mexico’s first legal step. On 13 July Mexico’s ambassador in Washington, Roberto Lazzeri, filed 20 complaints with state and county prosecutors in eight states over 17 deaths of Mexicans in immigration operations or custody, the SRE said on 22 July.

On 14 July the embassy also passed Mexico’s federal prosecutor’s complaint on those 17 cases to the US Justice Department through the State Department, and Foreign Secretary Roberto Velasco Álvarez wrote to the UN human rights chief, Volker Türk. In June Velasco told reporters the United States had given Mexico no updates on the deaths, KJZZ, a public radio station in Arizona, reported.

Texas Deaths and the Wider Toll

The Texas Tribune counts Andrade-Covarrubias as the seventh person to die in ICE detention in Texas this year and the second at an ICE facility in Laredo. The earlier Laredo death was that of Felix Alcorta-Rodriguez, a 63-year-old Mexican who died on 19 June at the Webb County Detention Center, which is run by CoreCivic.

Nationwide, the Texas Tribune counted at least 20 deaths in ICE custody in 2026 by 24 June, after 32 in 2025, a record in federal data. Families of other Latin American detainees are asking similar questions, as in the case of a Peruvian man who died in ICE custody in Louisiana on 29 September.

TRAC, a data project that compiles ICE figures, shows in its latest snapshot, dated 11 July, 65,765 people in ICE detention, 70.6 percent of them with no criminal conviction. Mexico’s foreign secretary put the number of Mexicans in US immigration detention at about 14,000 in June, KJZZ reported.

What It Means for You

If you hold a green card and travel to Mexico, this case shows how long a detention at the border can last. ICE says officers detained Andrade-Covarrubias on 26 June at a Laredo port of entry because they believed he obtained his status by fraud, having failed to disclose a 2004 theft arrest, and that he was in removal proceedings.

His daughter told the Texas Tribune that he had disclosed his record and that officials approved his green-card application. Online court records showed an immigration hearing set for Monday 2 November, the Tribune reported.

On Tuesday 23 June the Supreme Court ruled, in the case of a green-card holder named Muk Choi Lau, that a border officer does not need clear and convincing evidence that a returning permanent resident committed a crime involving moral turpitude before treating that person as an applicant for admission. ICE has not said whether the ruling played any part in this detention.

Consular access is a treaty right, and Mexico and the United States are both parties to the 1963 Vienna Convention on Consular Relations. Article 36 lets consular officers visit a national in custody, speak with him and arrange his legal representation, and Article 37 says the host state must tell the consulate without delay of a death.

Congress is already asking questions. Cuellar visited the Rio Grande Processing Center on Sunday, was told staff could not give details because the death is under investigation, and sent ICE written questions, adding in a Monday statement: “Any death in federal custody is a serious matter, and we need to know what happened.”

In its death notices, such as the one of 8 May 2025, ICE says it posts a news release within two business days of a death and that congressional requirements in the 2018 homeland security spending bill oblige it to make public every report on an in-custody death within 90 days. If the clock runs from the death on 17 October, that would be Friday 15 January 2027.

What Is Not Known

The cause of death is not officially settled. ICE’s statement says it is unknown pending an autopsy, while KGNS reported that the Webb County medical examiner called it a natural death after an autopsy on 19 October, a finding the Texas Tribune’s account of ICE’s statement does not include.

It is not known whether ICE or the GEO Group will answer the daughter’s account of his medication and medical requests. ICE says he received medical care and was seen by health professionals, and that it is committed to safe, secure and humane conditions for everyone in custody.

No US prosecutor or Justice Department response to Mexico’s planned complaint had been published by late Monday. It is also not known whether any of the 20 complaints filed in July has led to an investigation.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who died in ICE detention in Laredo?

ICE confirmed the name Emiliano Andrade-Covarrubias, a 56-year-old Mexican citizen who held lawful permanent resident status. He was found unresponsive on Saturday 17 October at the Rio Grande Processing Center and declared dead at 10:10 a.m.

What will Mexico do about it?

Mexico’s foreign ministry announced on Sunday 18 October that it will send a complaint to the Webb County prosecutor, and President Claudia Sheinbaum confirmed on Monday 19 October that Mexico will file a complaint in the United States. The ministry also says Mexico will ask for consular access to detention centres.

How many Mexicans have died in US custody?

Mexico’s foreign ministry counts 18 Mexicans who died in US custody or during immigration operations since 20 January 2025. The Texas Tribune counts this as the seventh death in ICE detention in Texas in 2026.

Can Mexico visit its citizens in US detention?

The Vienna Convention on Consular Relations gives consular officers the right to visit a national in custody and arrange his legal representation. Mexico says it will ask US immigration authorities to guarantee that access in its detention centres.

When will ICE publish its death report?

ICE says congressional requirements oblige it to make public every report on an in-custody death within 90 days. If the clock runs from the death on 17 October, that is Friday 15 January 2027.

Lau, 23 June 2026, UN, Vienna Convention on Consular Relations, 1963, TRAC, immigration detention quick facts. All retrieved 19 and 20 October 2026. World.title: Mozambique Titanium Tax Fight Ends at US$30M
World.content:
RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. Ask Answers are generated from Rio Times reporting only — every claim links to its source article. Open the full Ask Rio Times → RT Ask Rio TimesCost of living, safety, visas across Latin America › RT Ask Rio Times 17 years of Latin America reporting, on demand. × Best for expats Cost of living Safest places Easy visas Tap a question, or type your own — the answer appears right here. Ask Open the full Ask Rio Times →

MOZAMBIQUE · CRITICAL MINERALS

Key Facts — The country Mozambique is a south-eastern African country on the Indian Ocean, known for natural gas, coal, aluminium and mineral sands. President Daniel Chapo, in office since January 2025, leads it.

— What happened On Monday 19 October, the Ministry of Mineral Resources and Energy announced the formal end of Mozambique’s dispute with Kenmare Resources, which runs the Moma titanium mine.

— The tax claim The tax authority had demanded about US$30 million in capital gains tax and royalties for 2019 to 2022, a claim Kenmare contested.

— The new terms The royalty becomes progressive, rising up to 5% with the ilmenite price, and 10% of the mine’s tax revenue goes to Nampula province.

— Jobs and power Kenmare is to keep 1,682 workers, 96% of them Mozambican, and finish a 15-megawatt solar plant by 2027.

— The mineral Ilmenite is a titanium ore used to make white pigment for paints, plastics and ceramics, and Kenmare says Moma supplies about 6% of world titanium.

— Still open Kenmare’s own account of the terms, and whether the US$30 million claim is paid or dropped.

The Mozambique titanium tax dispute is over, the government said on Monday 19 October, ending a fight with Kenmare Resources that began in 2023. The tax authority had demanded about US$30 million from the miner, which says its Moma mine supplies about 6% of the world’s titanium.

Kenmare, listed in London and Dublin, sells ilmenite that ends up in paints, plastics and ceramics. The Mozambique titanium tax deal also comes while a bidder from the United Arab Emirates weighs a takeover offer.

What the Mining Ministry Announced

The Ministry of Mineral Resources and Energy announced on Monday 19 October the formal close of the Mozambique titanium tax dispute with Kenmare Resources. The Maputo daily Notícias carried the statement, and the English-language site Club of Mozambique reported the same terms.

Kenmare holds the concession for the Moma mine, a heavy mineral sands operation in the Larde district of northern Nampula province. The new agreement replaces the 2004 local development agreement, the ministry said.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Africa Critical Minerals Email address Follow Free. One email a day at most, and only when there is news. This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

A Three-Year Fight Over Tax and Royalties

Since 2023, the tax authority’s Mozambique titanium tax claim stood at about US$30 million in capital gains tax and royalties for 2019 to 2022. Kenmare disputed the sum, arguing that it had used international market reference prices.

In March, Kenmare warned it might seek international arbitration after the tax authority tried to impose terms the company said it had not agreed. The government denied a formal conflict, saying the talks sought a fairer split of mineral benefits, according to 360 Mozambique, a Maputo business site.

The mine’s original rights under its Implementation Agreement, the contract that sets its tax and export terms, expired in December 2024. Operations continued under written government confirmations while the two sides negotiated, Mining Weekly reported.

President Daniel Chapo said in March 2025 that he would renegotiate major contracts, and he met Kenmare’s chief executive Tom Hickey in Maputo that June. On Thursday 15 October, Kenmare’s third-quarter report still called renewing its agreement a priority.

New Royalty, Local Fund, Jobs and Solar Power

The new framework follows Mining Law No. 7/2026, and its royalty is progressive, reaching up to 5% with the world price of ilmenite. The ministry also said 10% of the mine’s tax revenue will go to the Nampula Local Development Fund.

That fund is expected to receive between US$8 million and US$10 million a year, Notícias reported. The provincial government will run it, and the Administrative Court, which audits public spending, will check the accounts.

Kenmare committed to keep its 1,682 workers, 96% of whom are Mozambican. It will also finish a 15-megawatt solar plant by 2027 to cut its use of diesel.

Villages Near the Mine and a Spending Gap

Residents of Topuito and Pilivili, two communities near the mine, had complained that the company’s Community Development Fund was not being honoured. The Inspectorate-General of Mineral Resources, the state mining inspector, found that only 42% of the US$12 million planned had been spent.

The money went to schools and water boreholes, according to Notícias. The statement does not say how the unspent balance will now be handled.

A Takeover Bid Adds to the Stakes

On 7 October, RTP, Portugal’s public broadcaster, reported that Emirati group International Resources Holdings proposed a non-binding cash offer for all Kenmare shares. The same group is in a separate dispute with Zambia’s state mining holding company over the Mopani copper mines.

Under Irish takeover rules, the bidder must say by Tuesday 17 November whether it will make a firm offer or walk away. No price has been disclosed.

Kenmare’s third-quarter report on 15 October showed ilmenite output of 233,600 tonnes, up 12% from a year earlier. It cut its 2026 forecast to 710,000 to 750,000 tonnes from about 800,000, citing delays at a new processing plant.

What It Means for US Readers

Titanium minerals from mines such as Moma are turned into the white pigment found in paints, plastics and ceramic tiles sold in American shops. A settled Mozambique titanium tax regime makes Moma’s supply and costs easier to predict for the companies that buy from it.

Investors who follow Kenmare now have a clearer view of the mine’s tax bill ahead of the Tuesday 17 November takeover deadline. The Mozambique titanium tax deal also shows a government rewriting its terms with foreign investors, as set out in our guide to the country.

What Is Not Known

The ministry statement carries no comment from Kenmare. It does not say whether the US$30 million claim will be paid, reduced or dropped.

The royalty rate at the ilmenite price on 20 October is unstated, as is the handling of the unspent community money. The bidder’s firm offer, or its withdrawal, is due by Tuesday 17 November.

More: Mozambique news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Mozambique announce about Kenmare?

On Monday 19 October, Mozambique’s mining ministry announced the formal end of its dispute with Kenmare Resources, the company behind the Moma titanium mine. The agreement replaces the 2004 local development agreement.

Who is Kenmare Resources?

Kenmare is a titanium minerals producer with its headquarters in Dublin and its shares listed in London and Dublin. It runs the Moma mine in Nampula province, which produces ilmenite, rutile and zircon.

How big was the Mozambique titanium tax claim?

The tax authority claimed about US$30 million in capital gains tax and royalties for 2019 to 2022. Kenmare disputed the figure, saying it had used international market prices.

What are the new royalty and fund terms?

The royalty is progressive and can reach 5%, depending on the ilmenite price. Ten per cent of the mine’s tax revenue goes to Nampula’s local development fund, estimated at US$8 million to US$10 million a year.

Why does the Mozambique titanium tax deal matter outside Africa?

Ilmenite is the raw material for white pigment used in paints, plastics and ceramics worldwide. The Mozambique titanium tax deal also comes as a bidder from the United Arab Emirates weighs an offer for Kenmare.
