World.title: Zelenskyy accuses US of delaying Patriot missile shipment
World.content:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused the United States of delaying deliveries of air defense missiles already paid for by European allies, as relations between Washington and Kyiv deteriorate.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused the US administration of delaying the delivery of crucial missiles needed by Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks.

He told US senators on Monday that "the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles" even though they had already been paid for by Ukraine's European allies.

The accusations come as Ukraine-US relations are strained. US President Donald Trump has eased sanctions on Russia and directly criticized Zelenskyy, calling for someone else to take his place.

What did Zelenskyy say?

The Ukrainian president said that the US was holding back interceptor missiles, with one shipment only waiting for the signature of US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth before it could be sent to Ukraine.

He also said that Ukraine's European allies had agreed to transfer some of their own Patriot missiles but that this too was pending the green light from the US .

"The missiles are ready, and they could already be in Ukraine," Zelenskyy said. "But unfortunately, there is still no approval."

Ukraine urgently needs more air defence missiles like the Patriot system Image: Valentyn Ogirenko/REUTERS

Earlier on Monday, he said Ukraine had again not received any early warnings about incoming Russian missile strikes. The country is dependent on the ability of US intelligence to spot fast-moving ballistic missiles fired by Russia.

There are also growing concerns over restrictions affecting Starshield, a military satellite communications network developed by Elon Musk's SpaceX. Ukrainian military communications and drone operations depend on using Starshield data.

The US government controls access to Starshield, but Trump has denied ordering any restrictions.

US says it's not withholding intelligence

The accusations come as Ukraine faces renewed Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure. In the night between Sunday and Monday, several Russian ballistic missiles struck the Ukrainian capital and its surroundings, cutting off electricity to more than half a million households.

"Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners," Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram about the attack.

The US, though, dismissed claims it was withholding information, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio insisting that Washington had not paused its intelligence sharing with Kyiv.

Regarding the easing of sanctions and the diesel deal between Washington and Moscow, Donald Trump strongly criticized Zelenskyy for calling out the deal.

"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said on Monday. "To be honest, I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine."

World.title: At least four dead after flooding in eastern Spain
World.content:
At least four people have died in Spain as torrential rain has battered the country's eastern Mediterranean coast. The severe flooding had left more than 450 people stranded on rooftops, in buildings or in cars.

At least four people have died after heavy rain and severe flooding across eastern Spain, forcing hundreds of people to flee. The worst-affected areas are in the Valencia and Alicante regions, on Spain's eastern Mediterranean coast.

In the town of Oliva, two bodies were recovered on Monday. One victim was a 79-year-old woman found at her home, while another was a man who died from a heart attack at a campsite.

In Sagunto, a man drowned while swimming at the beach, while in Catalonia, a woman died after falling into a rain-swollen stream in Catalonia.

Emergency services have rescued more than 450 people who were stranded by the rising water. Some had to be airlifted from rooftops, flooded buildings and vehicles, while others were brought to safety by boat.

Roads were underwater on Monday Image: Rober Solsona/EUROPA PRESS/dpa/picture alliance

Residents use buckets to drain water from their homes in Daimuz Image: Ana Beltran/REUTERS

Pile of furniture on a muddy street Image: Rober Solsona/EUROPA PRESS/dpa/picture alliance

Emergency restrictions

Authorities imposed emergency restrictions across several municipalities, asking people to stay indoors. Most restrictions have since been lifted.

The Balearic Islands in the Mediterranean, including Mallorca and Ibiza, were also affected, with schools closed, and some flights cancelled or delayed.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said military emergency teams were assisting with the rescue efforts and pledged full government support.

The latest flooding comes almost two years after the Valencia region suffered a devastating flood disaster that killed more than 220 people.

World.title: French authorities impose partial curfews in Paris, Nice
World.content:
Several countries around the world, including China, Malaysia, Germany and the United States, have advised citizens traveling to France to avoid large crowds and exercise caution in the wake of large-scale protests and looting in major cities.

China's Foreign Ministry urged Chinese nationals in France to remain alert to potential risks, increase safety precautions, and avoid ​areas where demonstrations are taking place.

Malaysia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that, while ⁠travel to France remains unrestricted, ​Malaysians are advised to consider postponing non-essential trips until the situation improves.

The Malaysian embassy in Paris has issued an advisory urging citizens already in France to exercise caution and remain vigilant.

The US State Department issued an alert on Monday warning Americans to avoid demonstrations in major French cities, while an alert issued by the American embassy in Paris noted new curfews ordered in cities including Paris and Lille.

"Avoid the areas of the demonstrations," the warning said.

And in Europe, some of France's direct neighbors have also issued travel advice to citizens.

The German Foreign Ministry said ‌further riots couldn't be ruled out and urged German nationals to follow instructions from local police. It warned citizens that they could face fines if they fail to adhere to requests to leave unauthorized demonstrations.

Governments in the Czech Republic, the Netherlands, Poland, Denmark, Sweden, ​Finland and Norway also issued warnings to avoid protests.

World.title: Bulgaria seeks suspects in Germany after Starlink sabotage
World.content:
A Bulgarian court has issued arrest warrants for two young German nationals suspected of setting fire to Starlink antennas. The case is reminiscent of another in Poland, which Warsaw says was orchestrated by Russia.

Bulgaria on Monday issued European arrest warrants against two 19-year-old German nationals, saying it suspected their involvement in the sabotage of a series of Starlink antennas near the capital Sofia.

"The evidence gathered makes it possible to conclude that there are reasonable grounds to suspect the involvement of the two defendants," the court in Sofia rules, granting a request from prosecutors.

Ukraine's military uses Starlink's military-grade satellite internet service Starshield for battlefield communications amid Russia's invasion.

Bulgaria does not directly border Ukraine, but it is on the Black Sea, one of the flashpoints of the conflict. A similar case in Poland, which does directly border Ukraine, led to a total of four arrests last week, also in Germany.

What do we know about the incident in Bulgaria?

The two teenage suspects are accused of deliberately setting fire to the antennas on the evening of October 9.

Of 18 in a mountainous region south of Sofia, three were destroyed entirely, two were partially burned and three more were damaged, according to prosecutors.

Prosecutors say the suspects entered from Serbia in a car with German license plates, claiming to be tourists, staying just a few hours around the time of the alleged crime.

Plamen Tonchev, the head of Bulgaria's domestic intelligence agency DANS, said he was working on the assumption that it was deliberate sabotage and said other such acts could not be ruled out in future.

What is the potential tie-in to a Polish sabotage case?

News of the arrests follow just a week after a total of four people were arrested in Germany, accused of sabotaging a Starlink satellite communications station in central Poland in late September.

German police detained three resident men and a woman, two of them Turkish nationals, early last week.

Polish officials said they believed that Russia was behind the sabotage attempt, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk calling it an act of "hybrid warfare."

The domestic intelligence agency also claimed that Russia had cooperated with organized crime elements in Germany on the alleged operation.

Meanwhile, in the Baltic, Lithuania's prime minister on Sunday said that Russia was likely behind an attempted arson attack on a company hosting communication hardware for Starlink satellites.

World.title: Germany news: Emergency at Leipzig airport sparked by novice driver
World.content:
A two-day conference entitled "Invest in Germany Summit" is to begin on Monday evening in Berlin as the government seeks to shore up public-sector spending with private money.

Chancellor Friedrich Merz will deliver the opening speech at the conference, which will be attended by an expected 200 representatives from large German and international companies.

The CEO of the US chip manufacturer Nvidia, Jensen Huang, is to be one of the key guests at the conference.

The German government is looking to cooperate strongly with the company, whose products are central to the boom in artificial intelligence, in a bid to help Germany catch up in the sector.

Nividia's Jensen Huang, seen here in Davos in 2026, is to be a key guest Image: Mattias Nutt/Avalon/Photoshot/picture alliance

Don't expect too much: Economic institute

The German Economic Institute (IW) has, however, warned against any too high expectations from the summit, saying that high costs for labor, energy and bureaucracy in Germany were a deterrent to investment in the country.

"It would be naive to believe that the summit will change that in the short term. Companies don't choose Germany because of a promotional event. What matters is whether they can make money here," IW director Michael Hüther told the DPA news agency.

He said it would be more effective if the government were to swiftly implement its reform agenda.

A study by Allianz Research has shown that investment in Germany fell by 6.4% between 2019 and 2025, while it grew by 6.7% in the rest of the eurozone and a whole 20.2% in the US.

World.title: Kenya: Cult leader guilty of murdering 190 children, 1 adult
World.content:
Preacher Paul Mackenzie was accused of encouraging his followers to starve themselves to death. He ran a Christian doomsday cult called the Good News International Church that claimed the end of the world was imminent.

A court in Mombasa, Kenya, on Monday found self-proclaimed preacher Paul Mackenzie and 28 associates guilty of murdering 190 children and one adult as part of a notorious Christian starvation cult.

Mackenzie established his so-called Good News International Church in 2003 and was alleged to have incited his followers to starve themselves to death in order to "meet Jesus."

He was arrested in April 2023 after a rights group informed authorities.

Some of his acolytes were rescued but the subsequent police operation exposed hundreds of mass graves at a forest site near the Kenyan beach resort of Malindi.

Local media dubbed the case the "Shakahola Forest Massacre."

Shakahola Forest Massacre: What did the judge say?

"I am satisfied that the prosecution has proved the case against all the 29 accused persons for the murder of 190 children and one adult," said Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache after a hearing which lasted over eight hours.

Justice Diana Kavedza Mochache delivered the verdict Image: Laban Walloga/REUTERS

The prosecution had said Mackenzie "initiated and directed" extreme fasting at his 800-acre (325 hectare) ranch in Shakahola Forest, claiming there was a "structured hierarchy of death" which said children should die first, followed by teenagers, women, and then men.

Post-mortems and police reports revealed that the children mostly died from starvation, but also from "asphyxia, neck compression and traumatic head injury," prosecutors said.

The court in Mombasa also heard that, in some cases, children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.

"This is a very, very important day," said Francis Wanje, 62, who lost eight family members, including his daughter and two grandchildren, at Shakahola.

"We are expecting a ruling that will be a lesson to the whole public, so that such kinds of things will not happen again," he told the AFP news agency, expressing anger over the government's initial inaction.

Kenyan doomsday cult leader convicted of murder To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Mackenzie facing even more Shakahola charges

Since the initial discovery of the graves, even more bodies of children, women and men have been unearthed, bringing the total to well over 400. The soaring death toll has even required sporadic pauses in excavations as local morgues ran out of space.

In January 2026, Mackenzie was charged over a further 52 bodies found at a nearby village.

There have been calls in Kenya for tougher regulations on religious organizations after it emerged that Mackenzie had been arrested twice in the past but released.

He was arrested in 2017 on charges of "radicalization" but was acquitted. He was arrested again in 2019 in relation to two child deaths at Shakahola, but released on bail.

His sentencing will take place on November 6.

World.title: Canada: Alberta votes on holding independence referendum
World.content:
Canada's oil-rich western province of Alberta is not deemed likely to vote in favor of a real breakaway plebiscite. Nevertheless the separatist movement hopes to gain leverage over Mark Carney's government.

Residents of Alberta in Canada are voting in a referendum on whether the province should begin a process that could ultimately lead to independence.

The motion does not appear likely to succeed but the vote taking place at all signifies economic and political grievances gaining some sway in the vast oil-rich region.

Separatist leaders hope that a comparatively strong showing for their cause could nevertheless pressure Prime Minister Mark Carney's government in Ottawa to pay them more heed in future.

What will happen during the vote?

Polls opened at 9 a.m. local time in the provincial capital Edmonton (1500 GMT/UTC) on Monday.

They are scheduled to close at 8 p.m. that evening (Tuesday, 0200 GMT/UTC).

Results will then be published as they come in.

At least based on opinion polls, the yes/no result is in no real doubt, but as many as 1 in 3 voters might support the proposal.

The 'no to the nine' campaign urges voters to refuse all nine proposal up for debate, not just the most significant one on setting the wheels in motion for a potential independence referendum Image: Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

What has led to the vote?

Monday's referendum is the first on the notion of breaking away from Canada in a province other than majority French-speaking Quebec, which has a better-known separatist movement founded in language and cultural differences.

The vast oil-rich state is almost double the size of Germany in terms of land mass, but is much more sparsely populated with around 5 million residents. Almost half of them live in its two main cities, Edmonton and Calgary.

Alberta's provincial government is led by Danielle Smith of the United Conservative Party while Mark Carney's Liberal Party lead the national government.

Smith herself does not advocate independence and has urged voters to oppose the motion. But she has nevertheless authorized the vote, seemingly in a bid to assuage an increasingly vocal flank within her own ranks.

Independence advocates accuse the government of stifling Alberta's oil industry, for instance through environmental regulations, and also say they contribute disproportionately to the national public purse.

"Canada has an imbalanced system which feeds the central population and government at the expense of the outlying producing provinces such as Alberta," said Cory Morgan, founder of a pro-separation organization called Pathway to Independence.

PM Carney has been campaigning in Edmonton and elsewhere, trying to maximize turnout among those who favor staying part of Canada Image: John Ulan/The Canadian Press/AP Photo/picture alliance

Canadian sovereignty under pressure from within and without

Carney, who grew up in Alberta, has spent much of the past week campaigning for the "stay" campaign, appealing to national pride and urging supporters to vote to provide as resounding a result as possible — even in what might not be a close race.

The renowned economist and central banker often argued that the separatist cause might be guilty of overlooking matters more significant than dollars and drilling permits.

"Canada is not a transaction between provinces. It's not about gross and net, gives and gets," he said at an event in Red Deer on Friday.

Although polls in French-speaking Quebec suggest that enthusiasm for independence — typically a minority cause — is lower than usual during Carney's premiership, the issue is never very far from the political debate. The success of the separatist Parti Quebecois in local elections this month served as a reminder of this.

Carney is also trying to maintain national unity amid pressure from Canada's nearest neighbor and biggest trade partner.

US President Donald Trump is conducting characteristically combative trade talks with Canada that have seemed in danger of breaking down in recent months.

When at his most agitated, Trump has even called for Canada to become the "51st state" of the US. He has also tried to rename bodies of water like Lake Ontario.

World.title: Can diplomacy stop another Ethiopia-Eritrea war?
World.content:
Ethiopia has installed a new administration in conflict-hit Tigray after federal forces pushed back Tigrayan fighters. But tensions with Eritrea continue to raise fears of a wider regional war.

Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed has announced an interim government in the country's northern Tigray region, giving it six months to prepare for regional elections and restore stability.

Abiy's announcement on Friday followed a military offensive launched in September by the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and six other armed groups. They were ultimately forced to retreat and lost control of the region.

"To attain the peace that has long eluded them, to secure their right to self-administration, ​and to finally enjoy the fruits of development — which have been out of reach for many years — the people of Tigray must break free from this cycle ⁠of conflict," ​Abiy said in a statement posted on X.

Shishay Amare, the new mayor of the regional capital Mekelle, said they would "create the right conditions for elections by ensuring peace and stability across Tigray," as reported by French news agency Agence France-Presse.

"I am confident that this will be done within six months, according to our plan," Amare said, adding that their priorities included restoring peace, helping displaced residents return home, reopening markets and ensuring humanitarian assistance reached those in need.

Why relations with Eritrea matter

The fighting has revived concerns about a return to the devastating 2020–2022 Tigray war. Around 1 million people remain displaced from that conflict. The African Union has estimated that the war resulted in around 600,000 deaths from combat, famine and the collapse of healthcare.

The new administration faces unresolved disputes over political authority and territory, including western Tigray, which is claimed by both Tigray and neighboring Amhara state.

Egypt and Ethiopia have repeatedly clashed over the construction of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, which is located in northwestern Ethiopia and opened in 2025 Image: Brian Inganga/AP Photo/picture alliance

Ethiopia and Eritrea were once bitter enemies but signed a peace agreement in 2018. Eritrean forces later fought alongside Ethiopian federal troops during the Tigray war. But the countries' relationship has since deteriorated.

Addis Ababa has accused Asmara of supporting Tigrayan forces and violating Ethiopian territory. Eritrea has denied the accusations.

Reports of Eritrean troop movements near the border have heightened concern, although the extent of any current deployment remains disputed.

Tsedale Lemma, journalist and publisher of the prominent Addis Standard magazine, told DW earlier this month that the danger reflects years of unresolved tensions and failures to implement the November 2022 Pretoria Agreement, which ended the Tigray war.

Lemma said the international community was "absolutely underestimating" the threat of conflict. She argued that international actors had failed to ensure effective monitoring of the agreement and respond adequately as the peace process weakened.

A wider regional risk

The confrontation comes amid instability across the Horn of Africa, including Sudan's war and tensions between Ethiopia and Egypt over the Nile mega-dam project.

Why northern Ethiopia is seeing growing violence once again To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ethiopia inaugurated the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam (GERD) in September 2025, a move that was not well received by neighboring Egypt and Sudan, both downstream countries.

Competition over access to the Red Sea has added another strategic dimension: Ethiopia became landlocked when Eritrea gained independence in 1993.

Journalist Martin Plaut, who specializes in the Horn of Africa, has warned that the region is at a crossroads. He has raised the possibility of Ethiopian forces entering Eritrea, but an invasion remains a scenario, not a confirmed decision by the Ethiopian government.

Any wider conflict could threaten regional trade and maritime security. The Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait connect shipping routes between Europe and Asia, making the region strategically important well beyond Africa.

Can diplomacy avert war between Ethiopia and Eritrea?

The United States and the United Kingdom have called on Ethiopia and Eritrea to exercise restraint and return to dialogue under their 2018 peace framework.

Speaking to reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland on Saturday, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that the military buildup on the Ethiopia-Eritrea border could escalate into a wider conflict.

Rubio said Washington hoped lifting some sanctions would improve communication with both sides and stressed the need for a "wise and measured" response to avoid a broader regional war.

The United Kingdom has also called for renewed talks between both sides. "We urgently call for de-escalation and a return to dialogue. We reiterate our support for the African Union's role in facilitating this," said a UK government spokesperson in a statement on October 15.

For now, the recapture of towns in Tigray has changed the military balance but has not resolved tensions in the region.

Whether international pressure can prevent a wider war will depend on whether the governments involved choose dialogue over further escalation.

Negash Mohammed, Tamirat Geleta and Christine Mhundwa contributed to this report.

Edited by: Keith Walker

World.title: Todos los ojos se vuelven al norte: lo que pasa cuando se empuja a los creadores
World.content:
Faro Santander, el nuevo espacio cultural y museístico del norte de España, lanza la II convocatoria de Ayudas a la Creación para artistas cántabros de cualquier disciplina, un programa que, además de ayuda económica, provee de asesorías especializadas y garantiza una muestra pública en el museo. Los ganadores de la primera convocatoria cuentan su experiencia

Suelen identificarse solo a toro pasado: aquel momento me cambió la vida. Hay oportunidades, sin embargo, cuyo brillo se deja ver desde el principio. Esta es una de esas. Faro Santander lanza su II Convocatoria de Ayudas a la Creación, un programa que ofrece a los proyectos seleccionados una dotación económica de 10.000 euros, seminarios y mentorías con profesionales, la ocasión de compartir proceso creativo con otros artistas y, como remate, una muestra pública en un espacio tan espectacular como el Edificio Pereda, convertido desde su reciente rehabilitación y apertura en Santander en uno de los grandes focos culturales de todo el norte de España.

Hasta el 15 de febrero de 2027 puede disfrutarse gratuitamente, comisariado por Ane Rodríguez, del resultado de los cuatro proyectos becados en la primera edición. Talento cántabro que, a partir de distintas manifestaciones culturales ligadas a esa verde tierra, ha generado un trabajo variado, muy contemporáneo y de vocación universal. En Flesh & Films / Pieles y pantallas, Itsaso Iribarren y Germán de la Riva recuperan materiales de un archivo de educación sexual de hace décadas; una obra, la que proponen, que cultiva la sensibilidad, que induce a la reflexión sobre gestos cotidianos como el abrazo. En Una forma minúscula, de Salón de belleza, nombre del colectivo formado por Manuela Gutiérrez y Cristina Somavilla, el cine de arte y ensayo sirve como pretexto para encontrarse y hablar, para crear comunidad y traer a la conversación la olvidada contracultura santanderina. La pintora Amaia Bregel, por primera vez en su carrera en piezas de gran escala, en Ludarquías muestra instalaciones y dispositivos impregnados de todo su saber pictórico (“Casi todo el arte contemporáneo es hijo de la pintura”, cuenta). El dúo Casapalma —Irene Atienza y Yoel Molina—, cuya música bucea en el folclore cántabro, ha logrado terminar el rodaje de un documental titulado La Suite de los Riconchos que se estrena el próximo 22 de octubre y nos trae ese ancestral conocimiento que se esconde en las danzas tradicionales y la etnografía.

Entre todos los aspirantes, el jurado escogió proyectos en los que, además de formatos convencionales, cupieran investigaciones artísticas y apuestas valientes: se valora documentación, proceso, método y pensamiento tanto como pieza final. Una característica de este programa de ayudas que los cuatro beneficiarios destacan, por inusual en el panorama nacional: “Ojalá mantengan este espíritu”, indica Germán de la Riva. La visibilidad que les ha otorgado este reconocimiento, sobre todo al verse expuestos en Marisma, en la primera planta de Faro, vecinos a una colección permanente que abarca obra desde El Greco a Frida Kahlo, es el otro gran privilegio que los artistas unánimemente señalan: “Para mí supuso un punto de inflexión”, confiesa Amaia Bregel; para ella, esta ha sido la puerta hacia otras becas o ferias de enorme prestigio, como la de Casa Velázquez o Estampa.

“Animaos a participar, sea cual sea vuestra idea”, ese es el mensaje común de los primeros beneficiarios para quienes les sigan.

Segunda convocatoria Ayudas Plazo de admisión 2026 15 octubre -

09 de noviembre Dotación económica 10.000 euros Beneficiarios Cuatro artistas (o colectivos de artistas) de cualquier disciplina, residentes o nacidos en Cantabria Así funciona el programa de acompañamiento: El proyecto debe desarrollarse en Cantabria, entre enero y junio de 2027

Se priorizarán aquellos que fomenten la generación de tejido artístico en el territorio

Se realizará un encuentro inicial entre comisarios, coordinadores y beneficiarios

Los beneficiarios dispondrán de cuatro seminarios y talleres con profesionales invitados, uno a la semana durante el primer mes de trabajo

Estos encuentros colectivos periódicos que estarán abiertos a otros artistas que deseen inscribirse

Los beneficiarios podrán solicitar tutorías personalizadas y seguimiento continuo

Al final del programa, se organizará una muestra pública en Faro Santander, a partir de septiembre de 2027

Amaia Bregel y

Ludarquías

Cuando Amaia Bregel volvió a Santander en marzo de 2020, con la pandemia, no tenía intención de quedarse. Se había graduado en Bellas Artes en Valencia, donde continuó con un máster de Producción de Arte y Pensamiento Contemporáneo y donde, sin aquel terremoto mundial, seguramente se habría imaginado residiendo todavía. Hoy, sin embargo, reivindica las posibilidades halladas en su ciudad: “Mucha gente de mi generación volvió y entre todos hemos creado una red. Soy la que más defiende Santander ahora mismo”, reclama entre risas.

05:15 Amaia Bregel | Fundación Santander

Al borde de la treintena, la ayuda de Faro ha supuesto para ella un cambio de escala, literal y profesional. Su proyecto, Ludarquías, le ha permitido abordar una producción que no habría podido llevar a cabo en las condiciones con las que venía trabajando. La artista lo resume sin rodeos: «Para mí a nivel profesional es un antes y un después». Ha podido tomar por primera vez decisiones plásticas sin ver constreñida su ambición por cuestiones estrictamente económicas y, además, ha contado, cuando la duda más quemaba, con el consejo de la consagrada artista limeña Andrea Canepa. “Fue un regalazo”, cuenta. Fruto de toda esa meticulosa labor es el objeto pictórico titulado Escalera de Jacob. Uno de los imperdibles de la muestra.

Amaia Bregel y

Ludarquías Las ayudas supusieron la oportunidad para Amaia Bregel de llevar sus objetos pictóricos a unas dimensiones nunca antes experimentadas. En la imagen, parte del trabajo de montaje final de la instalación móvil. (Crédito: Jabata Films) Antes de llegar al objeto pictórico grande, Bregel trabaja con maquetas. La propia escala presenta problemas que ha de ir afrontando en el proceso plástico y que necesitan de ingenio. En este proyecto, contó con la asesoría de la artista peruana Andrea Canepa. (Crédito: Jabata Films) Su obra parte de lo pictórico y lo deriva hacia objetos donde el color y sus vibraciones son habitables. Amaia Bregel sigue considerándose, ante todo, pintora, aunque se maneje en muchos lenguajes y métodos. Esta pieza expuesta en Marisma, en Faro Santander, lleva por título ‘Escalera de Jacob’ y puede contemplarse así, como un cubo completo, o abierta. (Crédito: Jabata Films).

Casapalma y

La Suite de los Riconchos

Su álbum debut, Montañesas (2023), mezclaba canción tradicional con sonidos electrónicos; con JOTAS (2025) profundizan en la importancia de la pandereta y de una música que, sobre todo, estaba hecha para bailar. Y ahí, en todo ese universo —de los ritmos de percusión y los pasos de danza a la alfayatería y los trajes tradicionales— encuentran el germen del documental La Suite de los Riconchos que ahora estrenan en la Filmoteca de Cantabria y que esperan que tenga un gran recorrido por festivales y salas. Música y patrimonio, arte y sociología.

08:08 Casapalma | Fundación Santander

Las ayudas, además del crucial aporte económico para completar el rodaje que finalizaron en agosto (“¡Hacer una película es muy caro!”, exclama Atienza), le han procurado otra experiencia de esas difícilmente olvidables. Tocaron en la inauguración de Faro Santander, pudieron, gracias a la celebración de ese concierto, “subir a un escenario enorme el folclore de Cantabria para que lo viera toda la ciudad”.

Casapalma y

La Suite de los Riconchos Fotograma de ‘La Suite de los Riconchos’, con Yoel Molina (izquierda) a la guitarra e Irene Atienza a la pandereta. Molina se formó en Musikene (País Vasco) y en el Conservatorio Superior de Ámsterdam. Atienza, que vivió varios años en Brasil, regresó a su ciudad, Santander, tras la pandemia. Para la grabación del documental han llevado a cabo una importante investigación musicológica y etnográfica. El baile estaba en el centro del propósito de estas músicas, y esa misma relevancia tiene en la película. Los trajes tradicionales de montañesa suelen componerse de camisa de manca ancha, saya larga de colores con detalles de terciopelo y detalles como pañoleta o faltriquera. La película documental musical, que contó con la asesoría de grandes profesionales coreográficos y estudiosos de la etnografía de la región, se estrenó en la Filmoteca de Cantabria el 22 de octubre y está pendiente de su distribución en festivales y salas.

Para una formación que trabaja con el patrimonio inmaterial, con buena reputación ya bien ganada y una trayectoria importante en el campo de la música, compartir el proceso de su película con otros artistas con métodos y objetivos más abstractos, inmersos en proyectos de lenguajes variopintos, ha sido otro de los aprendizajes más enriquecedores. Cuenta Irene que, tras esta experiencia en común, Aurelio Vélez, vinculado al colectivo etnográfico Brañaflor y asesor fundamental del filme, tomó la determinación de presentar una propuesta sobre costura y cuadros de la colección permanente a la convocatoria que ahora se abre. “Él no se imaginaba que pudiera ser candidato a unas ayudas de arte, pero programas como este son una forma de abrir la mente”.

Salón de Belleza y

Una forma minúscula

Una conversación entre dos amigas, Manuela Gutiérrez y Cristina Somavilla, que eclosiona al abrirla al resto: así podría definirse qué es Salón de Belleza, el colectivo artístico que ambas fundaron y para el que ver películas, discutirlas y cuestionar ideas anquilosadas sobre el gusto o la cultura es la razón última de ser. Una forma minúscula parte de un hallazgo accidental: se toparon con el largometraje de Jesús Garay Manderley (1981) sobre la figura del artista y activista LGTBIQ+ José Pérez Ocaña y se obsesionaron con la peli: “Le pregunté por ella a mi padre”, cuenta Somavilla, “y me contó que él había conocido aquí a Ocaña”. Ahí comienza su investigación, ¿qué relatos de aquella Cantabria habían quedado fuera de la historia oficial? “Hemos abierto fisuras en lo que se supone que es Santander: hay mucho más”, explican.

06:42 Salón de Belleza | Fundación Santander

La ayuda les ha permitido poner en marcha un grupo de investigación intergeneracional en el que la memoria oral y el intercambio de pareceres ha ido hilando una conversación inacabada e inacabable (“¡seguiremos con estos encuentros y clubes en el futuro!”), siempre dispuesta a fluir fuera de cauce y al vaivén de las sorpresas, una investigación recogida parcialmente en textos y materiales de archivo disponibles en la muestra. “Nos gustaría ahora que la gente se acercara al espacio museístico, que Faro Santander se convirtiera en ese lugar de participación y encuentro que ha sido para nosotras”.

Salón de Belleza y

Una forma minúscula Sesión de trabajo del proyecto ‘Una forma minúscula’, en la que, a partir del visionado de una película y de ciertos materiales de archivo, se abre una conversación. Fotograma del drama dirigido por Jesús Garay ‘Manderley’, estrenado en 1981. La trama acompaña a tres jóvenes homosexuales que, en un mal momento personal, deciden pasar un verano juntos en Cantabria. Entre los protagonistas, destaca el ‘performer’ José Pérez Ocaña. Además de la película, las sesiones del proyecto utilizan material que reconstruye el contexto cultural en que surgió el filme para indagar más allá del relato oficial. En la imagen, el informe de calificación por edades de ‘Manderley’ (Archivo General de la Administración). Otro de esos materiales empleados fue el libro del artista e historiador Adolfo Fernández-Punsola ‘Nuestras vidas’, editado en 1996, que recoge fotografías y documentos de las décadas que retrata la película.

Itsaso Iribarren y Germán de la Riva y

Flesh & Films / Pieles y pantallas

Nunca sabe uno adónde le va a llevar abrir unas cajas viejas. Germán de la Riva recordaba vagamente el contenido de las que sus padres habían acumulado en la consulta. Psicólogos, fueron pioneros en materia de educación sexual en Santander en los años 80 y 90, con métodos traídos de su experiencia en Latinoamérica y EE UU. Dentro de las solapas de cartón, películas con imágenes artísticas pero explícitamente sexuales convivían con artículos y tesis científicas, un archivo que resultó idóneo para la labor investigadora que De la Riva lleva tiempo desarrollando junto a la también doctora en Bellas Artes y bailarina de danza contemporánea Itsaso Iribarren. Para ellos, toda su obra empieza en el cuerpo.

06:28 Itsaso Iribarren y Germán de la Riva | Fundación Santander

Memoria, sexualidad o cómo nos relacionamos físicamente son cuestiones que se pueden abordar apelando a los sentidos y la intuición. El arte tiene su propio camino hacia el conocimiento y, para Iribarren y De la Riva, mostrar ese proceso junto a la obra puede ser la mejor manera de hacer pedagogía: “El público entiende más o menos lo que ocurrió en las artes hasta las Vanguardias, pero existe un vacío, una desconexión, con las artes vivas y el presente de la creación”. Justo por ello, valoran y agradecen el compromiso de Faro Santander al generar un espacio que puede proveer al espectador de las piezas de puzle que le faltan.

Itsaso Iribarren y Germán de la Riva y

Flesh & Films / Pieles y pantallas Itsaso Iribarren y Germán de la Riva, doctores en Bellas Artes y practicantes de danza contemporánea y artes vivas, inician todas sus investigaciones plásticas a partir del cuerpo: el movimiento, el tacto, los sentidos. Es otro de los caminos de conocimiento que permite el arte y que merece exploración. Para documentar el proceso del proyecto ‘Flesh & Films / Pieles y pantallas’ y generar un resultado expositivo, han empleado, entre otros métodos y lenguaje, la filmación analógica en 16 milímetros. Las artes vivas son una disciplina contemporánea en la que las fronteras genéricas se borran, donde conviven ‘performance’, danza, teatro físico, música, texto y artes visuales. De la Riva y Iribarren aplauden la apuesta de Faro Santander por proyectos así, donde mostrar el proceso creativo es casi más importante que alcanzar un resultado final.

Son cuatro historias, cuatro pulsos creativos distintos que, sin embargo, pintan un mapa justo de los derroteros del arte español de hoy, siempre vivo y siempre a punto del naufragio, sin tablas de salvación como la que ofrece esta convocatoria de Faro Santander. Hay oportunidades que de verdad cambian vidas, instituciones que verdaderamente tienen la capacidad de generar un tejido cultural que cosa todo el norte de España y enseñe el tapiz con lo mejor de nuestra creación fuera.

Para presentarse a la nueva convocatoria no hace falta tener respuestas, tan solo ganas de pelearse con el runrún que provocan esas preguntas que merece la pena hacerse.

World.title: Albert Heijn owner files police report over cyberattack
World.content:
Ahold Delhaize, the parent company of Dutch supermarket chain Albert Heijn, filed a police report on Monday over the cyberattack that forced it to take systems offline more than a week ago.

The company said in a statement on Monday that its investigation had confirmed the suspicious activity in its IT systems was caused by “the malicious actions of others”. Until now it had described the problem only as a “cybersecurity incident”.

Police and the public prosecution service (OM) urged the company to file a report last week, because a criminal investigation cannot start without one.

It is not clear why Ahold Delhaize has now decided to do so, broadcaster NOS reported.

The company did notify the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), the justice ministry’s cybersecurity agency, within 24 hours of discovering the attack, as required under a new cybersecurity law that came into force on August 15.

Albert Heijn’s website and app are back online and home deliveries are expected to resume on Friday, October 23, the company said. The websites of drugstore chain Etos and drinks chain Gall & Gall, also owned by Ahold Delhaize, are available again.

Ahold Delhaize said it had so far found no evidence that sensitive data belonging to customers, staff or business partners had been taken. It declined to give further details while the investigation continues, saying they could compromise its security.

The Albert Heijn hack is one of the first major incidents since the new reporting law came into force. It covers some 8,000 organisations seen as vital to the country, from healthcare, drinking water and banks to the food sector, including supermarkets.

The problems began on Sunday, October 11, when Albert Heijn switched off part of its IT systems, halting home deliveries and work at its distribution centres and leaving empty shelves in some stores.

Security sources told NOS last week that servers in the US, Poland, Moldova and Turkey had been used in the attack. Sector insiders told the Financieele Dagblad that the outage was costing the company “tens of millions” of euros a day.

World.title: POW campaigners keep up fight after cabinet limits compensation
World.content:
Campaigners for the widows of former Japanese prisoners of war have said they will keep fighting for compensation after the Dutch government said only surviving partners would be entitled to receive their spouses’ unpaid wages.

Long-term care minister Mirjam Sterk announced last Friday that the partners of civil servants and servicemen who were held captive following the invasion of Indonesia in 1942 would receive 42 months’ back pay, covering the period until the liberation in May 1945.

But Sterk said only widows who are still alive when the compensation scheme is launched on February 1 next year, all of whom are well into their nineties or older, would receive the payouts because a more extensive ruling would be “too complicated”.

The government has also cut the total size of the fund from the €50 mln announced in its last spring budget statement to €11.5 mln, on the basis that only a few hundred widows of the 40,000 men who were captured by the Japanese still survive.

The decision follows decades of campaigning for victims of the camps to be given the same treatment as Dutch government employees who were forced to work in Germany during World War II.

Moluccans

They include Moluccans who later fought on the side of the Dutch during the Indonesian liberation war and were subsequently persecuted by the independent government, prompting them to flee to the Netherlands.

Earlier this year prime minister Rob Jetten apologised to the Moluccan community for the way they were treated when they arrived in the 1950s.

Peggy Stein, of campaign group Indisch Platform 2.0, called for the ruling to be backdated to include widows who were alive when parliament approved a motion by farmers’ party leader Caroline van der Plas on the issue last April.

“That was when these people heard they were going to get their wages, but some of them have died in the meantime,” she told Dutch News.

Stein added that the cabinet appeared to have pushed through the ruling without waiting for parliament to debate the extent of the compensation scheme first.

“We still had to talk to MPs and had asked for a committee debate, but never had a reply,” she said.

“This isn’t about care or morality, it’s purely and solely about the technical settling of a case for the lowest possible cost.”

No official records

Sterk said it was “practically impossible” to compensate relatives of former camp inmates who had died because the government had no central records, but Stein said her campaign group had compiled its own list of detainees and could provide documentation showing they worked for the colonial administration.

“I have a list, but they say the SVB [Dutch social security bank] is legally not allowed to use it,” she said. “But if they have €50 million to spend, why can’t they find other parties to distribute the money who are able to work with us?”

Stein said she was not calling for the regulation to be scrapped, but it should be backdated to 2025 or 2015, when the government first acknowledged that the POWs were in its service. Prior to that it had argued that the colonial government in Indonesia was a separate entity.

Stein said the campaigners would continue to press the cabinet to compensate all victims of the Japanese occupation, including those who were no longer alive. “We have made a promise to these elderly people, we have signed a petition, and we are going to keep fighting for it,” she said.

World.title: Body of missing woman from Amsterdam found in suitcase
World.content:
The body of a woman who went missing after taking a lift on a bike with an unknown man has been found in a suitcase in Amsterdam.

Police said the remains were discovered last Friday in the Amstel river and identified as a woman named as Hajar, who was last seen two weeks ago near the Rai conference centre.

She left in the direction of Buitenveldert on October 4 on a black ladies’ bike with a man whom police are now trying to trace.

Police would not confirm reports on AT5 that a passer-by found the suitcase containing the body on Saturday morning, or that messages were sent to local neighbourhood app groups later that day asking if people had noticed anybody acting suspiciously with a suitcase.

She is described as between 1.65m and 1.70m tall with dark curly hair and dark eyes. The day before she was last seen alive she was wearing a tiger print dress and white New Balance shoes.

Anyone who saw Hajar between October 4 and October 17 or has any information can contact police on 0900 8844, via www.politie.nl, or anonymously via 0800 7000 or at Meld Misdaad Anoniem.

World.title: How expats tackle Dutch language issues without giving away data
World.content:
A letter from the Belastingdienst has landed on the doormat, and it might as well be written in code. At work, the team meeting that began in English has drifted into Dutch, and you’re nodding along while hoping nobody asks for your opinion. Sound familiar? We spoke with OmniForge, a tech company helping expats tackle the language barrier online.

Why the usual AI tools fall short

AI assistants promise to help with both of these challenges, but they have their limits. Firstly, many recording and transcription tools only support a handful of major languages, which leaves plenty of expats working in English by default, says Daniel G. Ríos, co-founder and CEO of OmniForge. Secondly, most of them process everything in the cloud, which is less than ideal when it comes to an employment contract, payslip or document with your BSN on it.

The risk is not theoretical. When hackers posted Odido’s customer data online, millions of people were reminded how far personal data can travel. “In the best case scenario, your data might be used to profile you for ads,” Daniel says, “but in the case of data exfiltration from cloud providers, your data might also be used for nefarious purposes.”

A local alternative, built by expats

OmniForge is a privacy-first AI desktop app for macOS and Windows that transcribes meetings and answers questions about your documents, all on your own computer. It was built by a team of expats in the Netherlands who, as Daniel puts it, “experience the exact same bilingual friction our users do.”

https://omniforge.online/dutchnews

“People should not have to compromise on their personal information in order to benefit from a service,” he says. In practice, the AI engine lives on your machine rather than in a data centre. “You could disconnect your WiFi entirely, and it will still securely transcribe your meetings and analyse your documents.” Only account login and subscription management are online.

There’s an environmental upside too, Daniel argues: running AI on your own computer’s spare processing power, what he calls “Green AI at the Edge,” can avoid the electricity and cooling water that big cloud models require from data centres.

When the meeting switches language

Language is where OmniForge stands out. It transcribes audio in 25 languages, including Dutch, English, German, French, Spanish and Polish, and can write summaries and answers in around 200 languages. In other words, a meeting held in Dutch can be summarised in whichever language you read most comfortably.

Then there’s the meeting that starts in English and slides into Dutch. Other tools make you pick a language in advance, Daniel says, whereas OmniForge listens for mid-sentence switches. He admits the transcript does not always get the spoken language right, but because the summary can be generated in any supported language regardless of the input, the gist still comes through.

A typical user, he says, is an international professional in a technical project meeting where half the team defaults to Dutch. Instead of stopping the flow to ask for translations, they record locally, having the assurance that a full English summary will be waiting the moment the meeting ends.

Decoding the paperwork

The same tool works on documents, not just audio. You can drop a Dutch PDF into OmniForge, whether it’s a letter from your landlord or your VvE, a payslip or a notice from the Belastingdienst, then ask questions and get an explanation in English.

Phone calls are covered, too. If you’re talking to the gemeente, put the phone on speaker and record the conversation: even if you feel lost during the call, OmniForge transcribes it so you have a comprehensive summary to review the moment you hang up. “It takes the stress out of local administration,” is how Daniel puts it.

Built for international teams

For employers, the same features make onboarding and internal meetings more inclusive: colleagues who are not fully fluent can follow along through a summary in their preferred language. And because OmniForge records locally, there’s no bot joining your video calls. A project manager juggling several projects can also keep a workspace for each, store meetings and documents together, and ask the assistant for recaps or highlights.

Moreover, local processing represents a win for compliance: HR handles sensitive employee data, and client confidentiality is non-negotiable. Companies are increasingly wary of staff feeding sensitive information to AI chatbots, Daniel explains. “Keeping everything in-house means GDPR compliance by default.” Many cloud tools go to great lengths to get certified, he notes, “but that just means they took steps to secure their customers’ data. With OmniForge, each customer is the sole owner of their data.”

Limitations and next steps

Daniel is upfront about OmniForge’s limits. Because everything runs on your device, transcription speed depends on your hardware: a brand-new machine will get through an hour-long meeting much faster than an older laptop. The assistant is above-average at summaries, highlights and finding information in your documents, “but it cannot compete with the likes of ChatGPT or Claude in terms of raw intelligence,” Daniel concedes, since it has a fraction of the resources.

OmniForge’s next steps will focus on speeding up the models on older hardware and adding more regional dialects. A mobile version is also planned, depending on how many people adopt the app.

Try it on your next confusing letter

The best first step, Daniel says, is to try OmniForge on your next meeting or baffling Dutch letter. Paid tiers start at €9.99 per month for unlimited quotas for individual users. But there’s a generous free tier so you can try before you buy: 40 complimentary minutes per recording and 50 indexed files. All you need to do is download OmniForge for Mac or Windows for free and register.

Prime minister Rob Jetten is going to become a father next year, he announced on social media on Monday.

He and his partner, Argentinian professional hockey player Nicolás Keenan, wrote on Instagram: “Someone very special is on the way. See you in 2027, little one.”

The couple posted the message with a photo of themselves holding an ultrasound scan.

The pair also posted a picture with the baby’s surrogate mother, named as Lisa.

“There are no words big enough to thank our egg donor, our surrogate mum Lisa and both their families,” they wrote. “None of this would be possible without you.”

The message was written in Dutch, Spanish and English. A statement on the website of Jetten’s party, D66, says the surrogacy is not commercial and that Lisa and the donor, who are both Dutch, are acquaintances of Jetten and Keenan.

“I grew up in a warm and loving environment and now have a fantastic family of my own,” Lisa said in the statement. “With the unconditional support of our loved ones, surrogacy feels like a very special way to contribute to making our dear friends’ dream come true.”

World.title: England’s Dutch coach Sarina Wiegman extends contract until 2029
World.content:
Dutch football coach Sarina Wiegman has extended her contract with the England women’s team by two years, taking her up to the 2029 European Championships.

Wiegman, 56, led the team to two European titles in 2022 and 2025, as well as their first World Cup final in 2023, when they lost to Spain.

Prior to that she won the European Championships with the Dutch national team in 2017 and reached the World Cup final two years later, losing 2-0 to the United States.

“I am so happy to be able to carry on with this squad and cannot think of a better job in football,” she said in a statement released by the English Football Association (FA).

“Working for a world-class organisation like the FA, and alongside so many people dedicated to winning England teams and the growth of our game, excites me every day.”

FA chief executive Mark Bullingham described Wiegman as “an incredible coach with an unparalleled record in major tournaments”. He added: “There is no one better to lead the Lionesses into the next two tournaments.”

Commentators had widely expected the Dutchwoman to leave her post after next year’s World Cup, after England failed to qualify automatically for the tournament.

A 4-0 loss to Spain in June, the team’s heaviest defeat since Wiegman took charge, means they will have to come through a play-off tournament with Greece, Ukraine and Slovakia to reach the finals in Brazil.

Wiegman said: “Anyone who knows me will understand that my main concern right now is absolutely the World Cup, and helping this squad realise their potential in the years to come.

“We have an important job to do to confirm our place in Brazil, and hopefully we can do that and give the country another special summer to remember next year.”

World.title: Border police won’t publish Schiphol e-gate investigation
World.content:
Hundreds of people missed their flights and thousands more faced long delays at Schiphol on Sunday after all 78 of the airport’s automatic passport gates went down at around 6am.

The Royal Marechaussee, the military police force responsible for border checks, said the outage was caused by an IT malfunction and that there was “no indication whatsoever” of a cyberattack.

The exact cause is still being investigated, but the results will not be made public, Marechaussee head of press, Major Mike Hofman, told Dutch News.

“For operational reasons, we do not comment regarding the further configuration, operation and technical details of our systems,” he said.

With the e-gates down, everyone flying to or from a country outside the Schengen area had to be checked manually by hand, including passengers in transit. The Marechaussee opened every desk and carried out less thorough checks to keep the queues moving.

Passengers waited an hour on average, and some waited up to an hour and a half, Schiphol officials said. The gates were working again by around 3pm.

KLM held departures where possible, and Transavia said it would be flexible with rebookings. A claims specialist told the Telegraaf the number of people affected in some way could run into the tens of thousands.

Few are likely to receive compensation, experts told the paper, because the outage will probably count as force majeure since the e-gates are run by the Marechaussee, not the airlines. The Marechaussee said travellers who missed their flights should contact their airline.

The outage happened during one of the busiest weekends of the autumn, as the one-week October school holiday began in the middle and south of the country and ended in the north. The Amsterdam marathon on Sunday also attracted thousands of runners to the city from all over the world.

World.title: Police investigate Grolsch beer tasting contamination
World.content:
Eleven people fell ill on Saturday afternoon after tasting water during a tour of the Grolsch brewery in Enschede. The water may have been contaminated with caustic soda, according to local broadcaster RTV Oost.

The group of nine visitors and two guides had been given shot glasses of the spring water used to brew the beer, a tasting that has been part of the tour for years.

One of the victims told RTV Oost that several people noticed a strange, sour taste and a burning feeling in their stomach after drinking it. Members of the group became nauseous and vomited, and the broadcaster said they may have suffered internal burns to the throat, oesophagus and stomach.

Several ambulances went to the brewery, and a German trauma team was called out but turned out not to be needed. All 11 were out of hospital on Sunday, and one spent the night in hospital, Grolsch told public broadcaster NOS.

Police have started a forensic investigation, and the labour inspectorate is also investigating. A police spokesperson told NOS it could have been an accident, “or something else could be going on”.

Grolsch said the tap the group drank from is separate from the rest of the production process, and that the quality and safety of its beer “are not and have not been at risk”. The company said it would not comment on possible causes while the investigation is ongoing.

World.title: Poland breaks up international criminal group accused of laundering €77 million
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Poland says it has broken up an international criminal group responsible for laundering an estimated 337 million zloty (€77 million) by using currency exchange offices to illegally process money obtained from internet scams. Nine suspects – eight Ukrainians and one Belarusian – have been detained in a series of raids, which also resulted in the seizure of gold and cash worth over 1 million zloty. Służby rozbiły międzynarodową grupę zajmującą się praniem pieniędzy z oszustw inwestycyjnych i kryptowalut. Zatrzymano 9 osób, a skala transakcji przekroczyła 337 mln zł. Zabezpieczono złoto i gotówkę wartą ponad 1 mln zł. @Straz_Graniczna @PolicjaCBZC @ABW_GOV_PL pic.twitter.com/g2NQoqaPvP — Marcin Kierwiński (@MKierwinski) October 19, 2026 The accused – four women and five men aged between 26 and 53 – were arrested in Łódź, Warsaw and Małopolska province, announced Krzysztof Kopania, spokesman for the Łódź regional prosecutor’s office, which is leading the investigation. The detainees are four female cashiers, three men running the exchange offices, and two couriers used to transport money. All have been charged with participating in an organised criminal group and money laundering. They could face up to 15 years in prison if convicted. Prosecutors say that the gang, which operated in the cities of Warsaw, Lublin, Wrocław, Katowice and Gdańsk, collected money that had been obtained through internet fraud and transported it to cryptocurrency exchanges. It was then processed without complying with anti-money laundering procedures. Proceeds were then transferred to bank accounts, sent abroad by car, or concealed in fictitious purchases of gold. Most money was ultimately invested in cryptocurrencies. “The scale of the operation was enormous,” said Kopania. “It is estimated that between February 2025 and July 2026, members of the group took steps to conceal the origins of approximately 337 million zloty.” The ringleader was a 34-year-old Ukrainian national who made the key decisions and oversaw the domestic and international channelling of funds obtained from illegal sources, according to the Internal Security Agency (ABW) and border guard, which were also involved in the operation. Seven of the accused have been placed in pre-trial detention for three (or in one case two) months, while two have been bailed and ordered not to leave Poland. World.title: Lithuania says Ukrainian drone that struck car entered its airspace from Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. This article has been updated to include a statement from Poland’s defence ministry issued on Monday afternoon. Lithuania says there is “no doubt” that a Ukrainian drone which exploded on its territory on Sunday, hitting a moving car, entered its airspace from Poland. However, Poland has so far said that there is no confirmation of an object crossing the border. Meanwhile, Ukraine has apologised for the incident, saying that Russian electronic warfare had diverted the drone’s path during an operation against military targets in Russia. Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and EU. This morning, NATO fighter jets stationed at Šiauliai Air Base scrambled once again after an unidentified object entered Lithuanian airspace. What appears to be a drone exploded… — Gitanas Nausėda (@GitanasNauseda) October 18, 2026 On Sunday morning, Lithuania confirmed that a drone had entered its airspace and exploded, causing damage to a moving vehicle. NATO jets were scrambled in response to the incursion but were not able to visually identify the object. President Gitanas Nausėda said that the incident was further evidence that “Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine is spilling over onto the Eastern flank of NATO and [the] EU”. Meanwhile, Lithuanian defence minister Robertas Kaunas revealed that preliminary information indicated the drone had entered from Polish airspace. “I have already contacted the Polish defence minister and asked Poland to join the investigation so that we can look into this incident together,” said Kaunas, quoted by broadcaster LRT. However, a spokesman for Poland’s defence ministry, Janusz Sejmej, told the Polish Press Agency (PAP) on Sunday that “there is no confirmation [from our radar systems] of [an object] crossing the border from Poland to Lithuania”. Polsat, a leading Polish broadcaster, cited unnamed sources at Poland’s defence ministry saying that they believed the drone in fact took off from within Lithuanian territory, around 30 kilometres from the Polish border, and then flew deep into the country. In response, Deividas Matulionis, an advisor to the Lithuanian president, told the Baltic News Service (BNS) on Monday that “I can say very unequivocally we have credible evidence that the drone crossed the Polish border”. Later, the country’s prime minister, Mindaugas Sinkevičius, said that “there is no doubt that it entered…from the Polish side”. He also confirmed that the evidence indicates the drone “is of Ukrainian origin”. We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia. We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have… — Heorhii Tykhyi (@SpoxUkraineMFA) October 18, 2026 Those remarks followed a statement on Sunday afternoon from Heorhii Tykhyi, the spokesman for Ukraine’s foreign ministry, who appeared to confirm that the drone was Ukrainian. “We regret the incident that occurred this morning in Lithuanian airspace, which may have resulted from Russian electronic warfare diverting drones during an operation against legitimate military targets in Russia,” wrote Tykhyi. “We apologise for any disruption, risks, and concern this may have caused.” The spokesman said that Ukraine would “share all relevant information with our Lithuanian partners to establish the full circumstances of the incident”. However, he gave no further information on what type of drone was involved, where it was launched from, and what its target was. Lithuania borders Belarus, an ally of Russia, and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, as well as Poland and Latvia. In March and May this year, a number of Ukrainian drones aimed at targets in Russia entered the airspaces of NATO members Lithuania, Latvia, Estonia and Finland, likely due to Russian electronic jamming. On Monday afternoon, Poland’s defence ministry issued a statement “strongly refuting” media reports suggesting that sources within the ministry had identified the drone as having taken off within Lithuania itself. It added that the ministry, in cooperation with its Lithuanian partners, was still “conducting a detailed analysis” of what had taken place. Poland has condemned an attack by masked Israeli settlers on a delegation of European diplomats – including Polish ones – that was visiting the West Bank. It called for a “decisive response from the Israeli authorities”, saying that the incident is “further evidence of the settler violence that the Palestinian population in the West Bank faces on a daily basis”. The attack has likewise been condemned by France and Belgium, whose nationals were also in the delegation, and the European Union, as well as by the Israeli foreign minister. Masked Israeli settlers attacked European diplomats, a French mayor and Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, prompting European condemnation. The violence comes amid unprecedented settler pogroms during the olive harvest. pic.twitter.com/wsP6edL62y — Al Jazeera English (@AJEnglish) October 18, 2026 On Saturday, the delegation – which included members from France, Belgium and Poland as well as representatives of the Catholic church – visited the mostly Christian Palestinian village of Taybeh near Ramallah in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. They had come to assess the situation following regular recent attacks by Israeli settlers on Palestinians trying to harvest olives on their own land. During the visit, the delegation came under attack, with parts of the incident caught on camera. France’s foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, reported that Bernard Baudoux, mayor of Aulnoye-Aymeries in northern France, had been “violently assaulted” during the incident. He demanded that Israel arrest the perpetrators and “urgently put an end to these criminal acts of violence”. Late on Saturday afternoon, the spokesman for Poland’s foreign ministry, Maciej Wewiór, issued a statement confirming that the attack had taken place and that the delegation had included an unspecified number of Polish diplomats, who he said had not been harmed. “We express our deep outrage and strongly condemn this incident,” added Wewiór. “Poland consistently opposes violence by Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank. Attacks on representatives of the diplomatic corps are absolutely unacceptable.” The spokesman said that Poland now “expects urgent and detailed explanations from the Israeli authorities” and for the perpetrators of the attack to be identified and held accountable. “We also expect effective measures to prevent similar incidents in the future.” ❗Potwierdzamy, że na Zachodnim Brzegu Jordanu doszło do ataku na konwój, w którym znajdowali się przedstawiciele korpusu dyplomatycznego, w tym polscy dyplomaci. Według wstępnych informacji za atak mogą odpowiadać izraelscy osadnicy. Polskim dyplomatom nic się nie stało. Z… — Rzecznik MSZ – Maciej Wewiór (@RzecznikMSZ) October 17, 2026 On Sunday, Poland’s foreign ministry issued a further statement in which it “condemned the attack by masked settlers…during a solidarity visit to a town known for its centuries-old Christian presence”. The incident “is further evidence of the settler violence that the Palestinian population in the West Bank faces on a daily basis”, they added, calling for a “decisive response from the Israeli authorities”. The attack was also “strongly condemned” on Sunday by the European Union’s diplomatic service, which said that it “expects full accountability as well as effective measures to prevent continued acts of violence and violent harassment against Palestinians”. Belgium’s foreign minister, Maxime Prevot, said that his country would continue to “press for EU sanctions against those responsible for this violence and those who support them”. 🇵🇸 I condemn in the strongest terms the attack by masked settlers in Taybeh, in the occupied West Bank, against Palestinians, our Consul General, French and Polish diplomats as well as catholic representatives. A French mayor was assaulted and a Belgian vehicle damaged. Our team… — Maxime PREVOT (@prevotmaxime) October 17, 2026 In the wake of the incident, Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu had urged people to show “caution before drawing conclusions” over what had happened. He claimed that there is “a coordinated campaign to smear Israel and the Jewish residents” of the West Bank. However, the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) said that it “strongly condemns the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters”. But it added that “the consulate’s visit was not coordinated with the IDF”, which is “important to prevent incidents of this kind”. Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, also issued a condemnation of the attack and said that police had opened an investigation. The IDF strongly condemns the severe act of violence that took place in the area of Taybeh, during which diplomatic representatives were attacked by Israeli rioters. Police forces and forensic investigators from the Judea and Samaria District are entering the area accompanied by… — Israel Defense Forces (@IDF) October 17, 2026 The incident involving the diplomatic group came a day after around 80 Israeli settlers had attacked Palestinians harvesting olives, with Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine among those injured. Levine told the Committee to Protect Journalists, an American non-profit organisation, that she had been pushed to the ground by a group of masked settlers, who “were kicking me for I think at least 10 minutes”. That incident prompted criticism of Israel from the United States, whose ambassador, Mike Huckabee, called it a “despicable act of terror carried out by masked cowards”. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, said he was “disturbed” by the incident and confirmed that “we’ve asked the Israelis to crack down on that”. .@SecRubio on reporter Heidi Levine being attacked in the West Bank: "We're very disturbed by those images and what we're seeing….the President has been very clear, he's said this repeatedly, he does not want to see friction or crisis going on in the West Bank." pic.twitter.com/Xg10vteeXK — CSPAN (@cspan) October 18, 2026 In August this year, Poland summoned Israel’s ambassador to express its “great disappointment” that the IDF had discontinued an investigation into the strikes on an aid convoy in Gaza in 2024 that killed seven humanitarian workers, including a Pole, Damian Soból. In May, Poland issued a five-year entry ban on Israeli national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir for his treatment of detained activists, including Polish citizens, from a flotilla seeking to reach Gaza. Last year, Israel criticised Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, after he suggested that Israeli politicians are causing the starvation of mothers and children in Gaza. The Israeli foreign ministry called the remarks “unacceptable” and urged Tusk to “remember the lessons” of the Holocaust. World.title: Poland moves to allow more municipalities to charge tourist fee
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Many more municipalities in Poland will be allowed to charge a daily fee for tourists and other overnight visitors after a change to the law dropping environmental requirements for levying such charges. Kraków, which received 8.7 million overnight tourists last year, had in particular been pushing for the change. However, Poland as a whole has seen a recent boom in visitor numbers, recording the EU’s second-fastest growth in the number of nights in tourist accommodation last year. #Krakow #opłataturystyczna #ustawa 🚨🔥Z OSTATNIEJ CHWILI! 🔥🚨 📢 Prezydent RP podpisał nowelizację przepisów dotyczących podatków i opłat lokalnych, PIT oraz PCC. 🏨 Najważniejsze zmiany dla branży turystycznej dotyczą opłaty miejscowej i uzdrowiskowej. 🗓️ Od 2027 r. za jej… pic.twitter.com/9ATvENvNol — Kraków (@krakow_pl) October 15, 2026 Until now, a “visitor’s fee” could be levied by municipalities with beneficial climatic features, “scenic qualities” and the capacity to accommodate people visiting to benefit from these attributes, as well as localities in areas with the status of a “spa protection area”. In practice, this largely applied to seaside and mountain resorts. Kraków did charge a visitor’s fee between 2004 and 2015, but was subsequently unable to do so due to a toughening of environmental requirements. The city has long suffered from bad air pollution, though it has taken significant steps to tackle the issue. Now, under new legislation proposed by the government earlier this year and signed into law by President Karol Nawrocki this week, the requirement for beneficial climatic features has been scrapped, meaning many more places will be able to charge the visitor’s fee. From 1 January, municipalities with scenic qualities will be able to charge visitors up to 5 zloty (€1.14) for each night they stay in hotels, guesthouses and short-term rental accommodation for up to one month, a rise on the current maximum of 3.46 zloty. Additionally, whereas previously only people visiting for the purposes of tourism had to pay, the fee now applies to all visits, including for work or health purposes, reports broadcaster TVN. People with significant disabilities, children with certified disabilities and their carers will be exempt from the fee. In another change, fees will be collected directly by accommodation providers, who will be required to maintain detailed records, reports the Infor news service. Passing fees on in a timely manner will entitle providers to receive at least 10% of the money they collect. Poland saw the EU's second-fastest growth in tourism in 2025, behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta https://t.co/WVkRbHtU7o — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) January 19, 2026 In 2024, Kraków appealed to the government to be allowed to charge tourists a fee, noting that “overtourism leads to tensions and social discontent”, as the “local community suffers” and “residents increasingly feel like tourists in their own city”. With its UNESCO-listed Old Town, Wawel royal castle, and former Jewish district of Kazimierz, Kraków is regularly named as one of Europe’s best tourist destinations. Last year, a record 16.25 million people visited the city, of whom 8.7 million stayed overnight. While that is a boon to the local economy, it also often causes tensions with residents, who complain about noise and disruption. In 2024, the city created the new position of “night mayor”, whose role is to reconcile the needs of tourists, businesses and residents. Poland’s government has approved legislation that would allow local communities to ban short-term rentals of the type offered through services such as Airbnb. Such accommodation has boomed in recent years, often prompting a backlash from local residents https://t.co/8MRfRWTDxd — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 3, 2026 Following this week’s change to the law, Kraków city hall confirmed that it would now again be able to collect a visitor’s fee “if the statutory conditions are satisfied and the municipal council adopts an appropriate resolution”. The city’s recently elected new mayor, Łukasz Gibała, who will be sworn in next week, said before Sunday’s election that he was in favour of a tourist tax of at least 20 zloty per night, four times the new maximum. “In western European cities there are rates of that size and higher,” Gibała said, quoted by financial news service Money.pl. “Maintaining the city in the face of the influx of tourists is costly. In Kraków, private business owners profit from tourism, whilst the city and its residents foot the bill.” Poland as a whole has also experienced a boom in tourism. Last year, the country recorded the European Union’s second-largest growth in the number of nights spent in tourist accommodation. Its increase of 7% was behind only the Mediterranean island state of Malta (9.9%). World.title: Poland drops proposal to criminalise providing help to illegal migrants following outcry
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
