World.title: Doha diary: A historian amid the Iran war
World.content:
(Renowned historian and author, Rila Mukherjee, was scheduled to fly from the USA to India by Qatar Airways [QA] on February 25, 2026. Her route—Shreveport–Dallas Fort Worth–Doha–Kolkata—was expected to bring her to Kolkata on the night of February 26 or in the early hours of February 27. However, as of March 8, she was still stranded in Doha. Qatar’s skies were closed due to the US-Israeli attack on Iran. QA’s commercial flights were suspended. At the time of writing, evacuation flights to India were scheduled to start soon. She reached home on 12 March.)

Today is 8 March. I am now camping out in Doha for the ninth day since 28 February. The Qatar airspace is shut and padlocked. The authorities have thrown away the key. Limited numbers of passengers are being flown to Europe and the Americas on evacuation flights (they are called ‘relief flights’) organised by QA, and relief flights to Africa and Asia will start from tomorrow. But for the time being, I am effectively marooned in Doha.

Doha is one of the largest airplane hubs in the world, and a cosmopolitan group of transit passengers has been put up by QA in the 4-star The Royal Riviera Hotel. The hotel is situated on Doha’s Corniche. It is an ageing hotel; not terribly posh, and the plumbing is a bit iffy. But it is well located, with comfortable rooms, and it is a clean and friendly hotel. I feel safe here. Its staff is composed of Asians (from Bangladesh, the Philippines, Sri Lanka, Nepal), North Africans (Algerians and Moroccans mostly) and some West Asians. All of them are helpful despite the pressures they are facing. They deal gracefully with the diverse demands and complaints of the passengers.

My room faces the Corniche and I can see the Persian Gulf from my window. As a maritime historian, this makes me very happy.

This country and its national airline are looking after us very well and, really, I have no complaints. QA’s representatives visit the hotel twice daily. There is no information forthcoming on my evacuation to Kolkata, and the greater part of passenger bags are still to arrive at the hotel. My South African neighbour says one of their bags has not been delivered; perhaps it is lost.

We are largely dependent on the clothes we have on our backs and those we had in our carry-on. Most of us are washing and drying them overnight. We have to use the hair dryer if they are still not dry.

My bags came in today, i.e., 8 March.

There are some elderly travellers. Many of them say that their medicines are running out. Mine will last another week.

Will I be able to get out by then?

We are told that a limited air corridor may open today; alternatively, we may be evacuated by the land route through Saudi Arabia to Riyadh (this would take around seven hours), where a leased QA aircraft may take us to India. But we have to make our own arrangements for the Saudi e-visa and overland travel. This seems a risky enterprise. And whether this potential leased aircraft would fly me direct to Kolkata is not known. There is no clarity to date.

***

But if I was scheduled to arrive in Kolkata on 27 February (and the war broke out a day later, on 28 February), how is it that I am still in Doha

Ah, thereby hangs a tale!

It is a cautionary tale on buying air tickets with multiple connections, and what ensues when the first connection does not take off as per schedule.

***

I had spent nine weeks in Shreveport with my son and daughter-in-law and was scheduled to leave on 25 February. Unfortunately, my flight from Shreveport to Dallas Fort Worth (DFW) by QA’s codeshare partner American Airlines (AA) did not take off. We were told that the incoming flight had nose gear problems and therefore could not land. Ultimately it made an emergency landing. Fire engines, firefighters, EMTs and ambulances were standing by. Luckily, there was no fireball and there were no casualties. The vice-chair of my daughter-in-law’s department was on that flight; I bumped into him in the terminal as he deplaned, and he said that the landing had been really scary.

There were no more AA flights to DFW that day. Roo and Stephanie came back to the airport and took me home. I spent a restless night. I hate flying at the best of times.

I was put on the same AA flight the next day, on 26 February, but when I reached DFW I was told that my connection flight to Doha was full. Apparently, the AA staff at Shreveport Regional Airport knew there were no seats on that flight; nevertheless they sent me on to DFW hoping I would ‘sort out’ the matter with AA’s customer care there. The only ‘sorting out’ that AA did at DFW was to put me on a later QA flight to Doha on the same day, that is, late evening on 26 February. It was a smaller aircraft (not the Airbus 350 on which I was ticketed), the flight was cramped and some of my co-passengers were not very well behaved. One lady kept on drinking; she skipped the meal service and was quite abusive. Another one, African American, told me that as an ‘American’ she was superior to Asians. Right, I thought, we all know how you as a Black person got there!!!

In all my years of travelling I have never encountered such blatant racism.

When we reached Doha very late on the night of 27 February (almost 24 hours later due to the time difference with DFW), I had missed that evening’s flight to Kolkata!

No problem, QA’s customer care said, we’ll talk with AA as it is their problem. This took a while, so I went off to buy myself a snack at Brioche Dorée in the airport’s food court.

By then it was early morning on 28 February.

Readers, note the date!

***

AA agreed to comp me a room for the remainder of the night at The Royal Riviera Hotel. I was granted a 48-hour emergency visa by Qatar Immigration and I was shifted to the hotel on 28 February at 2 AM. QA’s ground staff helped me throughout. The room was comfortable, the bed looked inviting, and I went to sleep, confident that my Kolkata flight would take off as scheduled at 18.45 hours on that day itself (that is, 28 February). At that point, I was going to reach only 24 hours behind my original schedule.

I informed Kolkata and asked my driver to collect me from the airport accordingly.

***

On 28 February, I was woken around 8 AM by a strange sound from my cell phone. It was a very loud, continuous screech. I don’t have international roaming and I wondered who was calling me and what was happening. I saw a ‘Security Alert’ on my screen but the text was in Arabic. I started hearing thuds and bangs. Another alert, still in Arabic, came in.

What was going on? I was mystified.

I was now getting alerts in English. It said the US and Israel had jointly attacked Iran. US bases and embassies and consulates across the Gulf were vulnerable. Qatar was in this critical area. Sirens were going off. I started watching Al Jazeera and Richard Engel on NBC.

This was Day 1.

Smoke rises following an explosion, after Israel and the US launched strikes on Iran, in Tehran, Iran, February 28, 2026. PHOTO: REUTERS

By Day 2, the Gulf was not just lying in a war zone; it had been converted into a theatre of war. Doha was undergoing regular drone strikes and missile attacks.

Day 3 was relatively quiet. Apparently, Qatar and Iran had a phone conversation, and Qatar urged Iran to stop the strikes. But our temporary visas were extended by Qatar. This was an indication that the phone call was not conclusive. This war was not going to end anytime soon.

The Qatar–Iran conversation does not seem to have yielded the desired result. There is no relief from Iranian attacks. These now form the backdrop to our daily life at The Royal Riviera. Drone attacks and missile strikes re-started from Day 4. None of them target the downtown area; they target only the US base and industrial areas in Qatar. Most of the drones and missiles are successfully intercepted; the few that are not cause localised fires. The attacks usually happen around breakfast and lunch, and sometimes they occur very late at night or in the early morning hours. This means we are always in a state of extreme alert. It is jarring on the nerves. We can neither eat properly nor rest. We are getting stressed out.

But I must also mention that the attacks and interceptions sound more like Diwali patakas than the very loud explosions that one expects.

*** Days 4 till 9 (that is, till date) have seen this regional war extending from land to sea: from the Hormuz Strait to the Indian Ocean. This is now becoming very serious. Critical choke points like this strait have become a curse. Ports across the Gulf are lying idle; almost no cargo is getting through. But we have had no alerts today. Does this mean that Iran will not strike Qatar for the time being? Is this a temporary reprieve? Will relief flights be able to take off? ***

Some bags arrived at the hotel on Day 5. Mine were not among them.

By Days 6 and 7 we have more or less settled into what is turning out to be our semi-permanent home. The hotel is no longer very ‘royal’; it has taken on the character of a London bedsit. Or a council housing estate in one of the UK’s inner cities! Children play noisy games in the corridors, an oddly comforting sound among the explosions, security alerts and sirens that go on regularly.

I see an enormous solidarity among the travellers, both on my floor and when we meet up at meal times. I have a very nice South African couple next door who check on me each morning, always asking how I am faring (‘please don’t hesitate to knock if you face any difficulties’). They have even offered to take me out to buy clothes (this was before my bags arrived). Elegant MENA (Middle East North Africa) people greet me each day at breakfast, a young Pakistani financial analyst from Toronto shares his insights with me at the breakfast table, and a British couple advise me to carry my passport with me at all times (especially when I leave my room in case of an attack and subsequent fire). They kindly offered to buy me my medicines, although they are at least a decade older than me. A young school teacher from Geneva shares my table at dinner. I have not seen her lately; perhaps she has already been repatriated on one of the relief flights to Europe which started operating from Day 7. The British couple and the South Africans are still here; the Pakistani man left for Toronto early this morning. He was given only two hours’ notice and he phoned my room to say goodbye at 1.15 AM this morning.

***

What does my daily schedule look like?

It is like what I imagine a day at boarding school would be. Because it is Ramadan, the hotel starts the breakfast buffet from 3 AM, lunch is from 12 noon, and dinner is over by 7.30. The food served (although mild in taste and quasi-institutional as regards the daily menu, which does not rotate much in terms of items), is nevertheless amazingly varied as regards the cuisine: Arabic, Turkish, Italian, Spanish and South Asian (the last is not good at all). A lot of lemon is used in the preparations, but practically no onions. This may be due to the fact that there was an onion shortage; onions came in from India only on Day 5. There are loads of different kinds of salads, some bland European cheeses and diverse types of hummus. In addition, there is feta cheese, stuffed vine leaves, green and black olives, veg and non-veg samosas and spring rolls, koftas, and baba ghanoush or baingan bharta. Good cappuccinos and lattes. Flaky croissants and brioches, pastries and amazing Arabian/Persian/Yemeni sweets. A decadent baked (and often caramelised) bread pudding called Umm Ali is served at dinner. Obviously, the Qatari supermarkets are still well-stocked with FMCG. The Indian-origin Lulu supermarket chain has flown in a whole lot of perishable and non-perishable food items.

Strangely, no fresh fruit!

***

Gas prices have shot up.

I have given up watching the death and destruction on TV, and watch Looney Tunes, Anthony Bourdain, Fawlty Towers and Mr Bean instead. Priyam Paul, my editor at The Daily Star, has sent me some e-books which help to pass the time.

When I am not reading, or watching sitcoms, cartoons and travel and food documentaries, I reflect on what brought us to this war. I see the Persian Gulf from my room; it is still a brilliant blue. But it is also desolate since the Hormuz Strait was closed off. I see no cargo ships or container vessels; there are no cruise ships or tankers. For a maritime historian like me, this is not the Persian Gulf I know. After all, it has been a crossroads since recorded history! My India in the Indian Ocean World (2022) documents this history of two thousand years at the very least. Now, mobility is severely constrained.

Persian Gulf. Photo: Collected

We are living now in a world of fragmented geopolitics, of accelerated climate degradation, and of critical demographic shifts. The world is undergoing these changes along with increasingly disaffected groups of peoples, perhaps terrorists, some of them. We are seeing the rise of AI which, to my mind, is linked, along with the toxicity of social media, with the increasing authoritarianism that we see worldwide. It horrifies me when I see a young nation declare it will bring ‘civilisation’ to Iran. It disregards the fact that Iran-as-Persia predates Arab culture and is one of the world’s oldest culture areas. Not just the glory of Shi’ite Safavid Persia (1501–1736), which political theorists and analysts invoke when describing this civilisational space and whose heritage modern Iran draws on: think of the period from c. 550 BCE to 651 CE (Muslim conquest and start of Islamisation by the Rashidun Caliphate), when four mighty Persian empires ruled a large portion of the then-known world: Achaemenid, Seleucid, Parthian and Sassanian. Persia challenged Egypt, Greece and Rome, and then it faced up to the Ottoman and Russian empires. This memory of resistance of 2500 years will not be easily erased.

However, the total disregard of international law and the collapse of the rules-based order will usher in a new regional order in West Asia. This will impact on the Gulf states. Once-biblical Lebanon is almost destroyed by a rampant Israel. Syria has closed its borders. As a rogue USA intimidates Persia and trains its eye on the Caucasus and Azerbaijan, it also destabilises Iraq. Iranian Kurds based in Iraq have been reactivated. How will this impact on the Turkish Kurds? Turkey, a NATO country, is already feeling threatened.

The relatively young post-WW1 statelets in the Gulf will lose out in the violent reshuffle in the greater region. The Dubai story was already over. And Oman had lost its sheen even earlier. Financial and service centres will shift eastward—to Singapore or perhaps to KL. As will global airline hubs. The Gulf states will see their importance in location, business and finance diminish. They will have to reconsider their dependence on the USA which has now become a double-edged sword. Iran will endure, but perhaps in a new form. But it will not be erased from the map of the world.

World.title: André Béteille: A sociologist Bangladesh should read
World.content:
My first encounter with the ideas of Professor André Béteille was in July 1966 in an introductory sociology course at the University of Dhaka (at that time in East Pakistan) through Professor Tom Bottomore’s book, Sociology: A Guide to Problems and Literature (1962). The emphasis on general theory of social stratification for an explanation of the Indian caste system found its empirical reflection, as Bottomore refers to, in the work of Béteille, especially in Caste, Class and Power: Changing Patterns of Stratification in a Tanjore Village (1965).

My second encounter with him was in the Fall of 1975 at Dalhousie University, Halifax where I was writing my Master’s thesis under Professor Bottomore, and he referred to read me Béteille’s “Closed and open social stratification” (1966). Reading Béteille after nine years under the Maple tree, I began to admire his empirical depth, comparative methodology, and theoretical clarity, which reshaped my understanding of social hierarchies in India.

In the Christmas of 1976, I had an occasion to share some of my understanding of Béteille’s work. At that time, I was at York University, Toronto where I was doing my PhD. Professor K. Ishwaran, one of our faculty members, who wrote Tradition and Economy in Village India (1966), invited me for Christmas dinner-- Turkey with cranberry sauce, cooked by his Dutch wife. There we talked about the contribution of both Béteille and his supervisor M. N. Srinivas towards understanding the impact of social change on Indian social stratification.

In order to realistically understand contemporary caste hierarchy, Béteille emphasised the “other factors such as class and power” that “have to be considered as independent variables” (1966). It appeared to me highly useful for comparative empirical research. It creates a distance from traditional essentialist and ideological perspective of inequality.

Borrowed from Max Weber, he focused on multidimensionality of stratification and examined how status, economic resources, and political control interact to shape multifarious social order. This was a tremendous contribution in the field of stratification studies. Though he focused on rural stratification, the model is also applicable to the study of urban social stratification.

It is puzzling that in Bangladesh universities, both sociology and anthropology disciplines overlooked and neglected the Weberian model of multidimensional stratification system: anthropology remained spell-bound under the dichotomous model of rural “ashraf-atraf”; and sociology was locked in the iron cage of simplistic Marxist model of “land ownership” under the name of peasant studies. In spite of teaching Weber’s “Class, Status, Party” (1922/1946) in the universities, there is a marked absence of the application of Weberian model in the study of rural and urban complex social hierarchy. Probably in Bangladesh, this shows the intellectual bankruptcy of these disciplines, which are suffering from morbidity.

In fact, in order to understand contemporary social change in Bangladesh, especially its regime of accumulation under crony capitalism, it is essential to understand the nexus between power and class. The determining power of traditional property ownership in the formation of classes and consequent class consciousness has diminished in Bangladesh.

The notion of political capitalism advanced by Max Weber is also useful in understanding Bangladesh social stratification, especially class formation. The party consciousness along with ruling party affiliation, may give legitimate or illegitimate access to economic resources, thereby determining class position in terms of life opportunities and life style. This in turn, heavily influence commodification of prestige and honour; and becomes marker of status.

André Beteille (1934 - 2026). Photo: Collected

The rural and urban dispossession, which is an integral part of neoliberal and crony capitalism’s regime of accumulation, is also the progenitor of emergent lumpen bourgeoisie, whose class position do not correspond with their demeaning status position. Again, the traditional status group in Bangladesh, as Béteille found in his Tanjore village study with respect to traditional caste, suffer from status dislocation, having less access to power and economic resources. The ontology of inequality and hierarchy can best be understood by the Weberian epistemology.

I think study of this process of social change, and its impact on inequality in Bangladesh, is vital towards understanding Bangladesh society. The internationally acclaimed Indian empirical model provided by Béteille can be one of the best guides to study the intersectionality of class, status and power in both urban and rural Bangladesh. It is unfortunate that social sciences in Bangladesh have neglected such a significant social dynamic that affects all our lives.

In March 1989, Professor Abhijit Dasgupta, a colleague of Professor Béteille, facilitated my direct meeting with him. Professor Dasgupta was kind enough to arrange a seminar talk by me in the sociology department of Delhi School of Economics. After the seminar, I paid a visit to Professor Béteille’s office room. He was very warm and hospitable to offer tea to me and my wife. He spoke in Bangla and affirmed his Bangali origin. I felt very comfortable to have a vibe of Bengal. I mentioned to him how I came to know of his work à la Bottomore and Ishwaran. I was so surprised to experience his stock of knowledge mediated by modesty and simplicity. The meeting with professor Béteille during the short-lived spring of Delhi was one of the most memorable events of my life. I wish his conceptual and methodological clarity inspire the young Bangladeshi sociologists to break the chain of ignorance, myopic framework, and the hegemony of intellectual infantilism.

A.I. Mahbub Uddin Ahmed is a professor in the Department of Sociology at the University of Dhaka.

World.title: In praise of Mymensingh’s Bangla folk ballads
World.content:
Folk-ballads are living archives that represent the imagination, values, ideas, and aesthetics of the people to whom they belong. Bangla literature has a rich repertoire of folk ballads. We are, however, quite oblivious of this treasure trove and, therefore, there is a dearth of research on these folk elements.

Czech Indologist Dusan Zbavitel's Bengali Folk-Ballads From Mymensingh And The Problem Of Their Authenticity can be called a wonderful exception in this regard. It is considered to be the first literary study of the beautiful folk-ballads from Mymensingh. The study was published by the University of Calcutta in 1963.

A brief background of the book may not be irrelevant here. In 1923, Rai Bahadur Dineshchandra Sen edited a volume of epic songs from the Mymensingh District of the then Eastern Bengal under the title Maimansimha-gitika. The ballads were mainly collected by Chandra Kumar De, a literary activist from the area. In the following years, Dineshchandra published three more volumes of balladic texts containing epic songs from different parts of Eastern Bengal. The beautiful ballads received enthusiastic response and admiration in India and abroad. However, for some scholars these ballads were too good, and they shared doubts about the ‍antiquity, authenticity and folk character of these lores. Dusan Zbavitel found this uncertainty "highly regrettable" and undertook a study to assign to the ballads their proper place—"one of the high points of Bengali literature". Dr Zbavitel tried to find out: "what is it that makes them so excellent?"

Zbavitel confined his analysis to the study of the ballads originating in Mymensingh—41 ballads containing more than 21,000 verses. He took an arduous effort of analysing each of these 41 ballads to prove their originality and, I must say, he achieved his goal with marked success.

One key argument put forward by Zbavitel in favour of the originality of the gitikas from Mymensingh is that these ballads are not collected by a single person and, still, there are similarities among the ballads: identical images, and similar artistic approach and common inventory of similes and metaphors. So these ballads couldn't be the creation of a modern poet as suggested by some detractors.

According to Zbavitel, the most significant aspect of these folk ballads is that they are devoid of any religious implications. They generally show harmonious co-existence of the Hindu and Muslim communities, without religious bias on either side. Zbavitel points out the fact that most of the Hindu ballads were collected from Muslim singers, which shows, according to him, that these folk poems were enjoyed and appreciated by both the communities with the same eagerness. The secular outlook of the folk ballads is diametrically opposite to the explicit religious connotation of the classical Bangla literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas and Vaisnava literature.

Zbavitel extensively discusses the ideological and artistic approach of the ballad writers, verse and rhyme technique, and use of similes and metaphors in chapter three and four of the book. The most dominant motif, according to Zbavitel, is love. Even the historical and heroic epics can be grouped into this category.

As to the literary techniques, the ballad writers, being true to the characteristics of folk epics, do not try to introduce innovations in their lyrical dictions. They are content with the poetic means offered by their predecessors. They want to tell an interesting and touching story in a simple garb, fresh with country scenes and feelings.

Zbavitel also discusses the manner of preservation of the folk ballads—preserved, in most cases, in torsos. Referring to two versions of the same ballad, Maishal Bandhu, he argues, "The 'original' ballads [were] sometimes rewritten by another folk poet, or other poets, quite freely, without any scruples; whole portions, as well as individual couplets and verses, were taken over, others were replaced by newly replaced passages, and the story itself was often changed." The reasons behind such changes, according to Zbavitel, might be an effort to offer listeners a 'better' story than the original one.

Due to this oral nature of preservation, it is always difficult to prove the originality of folk elements. If we undertake an effort to study the folklore of Bangladesh, Zbavitel's book will be an invaluable companion guide.

Rabindranath Tagore wrote to Dinesh Chandra Sen in appreciation of the book Maimansimha-gitika, "Classical Bengali literary texts such as Mangal-kavyas are ponds dug on by order and at the expense of the rich, but Maimansimha-gitika is a source of exuberance from the deepest level of the heart of rural Bengal, a clear stream of genuine pain. There has never been such a creation of self-forgetting rasa [aesthetic joy] in Bengali literature." [translation by the author]

While celebrating the Bengali new year this Pohela Boishakh, may we remember the melody and the essence of communal harmony embedded in Maimansimha-gitika.

Shamsuddoza Sajen is a journalist and researcher. He can be contacted at [email protected].

World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Japan considering paper-digital hybrid textbooks as standard
World.content:
The education ministry plans to adopt a paper-digital hybrid format as the standard for textbooks in elementary, junior high and high schools from fiscal 2030, sources familiar with the matter said Monday.

The plan calls for placing more emphasis on paper-based materials while giving a supplementary role to digital materials.

The ministry will present the plan as a draft of the education minister’s guidelines on school textbooks to a meeting of an expert panel Thursday, aiming to formalize the guidelines by the end of the year after soliciting public comments.

Under the country’s revised school education law, which was enacted in June, three formats — paper-only, fully digital and paper-digital hybrid — will be allowed for school textbooks from fiscal 2030.

The draft guidelines propose that hybrid textbooks be the standard format for all subjects in all grades in elementary, junior high and high schools, the sources said.

The draft states that hybrid textbooks should mainly comprise paper-based materials for elementary school fifth grade and above, and basically be made up of paper materials with a more limited role for digital materials for fourth grade and below.

The digital-only format should not be used for textbooks for fourth grade and below and should be allowed in limited subjects such as English, music and art for fifth grade and up.

Textbook publishers will choose appropriate formats in accordance with students’ development and subjects based on the minister’s guidelines.

In April, then education minister Yohei Matsumoto told a parliamentary meeting that fully digital textbooks should not be adopted for fourth graders and younger students. He also said that digital-only textbooks should not be allowed for the time being in such subjects as Japanese language, social studies and moral education.

World.title: As midterms loom, Trump seizes on France unrest for political gain
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump used the protests roiling France to score some quick political points Monday, as the upcoming midterm elections force his Republican Party to face strong headwinds.

At a rally in Kansas, the U.S. president launched into a lengthy tirade about France, which he said was being “conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists, and communists.”

“And we’re not going to let that happen to this country,” he added.

World.title: Lakers release former first-round pick Dalton Knecht
World.content:
The Los Angeles Lakers waived former first-round pick Dalton Knecht on Monday to reach the NBA roster limit of 15 players ahead of the 5 p.m. ET deadline.

Knecht, a forward, averaged 4.2 points and 1.4 rebounds in 10.2 minutes across 54 games (one start) last season.

The previous season, Knecht averaged 9.1 points and 2.8 rebounds in 78 games (16 starts) as a rookie and looked like a promising rotation player.

During the 2026 preseason, Knecht averaged 2.8 points and shot 25% (3 of 12) from the field. The 25-year-old scored 11 points in 22 minutes against the Golden State Warriors on Oct. 6 and was scoreless in each of his other three appearances.

The 6-foot-6 Knecht was the 17th overall selection of the 2024 NBA Draft after being the Southeastern Conference Player of the Year and a consensus first- team All-American at Tennessee. That was his lone season with the Volunteers. He spent the previous two seasons at Northern Colorado after playing two seasons at Northeastern Junior College in Colorado.

The move to release Knecht means that Bronny James and Jaden Hardy will make the Lakers’ opening-night roster.

World.title: Trump open to trilateral summit with Putin and Xi but wants denuclearization focus
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump said he is open to holding a trilateral summit with Russian leader Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping, but that any meeting would focus on nuclear issues — not the war in Ukraine.

Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday that such a meeting would be “based on denuclearization,” after a report said Putin had proposed an unprecedented three-way summit to talk about how to end the 4½-year-old Ukraine conflict.

“I would do it, not so much for Ukraine, because Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine. They haven’t been doing much,” Trump said. “We would have it to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearization.”

World.title: Empress Emerita Michiko turns 92 while enjoying peaceful life
World.content:
Empress Emerita Michiko turned 92 on Tuesday as she enjoys a peaceful life with her husband, Emperor Emeritus Akihito, also 92.

Her advanced age has caused a decline in her physical strength and makes her tired more frequently than before, which has led her to take shorter walks. Still, there is no major change in the Empress Emerita’s overall health condition, according to the Imperial Household Agency.

Despite spending less time in the public eye, the Empress Emerita, along with the Emperor Emeritus and other members of the Imperial Family, appeared before the general public in January this year for New Year’s greetings at the Imperial Palace in Tokyo.

World.title: Milan luxury shops close for fear of new unrest as government prepares to deploy troops
World.content:
The Italian government will dispatch 500 army troops to “defend Milan” after two days of unrest that saw demonstrators clash with police, loot shops and vandalize property, Italian Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini said on Monday.

The deployment is expected to be included in a package of security measures to be approved at a cabinet meeting expected on Tuesday.

Shops in central Milan closed early on Monday and boarded up their windows, fearing a fresh outbreak of violence in Italy’s financial capital.

“From words to action: 500 more troops to defend Milan,” Salvini, head of the co-ruling right-wing League party, wrote on social media.

Most stores in Milan’s Via Montenapoleone luxury shopping district, home to brands including Chanel, Tiffany and Dior, had removed merchandise from their windows as a precaution, while police patrolled the street and a handful of tourists looked on.

Several hundred hooded protesters, many believed to be minors, set bins ablaze and looted shops in the city center over the weekend after an initially peaceful demonstration on Saturday over poor public services and rising costs.

Among the stores ransacked were sports retailers Decathlon and Arc’teryx and mobile phone operator Vodafone, television footage showed. Stores such as clothing brands Levi’s and Under Armour, as well as Decathlon, covered their shop windows with cardboard and wooden panels.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who faces a national election next year, condemned the violence and chaired a meeting with ministers and security chiefs on Monday to discuss the situation.

“The government will respond firmly to these attacks on the state, including through measures aimed at curbing violence by minors,” Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani, who also serves as deputy prime minister like Salvini, wrote on X.

As part of the planned crackdown, Corriere della Sera newspaper said Meloni was considering extending preventive detention for minors and cracking down on youth gangs, bringing forward some provisions contained in an existing security bill currently being examined by parliament.

Italian police said it had detained 271 young people during unrest in Milan on Sunday. Of those taken to police stations, 32 were arrested, including 23 minors and 13 foreign nationals, police said on Monday. A further 28 people were reported to judicial authorities.

The unrest followed clashes on Saturday in Milan and other northern cities including Bologna, Brescia, Bergamo and Turin, where 28 protesters were arrested, according to a police report released on Sunday.

The disturbances echoed unrest in neighboring France, where hundreds of thousands of people angered by rising living costs and declining public services took to the streets on Saturday in some of the country’s most violent protests in years.

World.title: Data-center firm Elice plunges 32% in debut after Korea IPO
World.content:
Data-center infrastructure company Elice plunged in its trading debut on South Korea’s tech-heavy Kosdaq market after raising 201 billion won ($151 million) in the bourse’s biggest initial public offering this year.

Shares of the Seoul-based neocloud service provider fell as much as 32% to 61,400 won in early trading on Tuesday. The company priced its shares at 90,500 won apiece in the IPO, the top of a marketed price range, for a post-listing market capitalization exceeding 1 trillion won.

The debut is a test of investor appetite for the sector after a series of setbacks around the world. Firmus Grid canceled its high-profile Sydney listing this month as concerns over borrowing costs, fierce competition and long-term returns from massive AI-related spending weigh on valuations. Coreweave’s shares have more than halved since their May peak, AirTrunk is delaying a planned IPO of a real estate investment trust, people familiar with the matter have said, while Nscale is facing pushback over its target IPO valuation, it was reported.

World.title: Svitolina announces end of marriage to Monfils as Ukrainian cites toll of war
World.content:
World No. 6 Elina Svitolina said on Monday that she and former tennis player Gael Monfils were ending their marriage, with the Ukrainian adding that the emotional toll of Russia’s war in her homeland left her needing to rediscover herself.

The couple married in July 2021 and welcomed a daughter, Skai, in October 2022.

Announcing the separation in an Instagram post, Svitolina described the personal struggles she has faced since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 and the impact they had on her life away from the tennis court.

World.title: Hong Kong mother spared trial over neglect of chronically underweight daughter
World.content:
A Hong Kong mother accused of neglecting her 12-year-old daughter who had been chronically underweight has been spared trial as the prosecution agreed to place her on a good behaviour bond, with the justice department saying public interest is generally a key factor in such decisions.

The South China Morning Post has learned that prosecutors at West Kowloon Court dropped a child abuse charge against the 53-year-old housewife earlier this month in exchange for her agreeing to a three-year bind-over order.

Her daughter dropped from 24.9kg to 20.9kg (55lbs to 46lbs) from March to April in 2023. The mother admitted she sometimes failed to follow doctor’s advice and feed her daughter three times a day.

The girl’s weight at the time was about 8kg below the third percentile for her age. She had been underweight since age six, and at one point in 2021 was placed on a feeding tube in hospital.

World.title: How smart will Hong Kong’s ‘AI city brain’ be?
World.content:
When Severe Typhoon Dolphin approached eastern China in August, more than 110,000 delivery riders across Hangzhou received automatic alerts and personalised safety guidance on their mobile phones every minute.

With a few taps, Hangzhou’s “riders’ code” system navigated them to the nearest shelters, which authorities said had reduced their occupational risks under extreme weather.

Behind the tailored and quick support was Hangzhou’s artificial intelligence (AI) urban management system, which had been in place and evolving for more than a decade.

This is what the Hong Kong government aims to build: an AI-powered system that links databases on landslide monitoring, fallen trees, water pipes, weather and public complaints, among others. The handling of extreme weather will be the first scenario to put the ambitious initiative to the test.

World.title: Elderly man dies after being pulled unconscious from flat during fire in Sai Ying Pun
World.content:
An elderly man died in hospital on Monday night after he was pulled unconscious from a flat during a fire in a residential building in Hong Kong’s Western district.

Police received a report at 8.57pm that flames had erupted in a flat in Hang Fai Building on Pok Fu Lam Road in Sai Ying Pun.

Firefighters deployed two water jet and breathing apparatus teams to tackle the fire, which was extinguished at 9.54pm.

Police received a report about the fire at 8.57pm. Photo: Facebook/HeartyFrog9491

A man in his 70s was found unconscious and was rushed to Queen Mary Hospital in Pok Fu Lam. He was declared dead at 10.40pm.

World.title: Hong Kong police arrest woman after dog allegedly thrown into sea
World.content:
A woman has been arrested on suspicion of animal cruelty after allegedly throwing a dog into the sea in Hong Kong.

The woman was reportedly seen throwing a dog from the waterfront near 29 Tai On Street in Sai Wan Ho into the water at around 1pm on Thursday. She then retrieved the animal and left the scene.

A passer-by who witnessed the incident alerted police.

Following an investigation, officers arrested a 59-year-old local woman on Saturday near the junction of Tai Hong Street and Lei King Road. She was detained on suspicion of cruelty to animals and later released on bail pending further inquiries.

World.title: Apec in Hong Kong: what to know as 500 delegates descend on the city
World.content:
Global attention will turn to Hong Kong this week as about 500 senior officials and delegates from the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation’s 21 members gather in the city for the Apec Finance Ministers’ Meeting on Tuesday and Wednesday.

It is the first time Hong Kong has hosted the meeting, with Beijing’s support, as mainland China prepares to host the Apec leaders’ summit in Shenzhen next month.

Hong Kong joined Apec in 1991 and has continued to take part in the economic forum’s affairs under the “one country, two systems” framework since the 1997 handover of sovereignty from Britain to China.

The South China Morning Post lists the key things you need to know about the meeting.

World.title: 5 hikers fall ill as hot weather grips Hong Kong on public holiday
World.content:
Five hikers fell ill in separate incidents across Hong Kong on Monday as hot weather gripped the city on the final day of the Chung Yeung Festival long weekend.

In one incident at Po Pin Chau, a popular hiking destination in Sai Kung, a 62-year-old mainland Chinese woman was hiking with friends near the High Island Reservoir East Dam when she became dizzy and weak at about 10.30am.

Suspected of suffering from heatstroke, she was rescued by the Government Flying Service and flown to hospital for treatment.

At about 12.20pm, a family of three – a couple and their son – were hiking from Tai Tong Country Park along the MacLehose Trail when the mother, in her fifties, felt unwell and vomited near Tai Lam Chung Reservoir.

World.title: Art or box office? How Hong Kong plans to measure the value of a play, ballet or symphony
World.content:
Established performing arts groups in Hong Kong should rely less on public subsidies to make way for emerging companies, industry experts have said, after the city’s leader announced a revamp of the funding model in favour of a more flexible, non-permanent and merit-based system.

But a few directors of the city’s nine designated major performing arts groups in music, dance and theatre said the economic downturn had made private funds harder to secure and urged the government to take a long-term view, noting that arts development goals could take years to achieve.

The new funding model will require policymakers to lay down targets for companies, prompting questions about how to assess merit in an industry where artistic quality does not always translate to commercial success.

The South China Morning Post spoke to performing arts groups, cultural critics and a lawmaker amid the debate over how to better spend public funds to develop Hong Kong’s performing arts sector and how to determine which groups are deserving of support.

World.title: Contractor injured as brief fire breaks out at Hong Kong Cultural Centre
World.content:
A brief No 2 alarm fire broke out at the Hong Kong Cultural Centre in Tsim Sha Tsui on Monday, leaving a contractor injured after she received an electric shock.

The Fire Services Department said it received an alarm at the venue at 11.23am. When firefighters arrived three minutes later, the fire had already been extinguished.

“After investigation, a female staff member was found to have been injured in an electric shock accident,” a department spokesman said.

The worker was taken to Queen Elizabeth Hospital in Kowloon for treatment.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019142/Rehab, Release, Repeat: Nana, the Seal Who Refuses to Return to the Wild
World.title: Rehab, Release, Repeat: Nana, the Seal Who Refuses to Return to the Wild
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019142/Rehab, Release, Repeat: Nana, the Seal Who Refuses to Return to the Wild
World.content:
In wildlife conservation, there are three steps to helping an injured or orphaned animal: rescue, rehabilitate, and release. “Returning” isn’t part of the plan, but try telling that to China’s celebrity seal Nana.

This 2-year-old wild spotted seal, a Class I protected species in China, was a must-see attraction this summer for visitors to Dachangshan Island, part of Dalian’s Changshan Archipelago in the northeastern Liaoning province.

Nana has been released twice far out into the Yellow Sea, with the hope he’d join a migrating colony. Both times he’s made his way back alone, once covering more than 200 kilometers in just six days.

When he first showed up on the island in June, he was wary of humans and swam away when approached. But over time, he grew braver. Tourists tempted him near with tasty fish, though this sometimes resulted in him receiving a prod or a kick, and often a startling camera flash.

Concerned for Nana’s welfare, the local government put up warning signs telling people not to feed him and to keep a safe distance, and vowed “not to use him to promote tourism.” Yet within months, a “Nana Line” shuttle service had opened, running directly from the island’s Yuanyang Port to its “best seal-watching spot,” while the local tourism bureau began working with a private business to make and sell seal-related merchandise.

For many locals, Nana’s presence has been bittersweet: he’s a cute addition to the neighborhood, but the risks to his safety outweigh the benefits, they say.

Despite the falling temperature, authorities have ruled out moving him again, much to the delight of those who feel the seal has “made his choice.” But as the tourist season ends and his steady, fan-fueled food supply dries up, others worry that Nana could face a harsh winter alone.

Hello, new neighbor

Nana was just a pup in the summer of 2024, when fishermen first spotted him resting on a buoy in waters off Beihai, in the southern Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region. Noticing he was thin and had wounds on his body, likely caused by boat propellers, they alerted the authorities, who transported him to the Beihai Aquatic Rescue and Rehabilitation Center.

The spot where Nana was discovered lies just off a migration route for spotted seals between the western Pacific Ocean and Dalian’s Liaodong Bay. Experts suspect he drifted from his colony and was stranded alone.

In November 2025, after being nursed back to health, Nana was transferred to a wild species rehabilitation center in Dalian operated by the Liaoning Ocean and Fisheries Science and Research Institute. There, he quickly went from 50 to 70 kilograms and grew a new coat of glossy fur. “You could see him looking better every day,” says Chai Yuqiao, a researcher at the base.

By this spring, Nana was deemed well enough to return to the wild. On April 16, the institute released him and two other rescued seals roughly 10 kilometers from shore in the Yellow Sea, thinking they would naturally head for the migration route and find a new colony.

Nana’s two companions did exactly that, but data from his satellite tag shows he never left the Yellow Sea. Two months later, he popped up at Dachangshan Island.

Locals first spotted the seal relaxing in a rocky tide pool on June 19.

“Back then he was wary and rarely came close,” recalls Feng Zhi, who runs a guesthouse on the island. “He’d just hang around, and if someone walked over, he’d swim away.”

But that changed the more he interacted with tourists. “Wherever the crowd was thickest, that’s where he’d be,” says Li Ai, who also works in the hospitality industry. “But he can be picky about people,” she adds, explaining that Nana appeared especially fond of a wetsuit-wearing livestreamer known as “Man in Black,” who has 24,000 followers on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok. Nana often chased him and snuggled up to him.

Zhou Long, another guesthouse manager, says Nana once squeezed in between him and several friends as they stood in the shallows. The seal was warm, slippery, and plump, “like a balloon that’s about to pop,” he says.

People soon began feeding Nana fish and petting him when he got close. A local boat captain says he often tried stopping tourists from doing this, but few listened. He worried Nana might accidentally be fed a fish containing a fishhook, “the consequences of which don’t bear thinking about.”

Some people were even captured on surveillance cameras throwing Nana barbecued meat, bread, and potato chips, foods that could seriously upset his digestive system, while others kicked him, and thoughtless children threw stones at him.

“I couldn’t bear to watch and couldn’t do anything about it. I could only turn around and walk away,” says Li.

Many locals breathed a sigh of relief on Sept. 7 when the authorities finally arrived to take Nana away.

Gone, but not forgotten

To protect and “re-wild” Nana, the Changhai County government, which administers Dachangshan Island, decided to again transport the seal out to the Yellow Sea, this time to a spot about 140 kilometers away by boat.

Nana was back on the island just six days later. His tracking tag had fallen off a month earlier, but Tian Jiashen, director of marine rare animal conservation research at the Liaoning institute, estimates the seal’s return journey must have covered at least 200 kilometers.

Zhou had an inkling he’d not seen the last of Nana. Social media users had been eagerly sharing news of sightings, and the seal was getting closer all the time. On the evening of Sept. 13, Zhou went to the shore, opened a livestream, and lay in wait, with nearly 200 followers logging on to watch.

As night fell, Zhou heard a splash, like “a huge creature leaping into the water.” When he ran over, Nana was beside the blue pontoon bridge that he’d frequented all summer.

Within hours, Lin Gao, an employee at a beachside water sports center, had reinstalled the giant inflatable yellow duck Nana had liked to sleep on. “We couldn’t let him come back and find it gone,” he says, adding that work had felt “hollow” without Nana around.

Tian admits he never expected the seal to return but now believes Nana’s interactions with tourists might have reawakened his memories of being rescued and fed by humans.

Staff at the Liaoning institute recall that Nana was initially more curious than cautious. Marine researcher Chen Yanyu says he was once scrubbing the rearing pool when Nana surprisingly pushed a long-handled brush toward his hand. He badly wanted to pat the seal’s head, but that would be against the rules of “rehab and release.”

In wildlife conservation, keeping a safe distance is paramount. Rescued seals are fed by pouring live fish into the pool, while researchers deliberately approach the animals with nets to condition them to avoid people. By the time of his release, Nana had begun watching the staff from afar.

On that first release day, Chen watched Nana slide down the boat’s ramp into the sea with tears in his eyes.

However, when the seal became a celebrity, the institute came under attack from netizens who felt it had failed in its responsibilities to rehabilitate Nana.

Tian, who has worked there since 2010, believes the criticism was unfair. He explained that the institute is manned year-round by researchers who volunteer their time for free, and that in the past two decades it has helped rescue 244 spotted seals, releasing 223.

“The sea is his home, and he should go home,” he adds, talking about Nana. “Keeping him here, in a human environment — that would be cruelty.”

The risks human behaviors pose to wildlife are obvious. Ah Nong, a spotted seal rescued late last year after spending 15 months in waters off Wenchang, in the southern island province of Hainan, was found to have diarrhea, elevated liver function, and ultraviolet skin burns from being fed, touched, and photographed by tourists.

When Nana returned a second time, Chai and some colleagues wanted to go see him, “to find out whether he still remembered us.” Others, like researcher Shi Hongyue, held another wish: that one day they would come across Nana naturally during a survey of a wild colony.

Sealing his fate?

Nana became even more famous after returning to Dachangshan Island last month. By 7 a.m., at least 10 livestreamers would already be set up on shore, waiting for the seal to wake up. These channels quickly became a key marketing tool for guesthouses and other local businesses.

In August, Chinese media quoted an unnamed local official as saying that authorities “would not use (Nana) for cultural tourism promotions.” However, that attitude appeared to shift after the seal’s return in September.

The Changhai Culture and Tourism Bureau opened the “Nana Line” on Sept. 25, and beachside stalls hawking Nana-themed merch began popping up this month.

More warning signs and loudspeakers have been placed along the beach, reminding tourists that feeding protected species is forbidden, while enforcement officers and volunteers now regularly patrol the area. The local government has announced it will not attempt to move Nana again and is planning to build him a shelter on the pontoon bridge, away from the crowds.

Residents say the feeding and touching has declined, but it still happens.

This will naturally trail off as the tourist and fishing seasons wind down ahead of the coldest months, leading some to worry that Nana could starve. Despite the rules, in October, Sun Zongjun, the owner of the water sports center, pledged on a livestream that “we’ll definitely keep feeding him when it gets cold.” The county government has yet to confirm whether live fish stocks will be provided for the seal over winter.

Tian says it’s hard to predict whether Nana will ever leave and fully return to nature; it depends on diverse factors like water temperature, his physiological state, and whether he meets any companions and joins a new colony.

Scientific studies using tracking data show that spotted seals tend to rest or breed in the same place, year after year. Tian believes this behavior, and his memories of human interaction, could be what led Nana back to Dachangshan Island.

While most locals were happy to welcome Nana “home,” his presence has also brought pressure. “Our island lives off tourism. If anything happens to him, the criticism of millions of people could crash down on us in an instant,” says Lin, who regularly volunteers to patrol the pontoon bridge in the early hours.

On most nights, Nana can be found sleeping soundly on his giant yellow duck as it rocks gently in the waves. Soon, he will be joined in these waters by other spotted seals. No one knows what will come next.

“It’s fine if Nana stays,” says Liu Yi, a guesthouse owner on the island. “But I still hope he leaves.”

(Due to privacy concerns, Lin Gao, Feng Zhi, Li Ai, Zhou Long, and Liu Yi are pseudonyms.)

Reported by Qin Bing and Feng Haoni.

A version of this article originally appeared in The Beijing News. It has been translated and edited for brevity and clarity, and is republished here with permission.

Translator: PaperBuddy; editors: Wang Juyi and Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Nana comes ashore at Dachangshan Island, Liaoning, Sept. 27, 2026. From Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019137/Over 150 Chinese Apps Deny AI Assistant’s Use on Smartphone
World.title: Over 150 Chinese Apps Deny AI Assistant’s Use on Smartphone
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019137/Over 150 Chinese Apps Deny AI Assistant’s Use on Smartphone
World.content:
More than 150 Chinese apps have forbidden ByteDance’s mobile AI assistant Doubao from operating them on smartphone manufacturer Nubia Technology’s newly released agentic AI smartphone.

In a list published Oct. 14 on Doubao’s official account on messaging app WeChat, its developers identified dozens of apps that prohibit its graphical user interface (GUI) automation. The technology interprets a user’s spoken command, reads what is displayed on their smartphone’s screen, and navigates across and operates apps to complete the task.

Doubao had released its Smart Assistant Execution Protocol on Sept. 14, giving developers one month to decide whether to let the assistant operate their apps.

Apps owned by ByteDance’s rival technology companies Tencent and Alibaba make up nearly 60% of the list, including WeChat from the former and digital payment system Alipay from the latter, according to domestic media outlet Cailian Press. Others include those from e-commerce giant Meituan, ride-hailing platform Didi, lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, e-commerce platform Pinduoduo, China’s three state-run telecommunications carriers, several banks, and rival AI apps DeepSeek and Kimi. The listed apps can still be installed and used manually.

Absent from the list are e-commerce giant JD.com and most apps from internet service company Baidu, with the exception of Baidu Maps. A Baidu employee told domestic media outlet Caijing magazine that the phone’s shipment volume remains too small to pose a meaningful concern for the company.

Nubia bills the NaviX Ultra as “the world’s first AI-powered smartphone,” bringing agentic AI to consumers. The company, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, said that within seconds of the smartphone’s Sept. 16 launch, it generated 100 million yuan ($15 million) in sales. The phone’s price starts at 5,999 yuan.

Nubia released a prototype of the current AI phone, the M153, for 3,499 yuan in December last year. Though it quickly sold out, users soon reported that whenever the assistant attempted to operate WeChat, they were automatically logged out of the app. Doubao’s developers later disabled the assistant’s ability to operate the super app.

On the same day Doubao published the list of restricted apps, Nubia announced a software update — including improved localized data search, call-recording summaries, and call screening functions — and offered users six months of free Doubao membership, worth roughly 400 yuan.

As of Monday, none of the included app developers have commented publicly on the news.

Liu Xu, a researcher at Tsinghua University’s Institute for National Strategic Studies, told Cailian Press that China has no regulations relating to how AI agents operate third-party applications.

Given the lack of oversight, Liu said, it is understandable that developers would deny such access over data security and user privacy concerns. He added that their resistance may also reflect a desire to protect their own AI ecosystems, particularly given Doubao’s already vast user base.

In its post, Doubao’s developers stated that other apps can opt out of its GUI technology at any time, and its list of cooperating companies would be updated every Wednesday.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019133/Duolingo Launches Shanghainese Lessons, Its 2nd Chinese Dialect
World.title: Duolingo Launches Shanghainese Lessons, Its 2nd Chinese Dialect
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019133/Duolingo Launches Shanghainese Lessons, Its 2nd Chinese Dialect
World.content:
SHANGHAI – Popular language-learning app Duolingo has released a Shanghainese course featuring lessons on modern culture and life in old Shanghai as well as offline activities in the city.

The course, launched Thursday, features roughly 50 lessons drawn from everyday life in Shanghai, from ordering street food and taking public transit to exchanging greetings and navigating the city’s landmarks. To access the Shanghainese course, users must first set Chinese as their display language.

Founded in the U.S. in 2011, Duolingo offers courses in over 40 languages. The launch of the company’s Shanghainese course marks its second Chinese dialect offering, following Cantonese released in 2022. China is the company’s fastest-growing and second-largest market.

The course revolves around aspects of modern life in Shanghai like workplace dynamics and coffee culture, while also featuring old Shanghai themes, such as life in the city’s longtang lane houses and local phrases for traditional games, Tan Xiuting, a senior course designer of Duolingo, told Sixth Tone at the launch event in Shanghai on Friday.

Lessons also extend beyond the screen, with offline check-in spots around Shanghai, as well as themed activities on buses and in subway stations. Duolingo has also partnered with local shops; for example, if a user orders a coffee in Shanghainese at a partner café, they will receive a gift.

Wang Chen, an official with Duolingo, said that the course underscores the company’s “long-term commitment” to the Chinese market and its linguistic diversity.

“We want to make dialects cool and help local language and culture stay alive in contemporary life through products that are digital, engaging, and easy to access,” Wang said.

Shanghainese, or the Hu dialect, is a Wu Chinese variety spoken by roughly 10 million people, primarily in Shanghai and the surrounding Yangtze River Delta region. Difficult for native Mandarin speakers to understand, it features more tones and numerous English and French loanwords due to the city’s opening as a treaty port in the mid-19th century. It also preserves many classical Chinese words and structures.

The dialect has declined in recent decades, as national policies have pushed Mandarin use in schools, workplaces, and the media. In the last decade, Shanghai has reintroduced Shanghainese in some kindergartens and on public transportation, and has held speech competitions to inspire younger generations to learn it. TV programs, films, music, and standup comedy shows in Shanghainese have also emerged in recent years.

Zhou Yuwen, a 30-year-old branding manager born and raised in Shanghai, told Sixth Tone that her generation was expected to speak Mandarin both inside and outside the classroom, but over time, Shanghainese-speaking environments decreased.

“I can understand Shanghainese, but when I try to speak it, it comes out so ‘Yangjingbang’ that I feel too embarrassed to keep going,” she said, referencing the colloquial name for the pidgin English used between European and local merchants in Shanghai in the 19th century.

Zhou said she felt “excited” by the release of Duolingo’s Shanghainese course, and shared news of the course’s launch on lifestyle platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, hoping to encourage others to learn. “It’s a pity that someone like me, who was born, grew up, and worked my whole life in Shanghai, can’t speak proper Shanghainese,” she said. “I absolutely love the dialect, and I hope to see it not just preserved, but truly flourish.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Xiaohongshu, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019128/In China, an AI Idol’s ‘Maternity Leave’ Backfires on Her Creators
World.title: In China, an AI Idol’s ‘Maternity Leave’ Backfires on Her Creators
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019128/In China, an AI Idol’s ‘Maternity Leave’ Backfires on Her Creators
World.content:
“I’m pregnant. After much consideration and thorough discussions with the company and my bandmates, I have decided to temporarily leave the group to focus on rest and recovery,” reads a statement signed by Mity, one of five members of the new girl group BABYQUEEN, alongside a selfie of her wearing pink pajamas in bed.

At first glance, nothing seems out of the ordinary, except that she and the entire BABYQUEEN pop group are AI-generated.

The announcement, published Tuesday on the group’s official Xiaohongshu account, also known as RedNote, has drawn criticism for turning women’s reproductive health into entertainment, as well as jokes and incredulity about the situation’s perceived absurdity.

AI girl group accounts have proliferated on Chinese social media in recent months, with virtual idols often maintaining social media accounts where they share glimpses of their daily lives and even secure and promote brand endorsements.

BABYQUEEN, styled as a South Korean girl group, launched its Xiaohongshu account on Sept. 7. As of Friday, the account, whose IP address is located in China’s northeastern Liaoning province, has roughly 1,000 followers.

Mity’s pregnancy was initially announced on the group’s account the day before, reading, “To prioritize her health during pregnancy and prepare for childbirth, she will temporarily suspend all group and individual variety show appearances and stage performances after thorough discussions with the team.” It also urged followers not to “over-speculate about her private life.”

Since it went viral on social media, the topic has attracted more than 6 million views on microblogging platform Weibo as of Friday.

Many users have expressed astonishment. “AI group members can get pregnant now? I don’t understand the virtual world anymore,” one highly upvoted comment reads. Others joked that the group’s creators might be running short on tokens, implying they had to let one member go because they lacked the computing power.

Users also accused the band’s makers of using the story for views while showing little respect for women. “Using ‘pregnant and preparing for childbirth’ as a marketing hook and a sensationalized narrative trivializes real women’s reproductive experiences by turning them into entertainment,” one comment reads.

The day of the announcement, the account also released a teaser post for a new song performed by the group’s four remaining members.

In a since-deleted Tuesday post on the BABYQUEEN account, the group’s creators cited pressures of running the group as the reason for the pregnancy announcement.

“We’re just a few girls who like K-Pop, and we’re still students,” they wrote, adding that they had “not earned a single cent” from the endeavor. They also said they had experienced personal attacks and online harassment.

On the group’s official parent account, BABYPVSSY Entertainment, the creators said Mity might next “explore two possible career paths: acting or becoming a maternity and infant content creator.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Xiaohongshu, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019132/The Northeast Chinese Meme That Found a Second Life as a Video Game
World.title: The Northeast Chinese Meme That Found a Second Life as a Video Game
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019132/The Northeast Chinese Meme That Found a Second Life as a Video Game
World.content:
In 2016, two groups of Chinese livestreamers began feuding on Kuaishou, a short-video platform popular in China’s countryside and lower-tier cities. Their leaders, Brother Hu and Captain Shamate, were both grassroots streamers from Northeast China, or Dongbei. Video after video, they traded insults, accusations, and challenges. These gang-style exchanges were loud, theatrical, and unmistakably regional, full of Northeastern Chinese dialects, bravado, and the kind of chaos that early Chinese livestreaming platforms thrived on.

The feud was widely believed to be staged, a scripted collaboration designed for dramatic effect. But that did little to diminish its appeal. Audiences couldn’t stop watching, and clips of the confrontations soon took on a life of their own. Over time, they spawned an influential body of memes that spread across various media, even video games, one of which has now become an unlikely hit on Steam.

The phenomenon emerged against the backdrop of Dongbei’s changing cultural identity. Once the heartland of China’s heavy industry, the region is often referred to as the country’s Rust Belt after decades of industrial decline. Locals have turned that history into both tragedy and comedy. TV dramas such as “The Long Season” have tapped into nostalgia for the region’s industrial heyday, helping make the “Dongbei Renaissance” a cultural buzzword. Northeasterners have long played an outsized role in Chinese comedy. On television, Zhao Benshan’s sketches made the Northeastern accent familiar to audiences nationwide; on Kuaishou, Northeastern dialects and slang became a rich source of humor and memes.

It was in this context that the feud between Brother Hu and Captain Shamate gained traction. Fans recorded and reposted clips to streaming site Bilibili, where they were remixed, quoted, and jokingly treated as “classics.” The saga became known as “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei.”

Seven years later, those memes were turned into a video game. A Summer in Northeast China (DongBeiZhiXia), released for free on Steam on Jan. 9, 2023, was developed and published by Zhuangbuchun Studio, led by Zhuangbuchun, a Bilibili content creator with over 2 million followers. Up till today, the game has since accumulated more than 12,000 positive reviews on Steam, earning an “Overwhelmingly Positive” rating despite being available only in Simplified and Traditional Chinese. Its success shows just how far a regional internet joke can travel when platform dynamics, an existing fan community, and a developer’s instincts align at the right moment.

A Summer in Northeast China is a “gal game,” a genre typically centered on interactions with female characters. Set years after the original Kuaishou incidents, the game follows Xiaoliang, who must recover her memories with the help of a cast of female companions, each loosely inspired by figures from the “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei” phenomenon. The game’s most conspicuous adaptation is its gender-swapping: the male roles at the center of the original memes are reimagined as women, retaining their names, signature visual traits, and personalities while being reshaped to fit the conventions of the gal game and ACGN (anime, comics, games, and novels) aesthetics.

In effect, the game translates its source material across cultural registers. “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei” ran on masculine confrontation, local bravado, and the rough-edged authenticity of Kuaishou livestreaming. A Summer in Northeast China recasts that material through the softer, character-driven lens of the gal game, while keeping enough recognizable references to reward those who remember the source. Events from the original memes return as callbacks for longtime fans, while the first-person linear narrative gives newcomers an accessible way into Xiaoliang’s story.

The game also draws on subcultures Zhuangbuchun knows well, including shamate — a Chinese youth subculture known for its flamboyant hairstyles and fashion — and otaku — intense fandom of anime, manga, games, and related media, originating in Japan — while its use of Northeastern dialect keeps it rooted in Dongbei. Together, these influences reflect the game’s broader approach: combining distinctly Northeastern humor and internet culture with the appeal of manga and anime.

Zhuangbuchun made the game the way many Chinese indie developers do: on a limited budget and in public. The project was self-funded, with a crowdfunding campaign on domestic creator-sponsorship platform Afdian covering part of the cost. He handled much of the design and direction himself, outsourced some work, and recruited voice actors for the female cast.

But developing the game in public was not simply a funding strategy. It also became central to how Zhuangbuchun built an audience around the project. Nearly a year before the game’s launch, in April 2022, he posted a video announcing his gender-swapped take on “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei.” The video received over 1.5 million views, 71,000 likes, 23,000 saves, and 11,000 reposts.

From there, Zhuangbuchun kept followers closely involved in development. He posted early character designs, solicited feedback on voice acting, and explained delays. When viewers complained about an accent or suggested a different look, he listened and sometimes changed the game accordingly. In that sense, the project was not simply marketed to its eventual players. It was partly shaped by them.

Zhuangbuchun also visited Shenyang, the capital of the northeastern Liaoning province, several times to document where the original Kuaishou events took place. On one return trip after the game’s release, he even ran into some of its fans. These travel vlogs reinforced the sense that the game was being made by someone invested not only in the memes but also in the places and culture from which they emerged.

The steady updates kept the project visible on Bilibili and positioned Zhuangbuchun as part of the internet culture that turned the original Kuaishou videos into “Once Upon a Time in Dongbei.” His existing followers helped attract attention, while the project’s local roots kept audiences engaged. The original Kuaishou streamers added another layer to this relationship, posting reaction videos and engaging with Zhuangbuchun’s posts, further blurring the line between the game and the people who inspired it.

A Summer in Northeast China is neither the first game to adapt internet memes nor the first to blend Chinese regional culture with global subcultural aesthetics. What makes it unusual is the particular combination: a free gal game with a gender-swapped cast, a distinctly Northeastern setting, a developer who was already a prominent Bilibili creator, and source material rooted in the unruly world of early Kuaishou livestreaming.

For indie developers working with limited resources, A Summer in Northeast China offers a distinctive example of how online culture can move across platforms and media. The same platforms that provided the game with its source material also supplied an audience, feedback, publicity, and a community willing to participate in its development. Rather than simply adapting an existing meme, Zhuangbuchun used the participatory culture surrounding it to carry the material far beyond its origins.

That process creates tensions between local authenticity and internet marketability, and between the crude energy of the original memes and the game’s polished presentation. Yet, A Summer in Northeast China never loses sight of its regional origins. Zhuangbuchun, who has told me he loves Dongbei despite not being from the region, is part of that story: an outsider drawn into its culture who now helps reshape it for new audiences. The game has traveled from Kuaishou to Bilibili to Steam, changing along the way. But for all the distance it has traveled, it has never really left Northeast China.

Zhu Siheng, a Ph.D. candidate at the University of Rochester, and Han Yisong, a postdoctoral researcher at the City University of Hong Kong, also made contributions to this research.

(Header image: Promotional art for the video game “A Summer in Northeast China” on Steam.)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019126/Chinese Users Find Little Money in ‘Selling’ Their Faces to AI
World.title: Chinese Users Find Little Money in ‘Selling’ Their Faces to AI
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019126/Chinese Users Find Little Money in ‘Selling’ Their Faces to AI
World.content:
Users in China who “sold their faces,” or licensed their likenesses, for use in AI short dramas and livestreams months ago report receiving few or no requests for their use, and consequently almost no related income.

Domestic media outlet Southern Metropolis Daily reported Monday that many users on multiple domestic face-licensing platforms, such as NCAIGC, Mirafans, and ActID, which promise steady income and payment after use of a person’s likeness in their licensing agreements, have not received remuneration.

Face-licensing platforms first emerged around May this year, fueled by the growth of AI-generated content, particularly ultrashort dramas. At a September press conference held by the State Council Information Office, it was announced that more than 90% of the 430,000 ultrashort dramas released in China in the first eight months of 2026 were AI-generated.

The platforms attract users by advertising a low barrier to entry and high returns, with claims such as “earn nearly 2,500 yuan ($370) in three days with face selling” going viral on social media, state broadcaster CCTV reported Tuesday.

Face licensing lets individuals license their digital likenesses — otherwise protected from use by others under China’s Personal Information Protection Law — to a platform for use in AI ultrashort dramas and ads, among other content.

According to CCTV, registration on face-licensing platforms usually requires users to undergo real-name authentication, upload photos of themselves, and set a desired price for each use of their likeness. Some platforms also require users to specify which roles and scenarios they allow companies to use their likenesses for, such as villains, death scenes, or romance.

Buyers can select single-use or single-project authorization, and the licensor must accept within 24 hours, after which authorization documents are generated and materials released. Platforms take about a 30% cut.

Regular users can earn about 100 yuan per short video that uses their likeness, with some platforms setting a 500-yuan minimum, while professional actors may reportedly receive up to 10,000 yuan.

Wang Jinlin, a model based in the southern city of Guilin, licensed her face on ActID in May. If a buyer selects her portrait for commercial use, she says they’ll typically offer a one-time payment of 500 to 1,000 yuan. But so far, no studio has asked to use her likeness, she told Sixth Tone.

“There are probably few companies making AI live-action short videos right now — there’s no complete pipeline yet,” Wang said. She sees joining the platform as a way to protect her portrait: storing her portrait data should flag unauthorized use, and require any creator to apply for authorization through the platform before using her likeness.

That many report never receiving payments after licensing their faces could be because demand for non-celebrity likenesses is low. The head of AI production at a film and television company, surnamed Zheng, told CCTV that companies mainly seek celebrity and short-drama influencer likenesses, leaving little opportunity for regular people.
