Liu Xiao, founder of ActID, told Southern Metropolis Daily that the platform ultimately provides users with an entry point to be seen and selected by buyers, rather than a contract that guarantees monetization.

Criminals may also steal others’ likenesses for AI use rather than go through official channels like face-licensing platforms. On Oct. 8, Beijing’s market regulator warned that lawbreakers tend to scrape selfies, videos, and voices from social platforms and use AI to generate avatars and clone voices from this material for commercial and livestream use.

“Many celebrities cannot fully guarantee their portrait and voice rights, let alone facial licensing in the AI field,” Zheng said. “It’s hard for ordinary people to define how large the gray area (of legal portrait use) is.”

Additional reporting: Xu Ruishuo; editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: An authorization page on face-licensing platform NCAIGC, Aug. 26, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019112/A Decade On, Can China’s ‘Yoga Village’ Still Hold Its Pose?
World.title: A Decade On, Can China’s ‘Yoga Village’ Still Hold Its Pose?
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019112/A Decade On, Can China’s ‘Yoga Village’ Still Hold Its Pose?
World.content:
HEBEI, North China — It began with a “crazy” idea: use yoga to lift the village out of poverty. And it worked.

In 2016, yoga put Yugouliang on the map. Tucked away in the northern Hebei province, about 300 kilometers from Beijing, the village began attracting experts, journalists, and advertisers to watch its mostly elderly population perform stretches, headstands, and the splits beside crop fields, chicken coops, and sheep pens.

New revenue streams followed: livestream sales, online classes, yoga festivals, TV appearances, and even a movie. By 2020, the annual per capita net income for households under the national poverty alleviation program had reached 12,335 yuan ($1,840), up from 2,800 yuan in 2015, taking the village above the poverty line.

Today, a large stone marker proclaiming Yugouliang a “National Fitness Yoga Demonstration Village” still stands at the village entrance, but the national attention has long faded.

As the officials who drove the trend departed and the locals aged, the streets fell quiet, and the young people who had returned to help with social media marketing and sales left once again for better opportunities in major cities.

Yet 10 years on from that viral fame, yoga remains a force in many households here, either as a source of income or simply as a memory of how it opened a door to another world.

Stretching the imagination

When Jin Xiuying, then Yugouliang’s director of women’s affairs, was first tasked with going door to door to promote yoga in March 2016, she didn’t even know how to write the word in Chinese.

Naturally, she had a hard time convincing villagers. She recalls typical responses like, “Are you crazy? Farm work is exhausting enough. Who has time to exercise?” Others were confused and thought she was offering free fish, as the phrase sounds similar to “yoga” in Mandarin.

“Do me a favor, have a try,” she urged them. “The new official wants us to do it.”

She was referring to Lu Wenzhen, then 50, who had recently been appointed the village’s resident first secretary as part of a national program that dispatched officials from major cities to help develop impoverished rural areas. He’d previously been the Party secretary of a vocational college in Shijiazhuang, the Hebei capital.

Lu arrived that February, taking a seven-hour car ride to a village so remote that he couldn’t locate it on his map app.

Its 100 or so residents — mostly the middle-aged wives and elderly parents of migrant workers — survived by farming crops, raising cattle and sheep, or renting out their land. More than half survived on incomes of less than 2,952 yuan a year, below the official poverty line, while chronic illnesses like bronchitis, arthritis, and rheumatism were common due to years of physical labor and the cold climate.

In early 2016, the village still had no internet access, and playing mahjong or card games were among the few forms of entertainment. While visiting people’s homes, Lu observed that many elderly women would sit cross-legged for long periods on their kang, a traditional heated brick platform.

It reminded Lu of the lotus position in yoga — and that’s when he struck on the idea that this 5,000-year-old Eastern exercise could be the village’s ticket out of poverty. The locals could learn through movements they already knew: sitting on a kang, pulling weeds from the fields, and pushing a stone mill to make tofu.

The only issue was that Lu had never practiced yoga. So he watched instructional videos online, then taught others what he’d learned on an open field outside the village committee office.

He started with breathing exercises, getting villagers to stand with their legs bent, extend their arms in a circle in front of their chests, and make long “woo woo” sounds. Then they would crawl on all fours to strengthen their shoulders and backs and improve their balance. Yoga poses came later.

Lu bought 50 pairs of white gloves to protect his students’ hands during floor exercises, as well as 100 red foam yoga mats. Soon, nearly 70 villagers were showing up to his twice-daily training sessions, mostly women aged over 65.

At first, Jin received complaints from villagers about soreness, and she was still convinced that “Lu was just trying something out and wouldn’t stay long.” But after three months, the symptoms from her herniated disc began to ease, potentially saving her tens of thousands of yuan in medical costs, and others were reporting that they also felt healthier. So she persisted.

In March 2017, a producer from Hebei TV called to invite the village’s “yoga grannies” to perform in its studio. A month later, the state broadcaster CCTV broadcast a clip of Yugouliang residents in various poses.

The unprecedented attention inspired the locals to train harder to master tougher positions, such as the one-legged tree pose, the Sirsasana handstand, and lateral splits. More men began joining Lu’s sessions, and even the village’s superstitious hawks stopped suggesting that female yoga practitioners would bring about poor harvests by “pointing their backsides at heaven.”

Rising fortunes

In the summer of 2017, Jin’s daughter returned from university for the holiday and helped register an account on the Kuaishou short-video platform to promote “China’s yoga village.” In just over a year, it gained more than 300,000 followers.

Then came livestreaming. Most evenings, villagers would gather beside a concrete road to film themselves practicing yoga under the streetlights. They sold local products — potato noodles, red beans, soybeans, oat flour, and quinoa — and prerecorded yoga courses, which brought in thousands of yuan on a good day.

The income was divided according to how often each villager took part. Frequent participants were making more than 1,000 yuan a month, five times the rural pension at the time.

The group practiced year-round. In winter, they filmed in an abandoned single-story house after blocking holes in the walls and windows with old clothes and installing two coal-fired stoves to stay warm.

Wu Qilian, 83, who then practiced yoga with her husband, said that her grandson quit as a gig worker in Beijing to return home and run a social media account for the family. Livestreaming helped them earn several thousand yuan a year in additional income.

Yoga competitions and festivals were organized to attract visitors, while the village women continued to perform on TV shows across the country, wearing their signature blue headscarves and red athletic outfits.

“If you couldn’t do a headstand, if you weren’t good enough, they wouldn’t take you out to perform,” Li Xiufang told Sixth Tone. The 69-year-old returned to the village from Beijing after retiring at 55 and found “everyone was doing yoga, so I just joined in.”

Netizens dubbed Yugouliang “China’s No. 1 Yoga Village,” while the national sports authority designated it as a “National Fitness Yoga Demonstration Village.”

In 2022, the Chinese media giant Tencent released the movie “Welcome to Yoga Village” via its streaming service. A dramatized account of Lu’s poverty-alleviation efforts, it features several locals in minor speaking roles.

“Look at this. I’m a movie star,” said Zhang Xiying, 72, who had a few lines of dialogue. Pointing to a wall of photos in her home dedicated to her on-screen appearances, she added, “If I didn’t do yoga, who would invite an old woman like me anywhere?”

The village also secured more than 2.69 million yuan in government funding to build a small quinoa processing plant, creating 16 jobs. Many locals had switched to growing the grain because of its popularity among fitness enthusiasts.

On Feb. 29, 2020, Yugouliang was officially declared out of poverty.

Twist of fate

The boom times didn’t last long. Compared with other crops, quinoa requires deeper and more intensive tilling, so the aging villagers soon stopped growing it. Lu’s attempts to introduce a new variety of potato also failed when negotiations to secure a wholesale buyer broke down.

Livestream sales, which led to competition as well as resentment from families not sharing in the revenue, saw a sharp drop-off. After only a year back home, Wu’s grandson returned to Beijing to look for work.

Meanwhile, several members of the yoga group died, including Wu’s husband, or moved away to live with their children. Many of those remaining in the village are either too old to achieve difficult positions or have debilitating health issues.

Jin stepped down as the village’s director of women’s affairs in 2021. Residents say her successor promised to pay for yoga participation, but the money never materialized, so they stopped attending.

Liu Runtao, 58, took the role this year and has been struggling to put the team back together. She’d never practiced yoga before returning to the village in recent years. Now, when she posts notices about training sessions, usually only her relatives show up.

In villages like Yugouliang, organizing events and upgrading infrastructure often depend on approval and funding from town or county authorities. However, as officials change, so do their offices’ priorities.

Lu told Sixth Tone that he would sometimes win a higher official’s backing for a project only to see them transferred out before anything was finalized, taking things back to square one. Even when the village was at its most popular, funding to update its tourism facilities was slow to come.

Lu stepped down as resident first secretary in 2023 and returned to the vocational college in Shijiazhuang. Now 60, he still returns for major events and helps promote Yugouliang, but he feels it’s now someone else’s responsibility to keep the “yoga village” narrative alive.

Winding down

On one sunny July afternoon, a group of villagers sat chatting at a bus stop. Services pass through here just twice a day. Apart from the occasional truck carrying agricultural supplies, the main road is largely silent.

Liu had arranged a yoga training session, but just nine elderly women showed up. Most residents can no longer achieve the poses that made them famous. Only the septuagenarian Zhang can still balance with both feet off the ground.

The new resident first secretary, Li Jidong, who worked for the same Shijiazhuang college as Lu, watched from the sidelines. He has little interest in yoga, apparently seeing it more as a liability. “What if someone has a brain hemorrhage while doing it?” he said, after interrupting the session to suggest the elderly women attempt a safer activity.

Li believes that Yugouliang’s remote location and climate make Lu’s vision of building a tourism industry here difficult to realize.

“I don’t have that kind of ability. No single institution or person can solve a problem this big on their own,” he said. Li has only been in the job for two years but admits that he already wants to leave.

During a recent yoga event, Li asked people to help with livestream sales of local farm products, but the results were disappointing.

The village Party secretary, Zhang Pengcheng, who took over from his father in 2021, said he has also tried encouraging residents to make short videos and livestream, but many struggle even to use smartphones, let alone speak standard Mandarin with viewers online.

Yet he sees the remaining yoga team as the “embers” to spark a tourism boom. In 2025, he organized a gala in which the team performed on ice beside a bonfire. A livestream of the event drew about 100,000 viewers.

But for now, the priority is improving infrastructure. In July last year, the township government and local businesses funded the opening of a guesthouse with room for up to 86 guests. It has yet to turn a profit. When Sixth Tone visited, its doors and windows were shuttered.

The village has also built a canteen for pensioners, with dishes starting at just 2 yuan. It was also temporarily closed in July because of a staff shortage.

Before stepping down, Jin earned a yoga instructor qualification in Nanjing, capital of the eastern Jiangsu province, and has since relocated to Zhangbei Town, about 60 kilometers from Yugouliang. She offers free classes to locals and teaches online six days a week.

Of the few residents still practicing yoga in Yugouliang, Zhang Xiying, despite her age, remains the most able and enthusiastic — though not for the village’s benefit, but for her own family’s.

“Exercise keeps me healthy,” she said, after wrapping up a practice session. “And I need to take good care of my old man.”

Additional reporting: Wu Huiyuan; editor: Hao Qibao.

(Header image: Villagers practice yoga together on a summer afternoon in Yugouliang, Hebei province, July 2026. All photos by Wu Huiyuan/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019121/Divorcés Starring in TV Romances? China’s Internet Isn’t So Sure
World.title: Divorcés Starring in TV Romances? China’s Internet Isn’t So Sure
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019121/Divorcés Starring in TV Romances? China’s Internet Isn’t So Sure
World.content:
Popular Chinese TV drama “Against the Current” has sparked debate about power dynamics between divorced male characters and their female counterparts after featuring a romantic plot between a low-ranking young woman and a high-status divorced man.

The discussion began after the 48-episode drama premiered Sept. 11 on Tencent Video, its international platform WeTV, and Disney+, and was bolstered by this month’s release of a similar drama also featuring a divorcé, “Irreplaceable.”

Set in the Ming dynasty (1368–1644), “Against the Current” follows Shen Jialan, whose privileged life is upended when her grandfather, a renowned academician, is falsely accused of treason, endangering the lives of her entire family.

In exchange for a previous act of kindness, a couple allows Shen to take on the name of their late daughter, Xu Lanxiang, to escape execution. Under her new identity, Shen goes to work as a maid for her former fiancé, Lin Jinqi, who has since married another woman. Lin eventually divorces his wife to marry Shen.

After its release, the series became the most popular series on Disney+ in markets including North America and Spain, and topped WeTV charts in the U.S. and at least seven Asian countries outside China. Domestically, it currently tops analytics platform Yunhe Data’s long drama most-viewed list, with over a third of market viewership on Oct. 12.

Though the drama has been applauded for its storytelling and nuanced character development, some viewers have criticized Lin’s characterization, arguing that the show romanticizes unequal relationship dynamics, fueled by his status as a male divorcee. Lin, who divorces his wife after she cheats on him, curries favor with the King, asking him to force Shen to marry him against her will.

The debate has spread to other Chinese romance dramas that increasingly feature divorced and remarried male leads, from past hits such as “The Story of Minglan” (2018) and “The Glory” (2025), to dramas like “A Splendid Match” and “Irreplaceable” released this year.

Viewers have critiqued the imbalanced power dynamics in these series, which feature powerful, wealthy divorcés who offer protection, stability, and emotional guidance, often to younger, naive heroines from lower social statuses.

The recent popularity of remarried male leads marks a departure from the decadeslong shuangjie, or “purity on both sides,” trope in Chinese romance dramas, which favors depicting couples with no prior romantic or sexual experience before they fall in love.

In these stories, male leads are usually portrayed as successful, devoted figures whose affection belongs exclusively to the heroine, while female leads are frequently portrayed as innocent and kind.

Social media users have linked the shift to changing social realities, including rising divorce rates and the growing visibility of divorce and second marriages. Others have criticized it as a cheap way to create attention-grabbing plot twists, adding that the trend risks turning divorced males into a symbol of maturity and status while reinforcing unequal relationship dynamics.

Viewers point to the gender gap commonly found in romance narratives between divorcés and their female counterparts. When dramas instead feature divorced female protagonists, the corresponding male leads are often single or younger, and the story follows them as they “catch up” to their female counterparts professionally.

In the modern drama “Sniper Butterfly,” for instance, divorced protagonist Cen Jin reunites with a younger man who later becomes a successful professional in his own right as well as her business partner.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A still from “Against The Current.” From Douban)

World.title: [The Laylo Lens] What a stranded container is really costing us
World.content:
Government should implement a 100-day plan to enhance container movement reliability, ensure transparency in port charges, and separate regulatory and operational roles to prevent conflicts of interest

A truck may finish delivering goods, but it cannot take another job while carrying the empty container. If the shipping company’s storage yard has no room for the box, the truck and driver are left waiting.

Port delays affect even people who never go near a port. When goods reach factories and stores late, businesses incur costs that can eventually raise the family grocery bill.

Hapag-Lloyd, an international shipping company, has stopped accepting new bookings to Manila, Batangas, and Subic Bay until December 31, 2026, although the date may change. The company says it lacks enough space to store and return containers. The ports remain open; the suspension applies only to Hapag-Lloyd’s new bookings.

On October 5, the Bureau of Customs, which inspects imported goods and collects import taxes, said empty containers were piling up because storage yards had limited space. Ten days later, shipping company CNC sent some empty containers to a different return site in Cagayan de Oro because the usual yards were full.

How the delay reaches the household

Each delay adds another cost. A waiting truck earns less, but its owner must still pay the driver and repay loans. Businesses waiting for imported goods may need to borrow more money to keep operating. Small shops can lose sales when shelves are empty.

Smaller businesses may have little choice but to raise prices to cover these added expenses.

Food is especially at risk when shipments are delayed. On June 21, Customs reported that inspectors at the Manila International Container Port found 26 unclaimed containers of red onions that were already spoiling. Delays in documents, payments, or collection can turn food into waste.

Faster handling must still protect public health. Documents must be complete, inspections timely, food kept cold when required, and owners ready to collect it as soon as authorities approve its release.

Make responsibility clear

Shipping companies must provide return sites for empty containers and arrange for their removal or reuse. When a yard is full, they should direct truckers to another site and state clearly who will pay the added cost. Records of failed return attempts can help resolve billing disputes.

Importers also have a duty to keep cargo moving. On October 11, the Association of International Shipping Lines reported that loaded containers left too long at the Manila International Container Terminal were taking up space. Owners should collect released goods promptly. If an agency is the cause of delay, it should explain why and say when the goods will be released.

Port terminal operators must coordinate operating hours and truck access with storage yards, warehouses, and local governments. Keeping a port open overnight does little if the next facility that must receive the cargo is closed.

Port charges must be transparent. Businesses should know what each fee covers, who collects it, and how to challenge it. Government should also review bills for duplicate charges and fees without a proper basis.

PortCalls reported on October 8 that a proposed joint administrative order — a common set of rules from several government departments — was still awaiting signatures. The government should disclose whether it has been approved. If so, it should promptly publish the rules, their legal basis, their effective dates, and a process for filing and resolving complaints.

Give the public a result it can check

The government should launch a 100-day effort to restore reliable container movement. One department secretary should lead it, with authority to coordinate agencies. Representatives of shipping companies, port operators, truckers, cargo owners, and government agencies should meet daily to resolve specific delays. Weekly public reports should show how often yards reject empty containers, how long trucks wait, how many containers await collection, and how many complaints remain unresolved.

Funding should target the bottlenecks delaying deliveries now. More docking space will not help a truck that cannot return an empty container. Alongside new construction, government and industry must address storage capacity, access roads, working equipment, and reliable schedules.

Government should also review the conflict that arises when the same agency sets port rules and operates ports. In 2018, the Philippine Institute for Development Studies recommended separating these roles. Where one agency still does both jobs, an independent body should review charges and service standards.

The test of recovery is simple: deliveries arrive on time, charges are transparent, businesses receive reliable supplies, and drivers can finish one trip and begin the next.

Filipino families deserve reliable deliveries at fair prices. They should not bear the cost when companies and agencies fail to resolve delays within their control. – Rappler.com

Junie Laylo is a former Philippine ambassador to Israel and the founder of Laylo Research Strategies, a public opinion research firm. This piece on Laylo Lens was previously published on Facebook.

World.title: Notarization is finally available online. Here’s how it works.
World.content:
eNotarization makes the service more accessible to the public because under the 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice, traditional notary publics can only perform notarizations within their respective territorial jurisdictions

After years of preparation, the Supreme Court (SC) finally launched the country’s eNotarization system on Monday, October 19.

Notarization, according to Cambridge, is the process of having a public official (in the Philippines, a public notary lawyer) sign a letter, affidavit, or any legal document. Apart from converting a private document into public, this is done to verify a document’s legitimacy and authenticity, among others.

By launching eNotarization, the SC made the service more accessible to the public. This is because under the 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice, notaries public can only perform notarizations within their respective territorial jurisdictions.

The SC initially introduced remote notarization in 2020 in response to the COVID-19 pandemic restrictions. Subsequently, the SC formed a technical working group (TWG) led by Associate Justice Alfredo Benjamin Caguioa as chairperson and Associate Justice Ramon Paul Hernando as vice chairperson.

The TWG studied practices from other jurisdictions and consulted with several experts before finalizing the rules on electronic notarization. SC’s eNotarization microsite may be accessed through this link.

Terms, rules you should know

In February 2025, the SC approved AM No. 24-10-14-SC or the Rules on Electronic Notarization to make notarization more accessible and efficient. It formed part of the SC’s Strategic Plan for Judicial Innovations launched by outgoing Chief Justice Alexander Gesmundo.

As clarified by the High Court, eNotarization supplements and does not replace the traditional mode of notarial practice under the 2004 Rules on Notarial Practice.

The program introduced Electronic Notaries Public (ENPs), or lawyers authorized by the judiciary to perform notary services anywhere in the Philippines. This service may also be availed of by Filipinos overseas, subject to certain grounds.

“The ENP shall be allowed to perform any of the electronic notarial acts in the preceding Rule for a principal located outside the Philippines, provided that at the time of the performance of the electronic notarial act, the principal is within the premises of any of the embassies of the Philippines, Philippine consular offices, or offices of Philippine Honorary Consuls abroad,” said the rule’s Rule IV, Section 5.

“The eNotarization Rules applies (sic) exclusively to electronic documents in Portable Document Format (PDF) or Portable Document Format Archival (PDF/A). Paper documents with handwritten signatures, notarial wills, and depositions will continue to follow the 2004 Notarial Rules,” the SC clarified.

Meanwhile, to ensure digital safety, the eNotarization system uses multi-factor authentication like facial recognition, biometrics, and one-time passwords. All data stored under ENF are also protected by the Data Privacy Act, said the SC.

The SC also recently signed joint memorandum circulars (JMC) with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and Land Registration Authority (LRA) to establish the rules on processing eNotarized documents with these agencies.

SEC is the government agency mandated to oversee the “corporate sector, the capital market participants, and the securities and investment instruments market, and the protection of the investing public.” Meanwhile, LRA is the government body in-charge of handling land titling and registration affairs.

“On paper, we have signed two Joint Memorandum Circulars that categorically clarify the acceptability of eNotarized documents. In reality, we have done so much more. In the larger context of this partnership and development, our JMCs are a significant step towards innovation and access to justice,” said Caguioa.

How does it work?

A person who wishes to avail him/herself of eNotarization service must register through SC-accredited ENFs. There are three so far: Twala, QLegal, and NotarizeIT.

Registration portals of these ENFs may be accessed here. Instructional videos on how to use ENFs are also available here.

After registering, the user may choose an ENP from the list of commissioned ENPs. There are 100 accredited lawyers or ENPs so far in the SC list.

There are three forms of eNotarization under the new rules:

InPerson Electronic Notarization (IEN) – principals and witnesses must be present with the ENP. These parties must use the Electronic Notarization Facility (ENF) – or the eNotarization system and tools – within the same location.

Remote Electronic Notarization (REN) – clients may virtually connect to ENPs through videoconferencing.

Mixed

“Notarial act performed in accordance with the Rules shall have the same validity, force, and effect and may be relied upon to the same extent as any other notarial act performed under the 2004 Notarial Rules, provided, however, that the Rules shall not apply to the execution of notarial wills, deposition taking, and paper documents and instruments with wet signatures or marks,” said the rule’s Rule I, Section 5.

Like in traditional notarization, one who avails of eNotarization will get an electronic notarial certificate that contain the ENP’s electronic signature and electronic notarial seal. – Rappler.com

World.title: Pope Leo to hold Wednesday audience for first time since cancer surgery
World.content:
POPE. Pope Leo XIV gestures as he leaves after Palm Sunday Mass in Saint Peter's Square at the Vatican, March 29, 2026. REUTERS/Remo Casilli

Pope Leo pledges that he would slowly resume his usual activities as the leader of the world's 1.4 billion Catholics

VATICAN – Pope Leo will hold a general audience with pilgrims at the Vatican on Wednesday, October 21, for the first time since undergoing surgery for lung cancer, the Vatican said.

The 71-year-old pontiff had an operation on October 13 to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, fueling speculation about how his illness might change his 17-month papacy.

Leo pledged on Sunday, in his first public event since the surgery, that he would slowly resume his usual activities as the leader of the world’s 1.4 billion Catholics.

The pope hosts a general audience with pilgrims on most Wednesdays of the year. It is held in St. Peter’s Square when there is good weather, and the pope often tours the crowds, usually in the tens of thousands, in an open-top popemobile.

Leo has been diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer. The diagnosis, for the youngest pope in decades, who was elected only in May 2025, caused shock.

The pope’s doctors have said his surgery was completed successfully, without complications. They have not yet disclosed the size of the tumor or whether the disease had spread to nearby lymph nodes, key factors in determining prognosis.

The Vatican has provided no indication of Leo’s schedule beyond Wednesday.

The pope is due to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17, in one of the most intense trips arranged for a Catholic leader in decades, but it remains unclear if that trip will go forward.

Leo’s lead surgeon has said the pope could be fully recovered in time for the trip, but the Vatican’s secretary of state has indicated the pope may need to adjust the pace of his schedule to aid in recovery. – Rappler.com

World.title: France in turmoil: What might follow a weekend of riots?
World.content:
A masked protester holds a French flag as French police use water canon during a demonstration by French high school and university students in Paris, France, on October 13, 2026, as part of a nationwide protest movement demanding better school conditions and concrete measures.

Elections next year will see President Emmanuel Macron step down after a decade in power. The unrest is likely to give a boost to far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in polls who has long talked tough on law and order.

PARIS, France – France saw some of the worst unrest in years at the weekend as huge protests across the country over the cost of living and underfunded public services descended into riots and looting.

Limoges town hall was torched and more than 3,000 shops were pillaged or damaged, according to the government, as violent groups clashed with police in cities across the country.

While mayors of France’s biggest cities demanded answers from the government on Monday, October 19, over what they say was a lack of preparation, authorities rushed to set up support measures for impacted businesses and bolster security as calm returned to the streets.

Here is the latest on the situation in France:

What will the government do to quell the violence, compensate victims?

Some 2,400 people were arrested during the weekend and police investigators are poring over online videos and images to track down looters. Partial curfews are being organized in some municipalities while the government has said it will increase police numbers on the ground, especially for next weekend if it sees renewed protests. It has not specified how many extra officers will be made available.

For businesses and victims of the violence, the government is putting in place state-financed furlough measures to help employers avoid layoffs, and funds are being set aside to help companies meet their immediate cash flow needs. The government has yet to provide full details of the funding or how the money will be distributed. Insurers are also expected to cover some of the damage.

How will the government address complaints about the cost of living and public services?

France’s extremely strained public finances mean the government has precious little room for broader measures to address protesters’ anger over the rising cost of living.

It has already hiked emergency spending this year to help certain sectors like farmers, fishermen and haulers cope with high fuel costs caused by the Iran war.

The protests in France began last month at high schools in Paris’ working-class northern suburbs, where anger over teacher shortages and shabby facilities evolved into a broader movement.

The government has so far not committed to a substantial increase in funding for schools. However, it has pledged to send some 3,000 teachers, who are fully qualified but have not yet started work, to fill staffing gaps.

Will protests escalate or have they peaked?

Some protesters have already called for a new round of demonstrations on Saturday, October 24. Unions have called for strikes on November 5 to protest budget cuts and support hiking wages.

The weekend violence has largely eclipsed the recent high school student protests. Schools are now on a break for two weeks, but there have been reports of protests at some universities.

How will the crisis affect France’s dire economic situation?

The unrest will likely deal a blow to business confidence, which is already fragile due to a fiscal crisis and high energy prices resulting from the Iran war.

The minority government is struggling to pass spending cuts in France’s deeply divided parliament as part of its 2027 budget and is at risk of being toppled by opposition parties if a compromise cannot be found with at least some of them.

The unrest has weighed on French stocks and the euro and put pressure on French government bonds, pushing the risk premium over the 10-year German benchmark up to 146 basis points, the highest in two weeks.

Will the unrest spread to other countries?

If France cannot contain the unrest, there is a risk that it could spill across its borders. In neighboring Italy, clashes erupted between police and protesters on Sunday during demonstrations over poor public services and the rising cost of living.

Albania has also seen a series of student demonstrations in recent days over corruption, a lack of jobs and poor education standards, while Spain and Portugal have faced protests over housing.

How will the unrest affect the 2027 presidential election?

Elections next year will see President Emmanuel Macron step down after a decade in power. The unrest is likely to give a boost to far-right presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, who is already the frontrunner in polls to replace him and has long talked tough on law and order.

“Le Pen no longer needs to spend any money to campaign,” Jean-Baptiste Moreau, a former lawmaker from Macron’s camp, told Reuters. “It’s not just a clear path ahead of her, it’s a six-lane highway.”

Hard-left candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon has come under pressure for backing protesters’ demands, criticizing the government’s handling and not clearly condemning the violence.

Meanwhile, Macron, who headed off to the Middle East on Monday, has emerged from the crisis further weakened. His former prime minister Edouard Philippe, now a center-right presidential candidate, said on X he wanted “decisions and initiatives” from the lame-duck leader to “restore order.”

Are Paris and other cities safe to visit?

There have been no reports of any injuries to foreigners caught up in the unrest. However, several European governments advised citizens traveling to France to avoid large crowds and exercise caution. – Rappler.com

World.title: Alex Eala kicks off Ningbo Open campaign with win over Diane Parry
World.content:
VICTORY. Filipina tennis star Alex Eala advances to the round of 16 at the Ningbo Open after defeating France's Diane Parry.

Filipina tennis star Alex Eala advances to the round of 16 at the Ningbo Open after defeating France's Diane Parry in straight sets

MANILA, Philippines – Alex Eala got off to a strong start at the Ningbo Open in China as she defeated France’s Diane Parry, 6-3, 6-1, in the round-of-32 match on Monday, October 19.

The match, which lasted one hour and 17 minutes, had seen the two players tie at 3-3 before Eala found her momentum to eventually defeat Parry in straight sets.

The 21-year-old Filipina will advance to the round of 16 and will face either sixth-seeded Diana Shnaider of Russia or qualifier Yulia Putintseva of Kazakhstan.

“I’m very happy with my performance. I think it was a really good first round, a tough first round. Diane is a great player and I think she’s had a really good year so congrats to her for the year she’s done. I’m really happy to be in the second round,” Eala, who’s currently ranked world No. 20, said in a post-game interview.

The Filipina tennis ace’s Ningbo Open victory came just after her early exit at the Wuhan Open, where she conceded to World No. 177 Shi Han of China, 6-4, 3-6, 3-6, in the round of 64.

Previously, Eala had also settled for bronze at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, after absorbing a 3-6, 6-3, 6-2 loss at the hand of China’s Wang Xiyu in the semifinals of the women’s singles. – Rappler.com

World.title: Sandiganbayan suspends Marcoleta as senator | The wRap

Here are today’s headlines – the latest news in the Philippines and around the world:
