Dozens of puppies crowd into the enclosure, piled almost on top of one another. They huddle together and walk over each other’s heads. The footage shows that they are dirty; some are wet, while others look extremely thin. Their living conditions are clearly distressing and incompatible with the principles of humane treatment.

The shelter soon issued a response of its own. The regional Agency for the Management of Stray Animals published a statement on its Facebook page, saying that staff had been carrying out routine cleaning and had therefore gathered all the puppies in a single enclosure.

Activists dismissed the statement as an excuse. They argued that even if the staff had been cleaning, this should not have caused the animals to suffer or put them at risk.

Protests and animal rescue

The footage from Gori outraged animal rights activists, campaigners, animal lovers and other concerned members of the public. The videos spread rapidly across social media, and users soon began organising a protest outside the shelter.

The protest took place in Gori the following day, on Friday 16 October. It was noisy and saw several incidents. One report, for example, alleged that a shelter employee attacked a protester.

Nevertheless, the protesters managed to secure the release of most of the puppies. According to various reports, between 100 and 300 animals were removed from the Gori shelter. People launched a fundraising campaign and an urgent search for adopters. Several veterinary clinics joined the effort, offering to treat the rescued animals free of charge.

Abuses and new risks

That evening, activists told journalists that many of the animals had been diagnosed with a serious viral disease and that the weakest puppies had died on the way out of the shelter. They said the rescued animals drank and ate voraciously, which they believed indicated that the shelter had not provided them with enough food or water.

Other alleged violations included a lack of quarantine facilities, missing documents identifying where the puppies had come from, cold conditions and appalling sanitation. One enclosure reportedly housed sick and healthy animals together, alongside the remains of dogs that had died.

Veterinarians who joined the discussion highlighted another concern: the conditions at the Gori shelter could trigger viral outbreaks among dogs in Tbilisi and other cities.

Veterinarian Mariam Chkhikvishvili, for example, wrote that people should, where possible, treat the puppies rescued from Gori in a dedicated facility that allows them to maintain proper sanitary standards.

“Taking the puppies from one clinic to another makes very little sense: it could contribute to the spread of mutated viruses. We need to follow at least the basic rules of disease control: do not move infected puppies from place to place or put other animals — both pets and strays — at risk. These cases require an isolated facility where staff can properly clean and disinfect surfaces,” Chkhikvishvili said.

She added that Tbilisi had faced a similar crisis in the past, with cases in which serious diseases spread from a shelter in the capital.

A bad reputation

The footage has reignited debate in Georgian society about stray animals and how people treat them. But before examining this long-standing problem, which Georgia has struggled to resolve for decades, it is worth explaining why the images from Gori caused such an uproar.

At first glance, the public reaction might seem to stem from surprise, as though people had assumed the shelter met all the required standards, only to discover that it did not. In reality, the opposite is true: the Gori shelter had long been dogged by grim rumours, and the videos appeared to confirm them.

Activists have been raising concerns about poor living conditions and staff cruelty for years. This spring, the shelter even faced accusations of killing dogs on a large scale.

In April, footage spread across social media showing smoke rising from the Gori shelter’s crematorium at night. The person who filmed it claimed the crematorium had operated throughout the night and that a strong smell of burning hung over the site.

Animal rights activists suspected that staff were killing dogs in large numbers, including live animals. However, no convincing evidence emerged that anyone had burned animals alive, and the authorities never officially confirmed the allegations.

JAMnews covered the case in detail in an in-depth report on the mass capture of stray dogs and growing distrust of the state agencies responsible for their fate.

The October scandal was therefore far from the first time the Gori shelter had come under scrutiny. More than that, the events in Gori formed part of a much broader conflict between the state and animal rights activists, which has continued in Georgia throughout much of 2026.

Where do stray dogs disappear to?

In spring 2026, protests against the mass capture of stray dogs broke out in several Georgian cities. The demonstrations followed numerous reports of missing animals, including dogs that had been sterilised, vaccinated and cared for by so-called community carers — people who regularly feed, treat and look after strays without taking them into their homes.

A JAMnews report published on 23 May featured accounts from residents of different Georgian cities who were trying to find out what had happened to the dogs in their care and secure their return. In interviews with the publication, activists voiced fears that authorities were taking animals away from familiar surroundings and relocating them to places where they could not find food or water, effectively condemning them to die.

The authorities categorically deny allegations of mass killings. According to the official account, staff capture dogs as part of a state population management programme that includes veterinary examinations, sterilisation, vaccination and the subsequent return of animals to their habitat. Activists, however, say the programme captures all dogs, including those that underwent sterilisation long ago.

This raises one of the main contradictions. Under the programme’s rules, authorities cannot return animals to every location. Restrictions apply in areas near schools, kindergartens, medical facilities, markets and food outlets.

Yet stray dogs tend to live precisely around shops, markets and cafés. In cities such as Tbilisi, it would be difficult to find a street without a school, clinic or shop nearby. This raises an obvious question: where do the authorities take dogs that they cannot release at the places where they captured them? And who monitors what happens to the animals after they leave the shelter?

Animal rights activists who spoke to JAMnews say they have yet to secure a transparent, accessible system for tracking the fate of every captured animal.

Countless strays

Nobody knows exactly how many stray dogs live in Georgia. Despite the problem having persisted for decades, the country still lacks reliable nationwide statistics.

Relatively reliable figures exist only for Tbilisi, where the municipal Animal Monitoring Agency tracks the stray animal population. According to figures from the agency cited by JAMnews, the Georgian capital had around 29,676 stray dogs in 2025.

Animal rights activists estimate that Georgia could have hundreds of thousands of stray animals, but independent nationwide counts have yet to verify that figure.

The scale of the problem is also reflected in public attitudes. According to a CRRC Georgia poll for the National Democratic Institute (NDI), conducted in October 2023, 22% of respondents considered stray animals one of the country’s main social problems.

This comes as little surprise. Stray dogs are a familiar sight on Georgia’s streets. People encounter them near shops, markets, bus stops, residential courtyards and tourist areas. Many dogs wear special tags on their ears, indicating that they have undergone registration and veterinary procedures. Local residents and tourists often feed them.

However, peaceful coexistence between people and animals does not always work. Reports of dog attacks on people regularly emerge in Georgia, while the risk of rabies remains a public health concern. Calls to control the stray dog population and protect public safety therefore have a real basis.

Simply removing dogs from the streets, however, does not stop the population from growing. As long as pet dogs continue to breed without control and people abandon unwanted puppies, new animals will take the place of those authorities capture.

New laws, old problems

In 2025, Georgia’s parliament passed a law on pets intended to establish a unified legal framework for their care, registration and breeding control. In February 2026, the government approved a dedicated programme to manage the overpopulation of dogs.

The programme centres on an approach known as CNVR: capture, neuter, vaccinate and return. The World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) also describes this approach in its guidelines. When properly implemented, it can gradually reduce animal populations without resorting to mass culling.

However, the way authorities carry out each stage is crucial. Sterilisation must cover a substantial proportion of the population, vaccination must prevent the spread of disease, and the relocation and release of animals must take their welfare and public safety into account.

Georgian animal rights activists have raised numerous concerns about how the authorities implement these measures. They accuse state agencies of lacking transparency, mistreating animals, violating shelter standards and failing to monitor what happens to animals after their capture.

The overall effectiveness of government policy has also come under scrutiny. The authorities have tried to tackle the problem before, regularly announcing tenders over the years for sterilisation campaigns targeting stray animals in the regions. Yet the scale of the problem suggests that these programmes have failed to deliver significant results.

According to animal rights activists, private individuals still carry out much of the sterilisation work in practice. Animal carers and volunteers pay for operations, specialist non-governmental organisations take part, and volunteers from European countries travel to Georgia to help run sterilisation campaigns. Activists say state programmes reach far fewer animals than necessary, and they also question the quality of the work.

“Let the dog go”: where stray animals come from

Another serious problem is irresponsible ownership. In Georgia, people even use the common expression “let the dog go” to describe a practice in which owners take unwanted animals far from home and abandon them in a forest or by the roadside.

In rural areas, owners may abandon a dog because it hunts domestic poultry or otherwise “misbehaves”.

Energetic breeds that need plenty of attention and exercise are particularly vulnerable, as are hunting dogs that fail to meet their owners’ expectations. Meanwhile, effective controls on animal breeding remain largely absent.

The legal framework to tackle such practices already exists. Georgia’s 2025 Law on Pets explicitly prohibits owners from abandoning their animals and requires them to register their pets, partly to prevent such cases.

The law also introduces restrictions on dog breeding. Since July 2026, a three-year moratorium on breeding certain breeds has been in force.

The footage from the Gori shelter offers a glimpse of how effectively these rules work in practice. If the authorities properly enforced the law, many of the puppies found there — along with the hundreds of other emaciated and abandoned animals that people encounter along Georgian roads — might never have ended up on the streets.

Diana Petriashvili, Mediaset

Gori shelter

World.title: “No to torture!” Saturday march in Tbilisi. “Protests in Georgia” video podcast
World.content:
The “Saturday marches” are part of an ongoing protest movement that has continued in Georgia for 689 days.

Protesters are demanding that Georgia return to the path of European integration and that all political prisoners be released. They are also calling for the repeal of all anti-democratic laws passed by the ruling Georgian Dream party over the past two years.

Protesters and opposition parties point out that part of Georgian society still does not recognise the results of the parliamentary election held in autumn 2024. They are calling for early parliamentary elections.

Over the course of nearly two years of protests, dozens of people have been arrested. Many have been charged with criminal offences and sentenced to prison.

For the first time in independent Georgia’s history, the country has around 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the independent media outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. She was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer.

The protests continue despite an intensifying crackdown on civil society and the media.

World.title: Georgia: Billionaire Ivanishvili meets ruling party leaders – what is known about their talks after silent video release
World.content:
Ivanishvili Georgian Dream meeting

On 17 October, a rare political event took place in Georgia.

Bidzina Ivanishvili, founder and honorary chairman of the ruling Georgian Dream party, chaired a meeting of the party’s political council, followed by a meeting of the parliamentary majority, at the party’s central office.

This was the first public appearance in several months by Ivanishvili, whom many consider Georgia’s “shadow” ruler.

Yet it could hardly be called an “appearance”. Ivanishvili himself said nothing to journalists. The party’s press office released only silent footage of the meetings.

What was discussed behind closed doors became known through three sources: Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze’s briefing, the party’s written statement, and a brief comment by parliamentary majority leader Irakli Kirtskhalia.

Kobakhidze emphasised that Ivanishvili had expressed “pain” over his former team-mates who are in prison. This likely refers primarily to former Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili, who for many years was considered Bidzina Ivanishvili’s closest and most loyal ally but has now been convicted of large-scale corruption.

However, in the party’s statement, this issue is presented in a different tone.

It is stated that corruption problems within the team have been “fully and effectively” overcome.

While the meetings were underway, citizens protested outside the building under the slogan “Georgia against Ivanishvili”. One of the banners read, “Supporting Georgian Dream = betraying the country”, while another said, “14 bloody years”, referring to the years Georgian Dream has been in power.

Who joined the political council

The only publicly announced decision from the meetings was to expand the political council. Parliamentary majority leader Irakli Kirtskhalia and Zurab Pataradze, head of the government of the Autonomous Republic of Ajara, joined the body.

Footage released by the press office shows Ivanishvili entering the meeting, shaking hands with MPs and taking his seat. Irakli Kobakhidze, parliamentary speaker Shalva Papuashvili, Tbilisi Mayor Kakha Kaladze and Irakli Kirtskhalia sat beside him at the head table. Ministers were also present.

According to Kobakhidze, both meetings addressed current domestic and foreign policy issues. The party statement referred to “political and economic processes” in the country. It also said time was devoted to initiatives and reforms recently announced by the government.

The context behind Ivanishvili’s meetings with ruling party leaders

Bidzina Ivanishvili rarely appears in public. He has been under US sanctions since 2024.

His participation in party meetings on 17 October came amid an apparent crisis within the government.

Former senior Georgian Dream officials have been arrested one after another on corruption charges.

The most high-profile case involves former Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili.

In January 2026, he was sentenced to five years in prison under a plea agreement. In August, prosecutors brought a new bribery charge against him.

Gharibashvili has been publishing letters from prison in which he accuses Irakli Kobakhidze and former Deputy Prime Minister Mamuka Mdinaradze. On August 27, Mamuka Mdinaradze resigned from his post and announced his departure from politics. He denied any connection to the letters.

Another important factor in the context of Ivanishvili’s meeting with ruling party leaders is that the Constitutional Court is due to hear the authorities’ case seeking to ban opposition parties in just a few days.

According to opposition representatives, hearings were scheduled for October 21, 22 and 23. In response, an alliance of nine opposition parties announced a rally in Tbilisi on 25 October under the slogan “Georgia without Ivanishvili. Georgia deserves better.”

Gharibashvili is Ivanishvili’s “heartache” – and the statement about “overcoming difficulties”

After the meetings at the ruling party’s office, journalists asked Irakli Kobakhidze whether the possibility of releasing former Prime Minister Irakli Gharibashvili from prison had been discussed.

Kobakhidze replied that there had not. According to him, Ivanishvili gave a general assessment of “the developments”.

“For all of us, including, of course, first and foremost, Bidzina Ivanishvili, what happened is painful, when events unfold this way and former members of the team are serving sentences for specific crimes (…)”, Kobakhidze said.

He added: “What happened is regrettable. It was, of course, something of a blow to the team.”

Gharibashvili was sentenced to five years in prison in January 2026 following a plea agreement. In August, prosecutors brought a new charge against him. According to the prosecution, the former prime minister accepted 750,000 lari (about $290,000) in bribes.

Gharibashvili’s lawyers say he denies the new charge.

There is no mention of “heartache” in the party statement’s account of the same subject. According to the statement, Ivanishvili reviewed the corruption challenges the team had faced in the past and said that “as a result of the effective work of the prime minister, the government team and the security apparatus, these challenges have been fully and effectively overcome”.

Kobakhidze: “Friendship is none of your business“

Kobakhidze said the team had also discussed Mamuka Mdinaradze, a former deputy prime minister who previously served as head of the State Security Service.

Mdinaradze resigned from his post on August 27 and announced his departure from politics. At the time, he denied that his resignation was connected to Garibashvili’s letters published from prison.

Kobakhidze declined to elaborate publicly. “Mamuka Mdinaradze has left politics”, he said, adding that he did not consider it appropriate to bring the issue to the fore in these circumstances. He said he remained in occasional contact with Mdinaradze. He did not give a direct answer when asked whether they were still friends.

“Why are you asking about friendship? Friendship is none of your business”, he told journalists.

Journalists also raised the issue of a controversial social media post by Georgian Dream party member Dito Samkharadze, who wrote that “rats” [informers] had been identified within the ruling party.”

Kobakhidze was asked whether Samkharadze also meant Mdinaradze and whether legal proceedings against him were expected.

“I don’t know what you’re referring to,” the prime minister replied. He said there was “no basis whatsoever” for such speculation.

Parliamentary majority leader Kirtskhalia: “Ivanishvili spoke mostly about Kobakhidze“

Journalists asked Irakli Kirtskhalia to comment on growing public speculation that Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze could soon resign.

According to him, Ivanishvili devoted more time to Kobakhidze than to anyone else, “expressing support and praise, which the entire team, of course, shares”.

“Ivanishvili said that the government is performing very well under Kobakhidze’s leadership, and that not only is there no reason for his resignation, but every day confirms that he is the best prime minister,” Kirtskhalia said.

He described the resignation rumours as gossip spread by the opposition.

Scandal over possible corruption in spending on the Patriarch’s funeral

At a press briefing, Irakli Kobakhidze addressed the main political issue: allegations of possible corruption in spending on the Patriarch’s funeral.

He said preliminary information from the Government Administration showed “no indication of any improper expenditure”. He also said a large portion of the allocated funds had been returned.

In September, speaking on Rustavi 2, Kobakhidze provided specific figures: according to preliminary data, 722,000 lari (about $275,000) of the 3 million lari (about $1,100,000) allocated had been spent. The questions he answered concerned former Culture Minister Tika Rukhadze’s possible involvement in the alleged embezzlement.

Kobakhidze said detailed information would be presented to the public in the near future. Asked whether investigative agencies should look into the matter, he replied:

“First, we will present detailed information to you, and if any questions remain on this issue, let us discuss them together.”

“Whatever they call us, we keep winning” – Kobakhidze on media restrictions

Irakli Kobakhidze also commented on restrictions on the use of various words and expressions in the media adopted by the Communications Commission.

On 9 October, Transparency International – Georgia reported that the Communications Commission had objected to expressions used by independent TV channels Formula and Pirveli. The commission compiled a list of 93 words and phrases that it banned from use, including “regime”, “oligarch” and “prime minister appointed by Ivanishvili”, according to TI. Fines for using words on the list were increased to 10,000 lari (nearly $4,000).

Kobakhidze explained the decision as necessary to uphold the principle of objectivity.

He said these rules had existed in legislation for years, but an enforcement mechanism had not previously been in place. News programmes are now required to maintain neutrality.

That requirement does not apply to programmes expressing their hosts’ own views, Prime Minister said.

“Nothing bothers us. We win elections and emerge victorious from every political confrontation. Whether they call us a regime or a dictatorship, we win either way”, Kobakhidze said.

News in Georgia

World.title: More than 2,500 people detained during protests in France
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. A total of 2,513 people have been detained during protests and riots in France that have been ongoing since October 17, while 67 others have been remanded in custody, French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin said.

Commenting on the arson attack on the town hall in Limoges, carried out by rioters and resulting in the complete destruction of the building’s bell tower, the minister said that the National Anti-Terrorism Prosecutor’s Office could join the investigation in the near future.

On October 17, mass demonstrations were held in Paris and other French cities to protest rising fuel prices and declining purchasing power. The organizers claimed that 800,000 people had taken part in the demonstrations, while France’s Ministry of the Interior put the figure at 550,000.

In several cities, the demonstrations escalated into riots and clashes between police and protesters. French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez stated that those involved in the riots and looting would be held accountable.

World.title: Uzbekistan’s textile exports rise 26.9% to $2.1B in eight months
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. Uzbekistan’s textile exports increased by 26.9% year over year to $2.1 billion in January–August 2026, accounting for 9.4% of the country’s total exports.

This was reflected in the statement by the National Statistics Committee of Uzbekistan.

The value of textile shipments rose by approximately $445 million compared with the same period in 2025, when exports totaled an estimated $1.65 billion, according to Trend’s calculations.

Finished textile products accounted for the largest share of exports at 51%, followed by yarn at 32%, knitted fabric at 8%, fabrics at 6%, hosiery products at 2% and carpets at 1%.

Based on the reported export value of $2.1 billion, finished textile products generated approximately $1.07 billion in export revenue during the first eight months of 2026. Yarn exports amounted to around $672 million, while knitted fabric exports totaled approximately $168 million. Exports of fabrics reached an estimated $126 million, followed by hosiery products at $42 million and carpets at $21 million.

Finished textile products and yarn together accounted for 83% of textile exports, equivalent to approximately $1.74 billion. This highlights the importance of these two categories to Uzbekistan’s textile export earnings.

Textile products represented 9.4% of Uzbekistan’s total exports during the reporting period, underscoring the sector’s role in the country’s export structure. The year-over-year increase in textile export value also indicates stronger export earnings from the sector compared with the first eight months of 2025.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s exports grow four times faster than imports
World.content:
Photo: Ministry of Investment, Industry and Science of the Moscow region of Russia

BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. Kazakhstan's exports grew by 19.5% year-on-year in January-August 2026, more than four times the 4.5% increase in imports, with the country's trade surplus reaching $17.8 billion, according to data from the Ministry of Trade and Integration of Kazakhstan.

Kazakhstan's foreign trade turnover reached $103 billion in the first eight months of 2026, up 12.8% compared to the same period in 2025.

Exports totaled $60.4 billion, while imports amounted to $42.6 billion. The trade surplus widened to $17.8 billion, compared with $9.8 billion in January-August 2025.

The country's agricultural sector recorded notable export growth, with increases in both agricultural raw materials and processed products.

Exports of sunflower oil rose by 48.5% year-on-year to $672.8 million. In physical terms, shipments increased by 35.9% to 611,400 tons.

In 2025, Kazakhstan ranked among the world's top six sunflower oil exporters and was the second-largest supplier to China. The country also ranked among the top three suppliers of sunflower meal to the European Union and China and supplies a significant share of demand in Central Asian countries, according to the ministry.

Wheat exports increased by 26.5% to $1.25 billion. More than 5.5 million tons of grain were shipped abroad, up 13.8% compared to the same period last year.

Exports of wheat and wheat-rye flour reached $400 million, an increase of 36%. In volume terms, shipments grew by 22.8% to 1.38 million tons.

Flaxseed exports more than doubled in value, rising 2.3 times to $387.8 million. Physical shipments increased 2.5 times to 780,800 tons.

Exports of prepared animal feed products also increased. Their value rose by 60.8% to $577.6 million, while shipment volumes grew by 44.2%.

Combined exports of sunflower oil, flour and prepared animal feed products reached $1.65 billion, up approximately 48% in value compared to January-August 2025, reflecting growth in exports of processed agricultural products.

Outside agriculture, export revenues from metals and mining products also increased. Shipments of copper and copper cathodes rose by 55.7% to $3.9 billion, while uranium exports increased by 26.9% to $3.1 billion.

On the import side, Kazakhstan increased purchases of industrial and energy equipment. Imports of electric generating sets rose by 86.5% to $916.5 million, while imports of turbojet and turboprop engines, including gas turbines, increased 3.3 times to $611 million.

China remained Kazakhstan's largest trading partner, with bilateral trade reaching $23.3 billion in January-August 2026, accounting for 22.7% of the country's total foreign trade turnover. Russia ranked second at $18.3 billion, followed by Italy at $11.8 billion. Together, the three countries accounted for more than half of Kazakhstan's foreign trade.

Italy was Kazakhstan's largest export destination, with shipments totaling $10.9 billion, slightly ahead of China at $10.7 billion. Russia remained the largest supplier of imported goods to Kazakhstan, with imports amounting to $13.2 billion.

"The growth in exports of agricultural products, primarily sunflower oil, flour and prepared animal feed, indicates an expansion in supplies of value-added goods and the potential for further strengthening the position of Kazakh products in foreign markets," the ministry said.

Kazakhstan is seeking to diversify its exports by reducing dependence on a narrow range of commodities and expanding supplies of non-resource goods to foreign markets. Kazakhstan's Vice Minister of Trade and Integration Aset Nusupov told Trend in an exclusive interview that the country sees significant potential for expanding cooperation with Azerbaijan in the agro-industrial and industrial sectors.

"Kazakhstan is one of the largest producers of grain, oilseeds and meat, while Azerbaijan represents a growing market; therefore, the potential for mutual food trade remains significantly underutilized," Nusupov said.

World.title: Iran's electricity imports from Azerbaijan reach over 33M kWh
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. Iran imported 33.16 million kilowatt-hours of electricity from Azerbaijan in January–August 2026, generating $942,000 in revenue for Azerbaijan, according to the State Statistical Committee of Azerbaijan.

According to Trend’s calculations, electricity exports to Iran increased by 12.237 million kilowatt-hours, or 1.6 times, compared with the same period in 2025. In value terms, exports rose by $348,000, also increasing 1.6 times.

Meanwhile, Azerbaijan imported 23.806 million kilowatt-hours of electricity from Iran worth $676,000 in the first eight months of 2026. Compared with the same period in 2025, the value of imports increased by $57,000, or 9.2%, while their volume rose by 2.011 million kilowatt-hours, or 9.2%.

In January–August 2026, Azerbaijan exported a total of 319.040 million kilowatt-hours of electricity worth $16.629 million to three countries: Russia, Georgia and Iran.

Compared with the same period in 2025, Azerbaijan’s electricity exports fell by $36.105 million, or 3.2 times, in value terms and by 600.885 million kilowatt-hours, or 2.9 times, in volume terms.

During the same period, Azerbaijan imported 143.724 million kilowatt-hours of electricity worth $7.0945 million from these countries. Compared with the first eight months of 2025, the value of imports increased by $2.146 million, or 43.4%, while their volume rose by 28.1 million kilowatt-hours, or 24.3%.

Economic cooperation between Azerbaijan and Iran continues to develop across trade, transportation, energy, transit and logistics. The two countries are deepening cooperation under the International North–South Transport Corridor and implementing joint initiatives involving electricity and natural gas exchanges.

The two sides are also working to increase bilateral trade, expand cross-border economic ties, strengthen industrial cooperation and promote investment projects, with energy remaining a key area of bilateral cooperation.

World.title: Azerbaijan reduces greenhouse gas emissions
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. Azerbaijan reduced its greenhouse gas emissions in 2025 compared with the previous year.

According to the 2026 report prepared by the European Commission’s Emissions Database for Global Atmospheric Research (EDGAR), the country’s total emissions fell from 58.52 million tons in 2024 to 57.72 million tons of CO₂ equivalent in 2025. This represents a decrease of 0.8 million tons, or approximately 1.4%.

The report puts Azerbaijan’s share of global greenhouse gas emissions at 0.11%, down from the 2024 level. This was recorded against the backdrop of a 0.7% increase in global emissions in 2025, bringing the total to 54.15 billion tons.

According to the 2026 EDGAR report, total greenhouse gas emissions in regional countries in 2025 were distributed as follows:

- Russia: 2.57 billion tons — 4.75% of global emissions;

- Iran: 1.12 billion tons — 2.07%;

- Türkiye: 610.78 million tons — 1.13%;

- Azerbaijan: 57.72 million tons — 0.11%.

According to the report, China was the world’s largest source of greenhouse gas emissions in 2025, accounting for 15.98 billion tons of CO₂ equivalent, or 29.51% of the global total.

U.S. emissions amounted to 6.02 billion tons, representing 11.11% of the global total, while India accounted for 4.51 billion tons, or 8.33%.

Thus, Azerbaijan’s reduction in emissions in 2025, despite the rise in global figures, serves as further evidence of the country’s commitment to its voluntarily undertaken environmental obligations.

World.title: Uzbekistan, U.S. sign agreements worth $12 billion
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. Business representatives from Uzbekistan and the United States have signed agreements worth a total of $12 billion following a meeting of the American-Uzbek Business and Investment Council held in Samarkand. This was reported by the press service of Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Investment, Industry and Trade.

“A package of 54 agreements in trade, investment and technological cooperation was signed as part of business events held during the visit of the U.S. delegation to Uzbekistan. Their implementation provides for investments totaling $12 billion,” the statement said.

The agreements are aimed at modernizing Uzbekistan’s industrial sector, transport and energy infrastructure, developing critical mineral resources, and advancing the financial sector, digital technologies, agriculture, healthcare and education.

In the transport sector, cooperation with GE Aerospace предусматривает the supply of engines for new Uzbekistan Airways aircraft. Meanwhile, initiatives with Wabtec focus on localizing the production of railway equipment and components, helping modernize the industry technologically and expand domestic manufacturing capabilities.

Agreements with companies including Franklin Templeton, Oppenheimer & Co., Citigroup and BlackRock are expected to help Uzbek companies access international capital markets, attract institutional investors and secure financing for infrastructure projects.

Agreements and cooperation with ReElement Technologies, Traxys and Trafigura in the mining sector are aimed at developing new deposits, promoting technological cooperation and supplying mineral resources. Particular emphasis was placed on strengthening Uzbekistan’s domestic capabilities in the critical minerals sector.

Meanwhile, projects in the digital and social sectors involving Amazon Leo, GE HealthCare and Valmont Industries предусматривают the development of satellite communications, the introduction of advanced medical technologies and improvements in agricultural efficiency.

“The signed package lays the foundation for a new stage in Uzbek-American economic cooperation, combining international capital and advanced technologies with Uzbekistan’s industrial potential. The next priority will be to consistently translate the agreements reached into tangible results,” the ministry’s press service added.

World.title: Chronicles of Victory: October 20, 2020
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 20. The Azerbaijani Army launched a counter-offensive operation, later called the "Iron Fist", on September 27, 2020, in response to the large-scale provocation of the Armenian armed forces along the frontline.

The erupted 44-day Second Karabakh War ended with the liberation of Azerbaijan’s territories from nearly 30-year Armenian occupation and the restoration of territorial integrity.

Trend presents the chronicle of the 24-th day of the second Karabakh war:

- President Ilham Aliyev addressed the people of Azerbaijan.

- In his address to the people, President Ilham Aliyev said that the city of Zangilan and 24 villages had been liberated from occupation.

- President Ilham Aliyev renamed the liberated Vang village of Khojavand district to Chinarli.

- First Vice President of Azerbaijan Mehriban Aliyeva shared a publication on her Instagram account about the liberation of the city of Zangilan and a number of villages of Fuzuli, Jabrayil, Khojavand and Zangilan districts.

- The Azerbaijani flag was raised in Zangilan.

- Video footage of the destruction of Armenian armored vehicles had been released. The list of destroyed Armenian military equipment had been announced. A group of mercenaries from the Armenian side refused to fight.

- Armenian Armed Forces shelled the territories of Tartar and Aghdam districts, killing two civilians.

- Video footage of the destruction of a large number of Armenian servicemen and military equipment had been released.

- Armenian anti-aircraft guns were destroyed in the direction of Ganja.

- Video footage of the destruction of units of the Armenian Armed Forces in the direction of Gubadli had been released.

World.title: Diamonds boosted by imminent return of vice-captain
World.content:
Diamonds vice-captain Kate Moloney is on track to return from injury and give Australia a much-needed boost for the Constellation Cup.

Moloney was forced to watch the netball world's number-one side suffer a shock 56–50 loss to the Silver Ferns from the sidelines after a finger laceration in the lead-up to the Auckland series opener.

The Diamonds were already without defender Jo Weston (managed), and the experienced duo was sorely missed against the Commonwealth Games champions.

Diamonds centurions forced to the bench in Constellation Cup loss It was defender Courtney Bruce's 100th milestone game to start the Constellation Cup but the brand new centurion and her captain Liz Watson were both sent to the bench in Australia's 56-50 loss to New Zealand in Auckland.

New Zealand stormed to a 15-goal lead in the first of four matches, forcing Diamonds coach Stacey Marinkovich to bench captain and midcourter Liz Watson alongside goalkeeper Courtney Bruce in her 100th game.

Jamie-Lee Price took over centre duties against New Zealand's Adelaide Lightning star Kate Heffernan, while Jessie Grenvold was tasked with containing Silver Ferns goalscoring superstar Grace Nweke on debut.

Australia were able to cut the deficit to just six goals in the fourth quarter, but the damage had been done.

Georgie Horjus was the only Diamond who remained on the court for four quarters, finishing with a game-high 19 gains and 38 feeds as wing attack.

With the Diamonds set to name their squad on Tuesday night, Marinkovich said Melbourne Vixens captain Moloney's return was imminent.

"We'll definitely see her back in the series," Marinkovich said.

"It was a bit of a nasty laceration to her finger, so we had to wait till it pretty much stuck back together.

"It's just one of those innocuous things that happen at training, but she's been able to do all the running and the movement, and yeah, look forward to having her back."

But the midcourt will not be the only area of focus for Wednesday night's game in Christchurch.

Looking to end their five-year drought on Kiwi soil, the Diamonds will need to find a way past the towering defensive duo of Kelly Jackson and Karin Burger.

With goalkeeper Jackson standing at 192cm and goal defence Burger at 184cm, Australia's attacking roster of Kiera Austin, Cara Koenen, Sophie Dwyer and Sophie Garbin struggled to fire.

Marinkovich is urging her Diamonds to start with "immediacy" on the court.

"We were slightly off our pace [in game one], and our numbers would show that we weren't as aggressive as what we needed to be on the ball," she said.

ABC Sport will have live blog coverage of Game II between the Diamonds and Silver Ferns on Wednesday, October 21.

AAP

World.title: Jockeys cleared over Ohope Wins's fatal Caulfield Cup fall
World.content:
A Racing Victoria investigation into the fall at the Caulfield Cup that resulted in the euthanasia of Ohope Wins has finished, clearing all jockeys involved of any wrongdoing.

Ohope Wins, ridden by Jye McNeil, and Half Yours, ridden by Mark Zahra, both went down in the final straight at the 150th running of the famous 2,400m race.

Zahra and Half Yours fell first after getting tangled up in the pack chasing eventual winner Kingswood, with Ohope Wins going over the top of the fallen gelding.

Loading...

Last year's Melbourne Cup winner Half Yours suffered superficial cuts and scrapes, but Ohope Wins was assessed on track as having a "serious racing injury" and was put down by on-course veterinarians.

Both jockeys were thrown from their mounts and taken to hospital, delaying the conclusion of the inquiry into the incident, which once again prompted calls for the racing industry to be made more accountable for racehorse deaths.

After hearing evidence from McNeil, Zahra and three other jockeys in the race, Racing Victoria stewards said they "could not attribute the incident to the careless actions of any one particular rider".

The hearing at Racing Victoria headquarters found contact between Kings Valley and Green Spaces with about 300 metres to go resulted in the latter becoming unbalanced.

Half Yours ran the rest of the course without a rider. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Green Spaces, ridden by Rachel King, then turned inward and made more contact with apprentice rider Jabez Johnstone's Kings Valley, who then turned inward, resulting in Half Yours being squeezed for room between Kings Valley and Zahrann.

"A short distance later, Half Yours subsequently fell," the stewards' report read.

"Ohope Wins that was trailing was subsequently brought down when unable to avoid the fallen Half Yours."

The incident has been referred to Racing Victoria's Veterinary Services Department, as is standard practice.

Trainer Tony McEvoy said Half Yours was recovering well from injuries and would be rested, while Zahra was meeting with doctors today about a timeline around his return to riding.

McNeil was cleared of any injury and is expected to ride at the Geelong Cup tomorrow.

World.title: NT senator says child protection 'needs to change' after niece's alleged murder
World.content:
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of her family.

Northern Territory Senator Jacinta Nampijinpa Price says the "culture of child protection" in Australia "needs to change" after the "utter failings" of the NT's child welfare system in the lead up to her niece's alleged murder were laid bare.

Kumanjayi Little Baby review finds extensive failings An independent review into the NT child protection department's conduct surrounding Kumanjayi Little Baby before her alleged murder has revealed extensive failings.

Speaking after a review into the department's contact with Kumanjayi Little Baby's family was tabled in NT parliament this morning, Senator Nampijinpa Price said her five-year-old niece had been "let down" by the system.

"It just exposes the stark reality of the utter failings of a system that is supposed to protect our most vulnerable, our children," she told the ABC.

"My niece was let down and I know so many other children who have been let down over the years and it's finally been revealed as to why this is the case and it's just not good enough."

Five-year-old Kumanjayi Little Baby went missing from the Old Timers town camp earlier this year. (Supplied: NT Police)

The report by former NSW Police Commissioner Karen Webb and longtime NT public servant Greg Shanahan found there were extensive failings by the Department of Children and Families before Kumanjayi went missing from an Alice Springs town camp in April, making 45 recommendations.

Jefferson Lewis, 47, was charged with the five-year-old girl's murder in May following a five-day manhunt.

He is yet to enter a plea and will return to the Alice Springs Local Court in December.

Ms Price said the report showed a domestic violence risk assessment had not been carried out for her niece and those who had been noted as "safety people were not safe individuals at all".

Angus Taylor and Jacinta Nampijinpa Price were among those to visit the memorial for Kumanjayi Little Baby in Alice Springs earlier this year. (Supplied: Country Liberal Party)

"The continued notifications, the lack of process … words sort of escape me as to how much failure existed, which ended up in the situation where I lost my niece," she said.

She also criticised the child protection response of some organisations, who she said had an "ideological approach" to Indigenous affairs "based on this idea that culture is the be all and end all over and above prioritising the safety of vulnerable women and children".

"They would probably have argued that my niece should not be removed and in the end we lost her," she said.

"I think the system treats Aboriginal women and vulnerable children, [it] doesn't treat them like Australian citizens, that's for sure, where their human rights and their safety need to be upheld."

In parliament earlier today when she tabled the review, NT Minister for Child Protection Robyn Cahill attributed the lack of progress in child safety to Labor governments who she said "put so-called progressive beliefs ahead of child safety".

"A child's culture matters but it can never come before safety," she said.

Earlier this year, vigils were held around the country in honour of Kumanjayi Little Baby. (ABC News: Emma Masters)

Ms Cahill labelled the child protection system as being "in crisis" across the country — a sentiment echoed by Ms Price who has called for a coordinated national approach to child protection.

"I think what the Northern Territory has just been through … every state and territory should go through the same process to ensure that child protection is working right around the country, not just for the benefit of Indigenous children, but for the benefit of all children," Ms Price said.

"The culture of child protection needs to change.

Ms Price said she hadn't yet had the opportunity to go through the report with Kumanjayi Little Baby's other family members, but that "they've all been really wanting to understand more deeply" what had happened.

Ms Cahill said the government accepted all 45 recommendations of the report in full.

World.title: Hit-and-run crash leaves cyclist dead in Perth's south
World.content:
A 40-year-old man has died in an apparent hit-and-run incident after being struck by an unknown vehicle while cycling south of Perth.

Police said the man was hit by the car while riding along North Lake Road in the suburb of Bibra Lake around 5:20am on Tuesday.

Police are searching for the driver of the vehicle. (ABC News: Jasmine Hughes)

The 40-year-old was declared dead at the scene, and police said the driver remains at large.

Major Crash investigators are examining the scene, and urge anyone who may have witnessed the incident, or has dash cam footage, to contact Crime Stoppers.

World.title: How childlessness grief can reappear later in life
World.content:
Allison Macaulay-Dear's best friend recently became a grandmother.

"I was thrilled for her obviously," the 62-year-old from South Australia says.

"But it's still painful."

That's because Allison couldn't have children of her own. And it's moments like these when the pain of childlessness feels sharper.

"It just hurts. I haven't got little babies around me and never will. That part is difficult," she says.

Sarah Roberts is a childlessness grief counsellor and lived experience advocate based in Brisbane/Meanjin.

She says while many women adjust to the grief of being childless not by choice over time, living in a culture geared towards families can highlight an "absence of intergenerational relationships".

A timeline of grief

For some childless people, the grief follows a timeline of the baby they never had, says Ms Roberts.

Loving one another through childlessness When IVF didn't work, Susanne and Mike Armour had to face the difficult decision to stop trying for a baby. The couple say their love for one another got them through.

"The child that they are grieving for can age as their peers' children do.

"Loss of a baby, then loss of the school years, then the young adult relationship.

"And then it can be the next generation having their own children."

Allison was only 20 when she had a hysterectomy due to a combination of medical issues. She saw a psychologist at the time who suggested a private writing exercise.

"He said, 'Write a letter to the child you you're never going to have with all the things you would have liked to have done with that child.'

"I [wrote] about me taking them to school for the first time. Those milestones when you're a proud mum.

"I thought it was a good thing, to put those feelings on paper."

The 'pain points' of menopause, retirement and aging

Sarah Roberts says chidlessness grief can follow a timeline of the baby someone never had. (Supplied)

Pain points past the "acute" initial grief of childlessness can happen during perimenopause and menopause, Ms Roberts says.

"We are hit in that sense that 'my biological fertility is really over.'"

During retirement, she says grandchildren can provide someone with a sense of validation — "like a meaningful role they can take on".

"Also that opportunity to just delight in children and have that meaningful relationship without having to necessarily be responsible for them. And it's an added layer of connection to their own children."

That can be quite "tender" for a childless person to witness, Ms Roberts says, for example when approached by friends enthusiastically sharing stories and photos of grandkids.

Aging can bring up fears around not having children to lean on for support, too.

Adult children can provide their parents with physical care, social connection, incidental care — "Help, my TV remote isn't working!" — and advocacy, Ms Roberts says.

"I will often have women downplay their anxieties, saying, 'You can't rely on kids' … but often when the shit hits the fan, kids do step in in some way."

For support with childlessness: World Childless Week (for counsellors, therapists and support networks)

(for counsellors, therapists and support networks) Lifeline on 13 11 14

on 13 11 14 Beyond Blue on 1300 224 636

on 1300 224 636 Red Nose Grief and Loss 24/7 Support Line on 1300 308 307

Grief and Loss 24/7 Support Line on 1300 308 307 Bears of Hope (infant loss support for families) on 1300 114 673 We have included a range of helplines here knowing people have many different experiences of childlessness.

Finding meaning and purpose

Ms Roberts is 57 and says she spent a "good decade" grieving not being able to have a child.

These days, she sometimes feels relief.

"When you're in the grief you only grieve for the bits that are lost.

"But I do have little moments that surprise me. Sometimes when I see the challenges parents are experiencing in their lives."

She says it's an ongoing bittersweet experience.

" There are beautiful things I love about my life, but I do have a sense of living with the ongoing absence. "

Finding meaning and purpose outside of having children can help when grief reappears, Ms Roberts says.

"It's a non-conventional life where women have to actively construct meaning and purpose and what that looks like for them.

"I have seen women doing extraordinary things."

The complex label of 'childless not by choice' While childlessness devastates some, not every person who once wanted kids feels crushed when that doesn't eventuate.

For Ms Roberts, that's land regeneration.

"I've found meaning in joining a local bushcare group.

"I also work on my own acreage property in terms of [attracting] native animals."

Building networks with people who aren't parents can be helpful, she says.

"Sometimes even empty-nesters. There is a bit more synergy there and they are also trying to build meaning outside of parenting."

Ms Roberts says every life has highs and lows, and it's finding ways to cope with what that looks like for you.

"While childlessness is challenging, childless women really are capable.

"Particularly when they have had the time and space to make sense of that."

World.title: Giant tuna puts coastal town in global spotlight after 230kg catch
World.content:
A team of anglers has become part of a fishing phenomenon that has drawn fishers from across Australia, sent records tumbling, and put a small coastal town in Victoria's east in the spotlight.

Off the coast of Lakes Entrance, about 300 kilometres from Melbourne, giant tuna, some weighing more than 200 kilograms, are turning the waters into a fishing hotspot.

Lakes Charter Fishing owner Ricky Grech was among the first to catch one of the giant tuna, landing one weighing 154kg while out fishing with his 10-year-old son Oliver last month.

From there, more anglers continued to reel in record numbers, varying from 140kg to 190kg.

Belinda Brogna recently reeled in a tuna at 204kg at Lakes Entrance. (Supplied: Lakes Charter Fishing)

'Fish of a lifetime'

The largest fish weighing 231kg was caught on Sunday by a team of five fishers calling themselves the A Team.

The Gippsland Lakes Fishing Club said the catch was a club record.

"Who's going to bring in the next one?" Mr Grech said.

Back on shore, car parks were filling with boat trailers and accommodation was in demand.

Tristan Rodgers (right) caught a tuna weighing 217kg. (Supplied: Facebook (Starlo Gets Reel))

Mr Grech said the scale of the activity was unlike anything he had experienced before.

"It's something that I don't think we've really seen so big and phenomenal in Lakes Entrance," he said.

"I think there was well over 150 boats.

"I spoke to one of the fisheries officers and he says it's busier than Easter."

Mr Grech said it was thrilling to hear the record kept getting broken as well.

"I understand it's a fish of a lifetime for some people, so go for it," he said.

Small town spotlight

The influx of anglers has also brought a surge in tourism to Lakes Entrance, with visitors travelling from Sydney, Queensland, Adelaide and Western Australia.

Mr Grech said the flow-on effects were being felt across the town.

"It was unbelievable. [People were] going out for dinner, pizza shops getting booked … Airbnbs and tackle shops being called," he said.

"It all matters for a small regional town."

Victorian Fisheries Authority (VFA) manager of recreational fisheries Taylor Hunt said the town had become a hub for anglers chasing the extraordinary fish.

Fishers have been reeling in large tuna near Lakes Entrance over the past few weeks. (Supplied: Lakes Charter Fishing)

"It's a buzz for the fishing community," Dr Hunt said.

"It's hard to get a car park; there are so many boat trailers there."

Suspected Pacific bluefin catches

Earlier this month, the CSIRO confirmed two tuna caught off Western Port Bay in July were Pacific bluefin, the first genetically confirmed fish of the species in Victorian waters.

CSIRO principal research scientist Peter Grewe said further analysis had strengthened confidence in the identification of the two fish.

"I'm extremely confident in these results following a secondary forensic-grade sequencing analysis further confirming our initial quick species ID test," Dr Grewe said.

Researchers are now working to establish whether the monster fish off Lakes Entrance are also Pacific bluefin.

A map illustrating the migration patterns of Pacific bluefin tuna across the Pacific Ocean, including their movements towards Australia and New Zealand. (Supplied: NOAA Fisheries Service)

Dr Grewe said the discovery also highlighted the value of information shared by recreational fishers.

"Information from people out on the water every day is invaluable to scientists," Dr Grewe said.

"Fishers are a wealth of knowledge; they see unusual things, they tell great anecdotes."

Dr Hunt said the suspected Pacific bluefin tuna caught off Lakes Entrance had features that distinguished them from the southern bluefin tuna more commonly caught in Victoria.

"And they look just like Pacific bluefin tuna, but we haven't confirmed that with the genetic testing yet," he said.

"But it looks highly likely they are because they've got some anatomical features which sort of set them apart from our regular southern bluefin tuna.

"They're very rare [in Australia]."

Fishers have travelled from across Australia to be part of the action. (Supplied: Victorian Fisheries Authority (VFA))

Researchers are collecting genetic samples and otoliths, or ear stones, including fish ear bones that can help determine their age, with recreational fishers and charter operators contributing to the research.

Discovery remains a mystery

Dr Hunt said why the tuna had appeared in such numbers off Lakes Entrance's coast remained a mystery.

He said the region's marine environment still held plenty of surprises.

"The eyes of the fishing community right now are on Lakes Entrance because it's just been amazing," he said.

"And it certainly sparks my sense of adventure to get down there and get on the water."

World.title: After 20 years, Adelaide is losing its leading Asian arts event, OzAsia
World.content:
OzAsia Festival has arrived with its usual, exciting iconography — lanterns illuminating the Elder Park lawns, bustling market stalls, and the buzz of audiences experiencing Asian art on a grand stage.

This year's festivities, however, have returned with an unexpected and grim addition. The Adelaide Festival Centre announced this year that 2026 would mark the final run of its full-bodied artistic programming.

While some prepared to celebrate the milestone, others inched towards the festival dates in a state of shock, rage and anticipatory grief.

"I never, ever guessed that it would be cancelled. I thought it was an institution," former OzAsia Festival community engagement coordinator Jessica Zeng tells the ABC.

Two decades of Asian art

For two decades, the festival promoted Asian and Asian Australian arts, music and food, rallying a dedicated following of more than 200,000 attendees in recent years that was anticipated to grow.

The Moon Lantern Festival sees Elder Park transformed into a theatrical illuminated extravaganza. (Franklin Yao)

What was widely recognised by the community as a hotbed for meaningful artist collaboration, cultural edutainment, and a familiar gathering place has now been replaced for some with a sense of cynicism about the future of the arts and festival landscape.

In a statement in August, Adelaide Festival Centre CEO Kate Gould said OzAsia Festival was expected to shift to a "year-round programming" format from 2027 with an annual presence of The Lucky Dumpling Market.

Zeng said the decision to cancel the festival was "unceremonious" and "short sighted".

"There's so much more to the festival than the market, she said.

" It's really about capturing a broader Asian diasporic experience that's not the traditional kind of cultural signifier. I think that's something so special that can only happen with a festival. "

Spaces of belonging

"A homecoming", is how Zeng described OzAsia Festival's overall effect on the community; for artists, vendors and audiences alike.

"There were so many beautiful moments. Memories that are bittersweet with the knowledge of OzAsia's end," she says.

The Demon explores the violence enacted against First Nations peoples, Asian migrants and Muslim Australians. (Supplied: OzAsia Festival/Xplorer Studio)

Zeng said a Chinese migrant once told her OzAsia was the first time she felt like she "truly belonged in this country".

"I have had multiple people say that OzAsia was the reason they thought that Adelaide could be their home. You know, new migrants," she says.

"What about using that as a measure of success? Why don't we poll how many people realise that Adelaide was a safe city for them because they experienced OzAsia Festival?"

Boram Lee, a senior lecturer at Adelaide University for festival and event management, can speak to this personally.

"I came to visit in 2017 where I first experienced OzAsia Festival. That was a big part of me deciding to move. I didn't feel like a stranger," Lee says.

"Festivals have always been my playground, but up until that point, I had never come across a festival that celebrated a shared cultural identity."

Lee said the traditional festival structure allowed for shared moments during a period of "friction, conflict and hatred taking place in Australia".

She said it also provided a platform for "strategic cultural diplomacy".

Where artists careers were born

Asian Australian artist and creative producer Danielle Lim credits OzAsia Festival as the launch pad for her career.

"If you were to ask an Asian artist where they started, I think it's very likely to hear OzAsia," Lim says.

First introduced to the festival through the Contemporary Asian Australian Performance (CAAP) Artist Lab as an emerging artist in 2021, Lim became a producer on the same program the following year.

"I met a lot of collaborators of mine through that program and through OzAsia, collaborators who I still work with very closely in my practice today," she says.

Danielle Lim, pictured with her Contemporary Asian Australian Performance cohort, says OzAsia Festival launched many careers. (Ben Searcey)

In 2024, Lim also participated in a theatre work-in-progress, All Things At Once, which was an international collaboration between Infinity Ensemble in Melbourne, OzAsia and a Hong Kong arts festival — bringing together a half Asian-Australian and a half Hong Kong cast.

"These kinds of collaborations aren't accessible to us anymore. We're losing those international connections," she says.

Could a new festival exist?

Former Contemporary Asian Australian Performance Artist Lab facilitator Valerie Berry, a local artist and festival attendee, said the festival would leave a lasting legacy.

Damien Shen's work bringing together the visual languages that shaped him as a child with the Ngarrindjeri and Kaurna heritage. It's part of this year's festival. (Supplied)

"The biggest thing is seeing Asian Australian stories — whether that's theatre, or on stage at The Lucky Dumpling Market — that sense of gathering and enjoying something that's either outside your experience or connecting to your culture," she says.

Berry is grieving the loss of the festival but she is also looking forward to slowly rebuilding an initiative with the broader community, like OzAsia Festival, that centres collaboration, "global majority" narratives, and connection.

" There's still a need for Asian Australian stories. There are still younger generations who want to connect with their identity, so there will need to be a platform for those emerging voices and emerging audiences as well. "

Kate Gould, CEO of the Adelaide Festival Centre and Joon-Yee Kwok, artistic director of OzAsia, declined an interview with the ABC for this article.

OzAsia Festival is on until November 1.

World.title: Desalination plant delayed, despite fears Eyre Peninsula could run out of water
World.content:
Work on a desalination plant in regional South Australia has been delayed by six months, past when the region was due to run out of clean drinking water.

SA Water has announced construction on the Eyre Peninsula Desalination Plant will be pushed back six months, to mid-2027, due to harder-than-usual granite affecting its underground boring

Consumer access to water will be "unchanged".

Residents of Port Lincoln and its surrounding areas were told they could run out of clean drinking water by 2026.

The 35,000 residents of the Eyre Peninsula draw drinking water from the Uley South Basin, which has been depleting at a rate described as "dire" by the state government.

The state government funded the then-$330 million Eyre Peninsula Desalination Plant project, which is now expected to cost approximately $470 million, at the Billy Lights Point coastal reserve.

Early works began in February 2025 and it was projected to deliver fresh water by the end of this year.

"We're a bit behind where we'd like to be," SA Water sustainable infrastructure general manager Peter Seltsikas said.

Peter Seltsikas says tunnelling delays have pushed out the plant's completion date. (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

"The pipelines are done, the desalination plant is substantially complete.

"But the tunnelling delay means the first water day is pushing out to the middle of next year."

Mr Seltsikas said higher-than-usual rains this year across the Eyre Peninsula had increased the water levels of the Uley South Basin.

"We have enough water this year to continue to supply our customers and when the desalination plant comes next year they'll continue to have secure water."

Cost blowouts and security concerns

Glen Ingham was the spokesperson for community action group Hands Off Boston Bay, which was opposed to the location of the desalination plant.

He said the delays were testing the government's claims the site is the "cheapest and quickest" option.

Glen Ingham was the spokesperson for Hands Off Boston Bay. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

"Here we are now at the end of 2026 and they're [pushing the end date] to the middle of next year.

"I'm certain it will be beyond that and the cost blowout will be huge," he said.

In a statement, the state government said the revised budget of the project would be detailed once "contractual processes with delivery partners are complete".

Mr Seltsikas said the authority recognised the ongoing need to reduce water being taken from the basin.

"So we are very much concerned about water security," he said.

The state government said a revised Water Allocation Plan for the Southern Basins meant SA Water could extract water from the Uley South Basin and River Murray to meet consumer demand.

SA Water's groundwater allocation will reduce to 3.5 gigalitres per year in 2027-28, as the plant comes online.

A spokesperson said "it is not expected that water restrictions will be needed".

World.title: Riders scramble to ‘lock’ e-scooters to speed limits
World.content:
PoliticsQueenslandE-Scooters Riders scramble to ‘lock’ e-scooters to speed limits Felicity Caldwell and Catherine Strohfeldt October 20, 2026 — 1:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A crackdown on e-scooter top speeds has cut the number of kids ending up in Queensland’s hospitals, the state government says, but some riders are struggling to work out how to make their devices legal. E-scooter owners have until the end of February to “lock” their device to a limit of 25km/h, while riders of already legal e-bikes will have to fork out up to $70 for a special check and sticker. Brendan Hemmings, from spare parts company eScootNow, said he took several calls a day from people confused about how to limit the top speed, while some people had difficulty getting help from retailers or manufacturers. Getting your e-scooter locked to a top speed of 25km/h is not as simple as just taking it back to where you bought it, owners say. Dan Peled Police Acting Assistant Commissioner Tim Partridge said new devices would have to be sold locked to 25km/h, and people who already owned an e-scooter could return them to “participating outlets”.



But Hemmings said tens of thousands of e-scooters were sold in south-east Queensland by retailers that had since closed or been liquidated. “There is no [mobility device] industry-wide approach, unlike the [Department of Transport and Main Roads] assurance scheme for e-bikes,” he said. Hemmings said speed limiting was specific to makes and models, but there were several methods. Some advanced models or devices sold into European markets were factory-limited to a top speed, or locked via GPS or upon registration. A speed-limiter wire could be installed under the deck to limit an e-scooter to 25km/h.



Another method was changing the “P-settings”. For example, if the unlimited top speed was 60km/h, users could set this to 41 per cent. Related Article City life Why this family is fighting to get their illegal e-bike back from police Or people could set the mode or gear somewhere between one and five, or change between eco to turbo, to get a top speed close to 25km/h. “For the average e-scooter rider, this is all too complex. It is all too hard, and they talk to different people and get different answers,” Hemmings said. “If you are not the original buyer of a Ninebot, impacting ability to register and log in and make speed changes, you are going to struggle. Often there is no pathway.”



Hemmings argued most higher-class e-scooters could not be set to 25km/h accurately, and speeds would be 22-27km/h due to a simplistic controller. And many e-scooters limited to 25km/h would realise 50 per cent torque, he said, meaning they would struggle to climb hills. Meanwhile, e-bike owners will have to pay up to $70 to get their already compliant ride verified as legal if they do not have an EN15194 sticker, under a statewide assurance scheme starting on November 2. The assurance scheme states higher-powered or higher-speed bikes modified to meet the 25km/h and 250-watt rules will not qualify for the sticker because that would create an “ongoing compliance and enforcement risk, as the modifications may be reversed after verification”. Transport Minister Brent Mickelberg said there was no equivalent compliance labelling for e-scooters “due to the absence of a consistent national or international standard”.



“The Crisafulli government’s nation-leading laws get the balance right between cracking down on those who do the wrong thing while backing those Queenslanders who do the right thing, and delivering sensible exemptions,” he said. On Tuesday, the government said seven children were admitted to the Queensland Children’s Hospital between July and September for more than 24 hours for serious e-scooter or e-bike incidents, compared with 18 between January and March, and 16 from April to June. Queensland Children’s Hospital paediatric surgeon Professor Roy Kimble. Catherine Strohfeldt “We’ve only had three months since the legislation came out, on July 1,” said Professor Roy Kimble, the director of paediatric surgery, burns and trauma at the Queensland Children’s Hospital. “But I’m very pleased to say that there has been a rapid decline in the number of children into this hospital after riding e-scooters and e-bikes.”



This masthead has seen high-powered e-scooters still for sale in Brisbane, including one with peak power of 3600 watts and a maximum speed of up to 60km/h. Police seized 595 non-compliant devices from July 1 to October 9. They would not provide a breakdown between e-scooters and bikes. Road Policing Group Acting Superintendent Gareth Bosley said people who rode illegal or modified e-mobility devices in public, combined with unsafe and reckless behaviour, posed a significant risk to others. “[Queensland police] utilise conventional speed detection equipment to identify devices that may reasonably be suspected to be non-compliant and/or modified, due to the fact they are able to exceed device-specific speed limits,” he said. Three people have died in Queensland while riding “personal mobility devices”, which includes e-scooters, this year.



From 2022 to 2025, 6089 people went to 36 Queensland Injury Surveillance Unit emergency departments at Queensland hospitals as a result of an e-scooter crash. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Melbourne Assembly live: Ex-New York mayor, PM share visions to improve liveability
World.content:
Architect Sarah Lynn Rees is arguing that Melbourne needs to pursue renting as a sustainable housing model, when the historical emphasis has been on home ownership.

We can use legal and regulatory structures to ensure renting is a decent option, says the Jackson Clements Burrows Architects principal.

From left: Steve Bracks, Sarah Lyn Rees and Bill de Blasio. Justin McManus

But former Victorian premier Steve Bracks disagrees, saying: “If you look at what’s happening in Footscray for high-rise developments, they’re all fully let.”

“If you look what’s happening in Box Hill, this is happening already. People are making different choices, particularly young people, and I think you’re going to see more of that in the future as well,” Bracks says.

Rees counters that there remains a need for diverse rentals, beyond one or two-bedroom units that only support the nuclear family.

“It’s not going to support intergenerational living. It’s not going to support families,” she says. “We need to design for how we live now – not how we lived in the industrial era.”

World.title: Look away now Royal Melbourne members, Fox prefers Kingston Heath, too
World.content:
SportGolfAustralian Open Look away now Royal Melbourne members, Fox prefers Kingston Heath, too Peter Ryan October 20, 2026 — 1:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Reigning Open champion Ryan Fox will attempt to become the first Kiwi to win the Australian Open after confirming he will join US Masters champion Rory McIlroy at Kingston Heath in December. It will be the first time the current titleholders of The Open and US Masters have played at the tournament since Gary Player in 1974, while Fox will be aiming to become the first Open champion to win the Australian Open in the same year since Bill Rogers in 1981. New Zealand golfer Ryan Fox holds the Claret Jug as he stands with his wife Anneke Ryff and their two daughters Isabel and Margot during a public reception in Takutai Square. He will get a huge reception at this year’s Australian Open. Getty Images Fox said it was an easy decision to fit the tournament into his schedule, which has become hectic since his dramatic win at Royal Birkdale in July, particularly when the 2026 version is being played at Kingston Heath. Look away now if you are a member at Royal Melbourne. Fox agrees with the controversial view McIlroy expressed ahead of last year’s Australian Open: Kingston Heath is the best sandbelt course.



“My favourite sandbelt course is Kingston Heath,” Fox said from Korea where he is preparing to play this week. Although keen not to upset anyone too much ahead of his return to the country where he learned to play the tough, uncompromising and sometimes brilliant golf which prevailed at The Open, he said rating one course above the other was splitting hairs. View post on X But his preference was clear. “I am definitely in Rory’s boat. I think my favourite is Kingston Heath on the sandbelt, but it is not like they are miles apart. You give me a chance to play either and I am very excited to play,” Fox said.



“It is just a personal thing. I just like the feel of Kingston Heath and the look of some of the shots. I have been lucky enough to play both in tournament conditions. [The chance to play] either of them I am not complaining. “They are some of the best courses anywhere in the world but for me Kingston Heath’s just got it by a hair basically.” Ryan Fox will bring the famous Claret Jug with him to Australia to play at Kingston Heath in December. Warren Little Fox said the automatic admission Australian Open winners were granted into the US Masters and The Open had increased the incentive for the world’s best players to play in the tournament. But he said it was not the only reason the best players in the world were considering making an Australian summer part of their schedule. He said the momentum was real. “If you look at who has won the Stonehaven cup, it’s pretty impressive. It’s the who’s who of golf, [and] it’s an event guys really, really want to play,” Fox said.



Fox finished equal 14th alongside McIlroy in last year’s Open won by Denmark’s Rasmus Neergaard-Petersen after being the joint leader at the end of the opening day. He said his major victory had helped him feel as though he belongs among the sport’s big names and playing in the high-profile groups. On the course, Fox has handled the expectation with comes with his new-found status, but he admitted he was battling to manage his time as effectively as he would like when it came to the increased expectations off the course. One of the most down-to-earth and likeable players on the tour, Fox said he had sought the advice of US Open champion Geoff Ogilvy during the President’s Cup. “He said it does calm down a bit, but the cool thing is it kind of never leaves you as well,” Fox said. “You will always be a major champion. There will always be a bit of extra buzz around.”



Fox said he has to get better at saying no to certain demands now that his downtime was not as free as it once was. He said he was looking forward to going on a fishing trip when the chance arose. Related Article Australian Open ‘One in 72 billion chance’: Sydney golfer does unthinkable with back-to-back albatross and hole in one But he is far from complaining. He will arrive in Australia, knowing he has the claret jug, but also the game and mental resilience to contend in any tournament. “[I know I] can deal with pressure. I can hit some good shots down the stretch when it really matters,” he said. “Playing that well under pressure ... there is just a bit more belief there now.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Friday.
