World.title: Dual international says Nawaqanitawase’s NRL stint proves Wallabies aren’t dead
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Dual international says Nawaqanitawase’s NRL stint proves Wallabies aren’t dead Christy Doran October 20, 2026 — 12:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Wallabies’ Bledisloe Cup drought might have stretched to 24 years, but dual international Michael O’Connor believes Mark Nawaqanitawase’s extraordinary two-year stint in rugby league proves the 15-a-side game in Australia still produces world-class talent. “You look at his ability and what he’s been able to do; to me, it reflects really well on rugby that we have a player like him come over to rugby league, and there are quite a lot of sceptics in rugby league around rugby union, and to see how he’s dominated the competition, I think it’s a good thing,” O’Connor said. Mark Nawaqanitawase and Robert Toia celebrate grand final glory. Getty Images Nawaqanitawase’s decision to sign with the Roosters following the Wallabies’ dreaded 2023 World Cup campaign caused a stir in Australian rugby. Rugby Australia boss Phil Waugh was shocked the talented back, who had only broken into the Wallabies in late 2022, was jumping codes just 12 months later.



But the athletic winger, who scored twice on his Super Rugby debut in 2020 and also bagged a double in his third Test against Wales in Cardiff, never looked back. Nawaqanitawase made an immediate impression in league, soaring high against the South Sydney Rabbitohs to score on debut. Loading He then topped the tryscorers list in 2025 (with 24) to earn Kangaroos selection for the Ashes in England, before bowing out with an Origin series win and an NRL title, where he scored twice in the Roosters’ 19-18 win, to cap an incredible 26 months. O’Connor, who played 13 Tests for the Wallabies before scoring 87 tries across 10 seasons of rugby league for St George and Manly, said he wasn’t shocked Nawaqanitawase had scaled such heights, having first seen him during his short second stint as a selector with the Wallabies in 2019.



But he added that the player returning to rugby, where he will join Japanese League One club Saitama Panasonic Wild Knights, was better than the one who left rugby in mid-2024 following the Paris Olympics. “The Roosters certainly did their homework when they signed him,” O’Connor said. Michael O’Connor believes Mark Nawaqanitawase’s successful transition bodes well for rugby union in Australia. Rugby AU Media/Stuart Walmsley “He’s a real athlete, and that was apparent even when I was a selector. “He made the Australian under-20 squad that went over to Argentina in 2019. He was scoring tries, he had a great instinct for the game and where the ball was, and his visual awareness was through the roof. But I think he’s just grown into a man, and he’s a far more complete footballer now.



“I think his move to rugby league has been a good thing; it certainly has brushed up some areas of his game … he’ll go back up with a lot of confidence.” Whether the Wallabies bear the fruit of his two years in rugby league remains to be seen. Mark Nawaqanitawase is a better player now than he was when he left rugby union in 2024, according to Michael O’Connor. Chris Hyde Wallabies coach Les Kiss wanted to pick the 26-year-old for next month’s Nations Championship campaign in the United Kingdom, but Nawaqanitawase ruled himself out after seeking time off. The decision means Nawaqanitawase could run out for Fiji or Italy next year, given the outside back would have missed the last three years of international rugby.



O’Connor said Nawaqanitawase’s availability would be critical for the Wallabies if they wanted to go deep at next year’s World Cup. “At a World Cup, it’s just apparent that you need world-class players, and a lot of them,” he said. ‘He’s a far more complete footballer now.’ Michael O’Connor on Mark Nawaqanitawase “Just watching New Zealand on the weekend, just the power of their lineup, there’s just no weaknesses, and that’s where we need to go. We need to get a complement of players who’ve played together and got no weaknesses. “He’s a world-class player, and that’s what we need. When we’ve had success in the past, we’ve had world-class players.”



While Nawaqanitawase might be unavailable for the Wallabies, fellow Origin cross-code star Zac Lomax could get the chance to push for a national call-up on Sunday when Australia A takes on the USA Eagles in Nashville. Lomax will be hoping to link up with another former Origin star, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, who will later this week be named for his third spring tour. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii on the attack against the All Blacks on Saturday. Getty Images O’Connor said he felt Suaalii, who was exposed defensively during the Wallabies’ 43-21 defeat in Sydney on Saturday, had been harshly rated since being catapulted into the Australian team in late 2024. “I feel a bit sorry for him in a way,” O’Connor said.



“He’s not complained once, but he’s played a number of positions, and he seems to be playing one position, and then someone says he’s a fullback or winger, or an outside centre. Related Article Analysis

Wallabies Why Wallabies are a better chance of winning World Cup than Bledisloe “It’s apparent that he has got great attacking skills. He’s very effective at running at the line and breaking through the line, and we need players to do that.” O’Connor, who made his Wallabies debut in 1979, a year before the great Mark Ella first ran out in gold, said today’s generation needed to play flatter at the line. “If you can look at where we can improve, we’re playing a lot behind the advantage line because of the rush defence, particularly from South Africa and also New Zealand,” he said. “But we need players to get through the advantage line and Suaalii can do that. He’s got good feet, he’s got good attacking nous, so there’s a spot for him there somewhere.”

World.title: The sinister meme that appeared just hours before the attack on Helen Haines
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsFederalHaines attack The sinister meme that appeared just hours before the attack on Helen Haines Jacqueline Maley October 20, 2026 — 12:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

“Not enough politicians are afraid for their lives right now & I think that’s a problem.” The comment had been made into a meme, with the words in fancy font printed on an image of a man pointing a gun. Social media vitriol is a strange amalgam of public and personalised. Marija Ercegovac It was posted on the official page of Nichole Overall, a NSW Nationals MP, by an account with a full name and a shadowy profile pic of a man’s back. “I’ve never had anything of this nature, this was quite shocking. I was taken aback,” says Overall of the post, which appeared on Monday, in the hours before the alleged attack on federal independent MP Helen Haines.



Related Article Live

Haines attack Helen Haines attack live updates: Federal Indi MP loses leg after being struck multiple times by car outside Wangaratta office; Brendan Nugent identified as alleged attacker “It’s just not the way, in a civilised society, we should be addressing things,” Overall says, becoming agitated. “It’s too much.” Such social media vitriol is a strange amalgam of public and personalised. It is posted for all to see, but it is deeply silo-ed, which is to say that I don’t know what’s happening in your feed, and you don’t know what’s happening in mine. You will only see the post on Overall’s Facebook page if it pops up in the online bubble that is perfectly tailored to you, courtesy of a tech company’s algorithm, breeding an isolation that is anything but pro-social.



We live in an age of bombardment, with overwhelming amounts of content coming at us all the time – more content than we could ever need or enjoy. But at the same time we are increasingly ignorant of the worlds, lives and viewpoints of those who don’t appear in our over-full feeds. NSW Nationals MP Nichole Overall was targeted in a post on social media hours before the alleged attack on Helen Haines. Alex Ellinghausen This confusion of content has metastasised threats to public safety, which are now splintered along strange fault lines that don’t necessarily follow traditional ideological positions of left/right. As Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said earlier in October of the terrorist threat: “We are getting some weird mixed ideologies, logically inconsistent, all cohering on violence.”



Related Article Haines attack Turn down the temperature: Spy chief’s urgent warning as Helen Haines remains in critical condition But extremists who deal in hostility do tend to share some common denominators – antisemitism being one, and misogyny being the other. These two ancient hatreds are useful bellwethers for talk that might turn violent. It is too early to know if Haines’ gender was a factor in the attack on her. But we are alive to the possibility because we know women politicians cop a degree of sexualised, highly personal abuse unique to their sex.





When asked if she thinks women politicians are singled out for particular abuse, Overall says: “I don’t want to make it a gender thing, but yes, it is most certainly the situation.” “Within the last 12 to 18 months there has absolutely been a heightened level of viciousness and sadly, it is misogyny.” She mentions a recent instance where she was called a “ho”. “It’s things that just simply aren’t said to men.” The political week took a horror turn with Monday’s attack on Haines.



But even before then, the political discourse had already entered a new era of coarseness. Independent senator Jacqui Lambie was mocked in a One Nation Please Explain video. Alex Ellinghausen Independent senator Jacqui Lambie has spoken before about her suffering from vaginal prolapse, in a laudable effort to de-stigmatise the condition from which hundreds of thousands of Australian women silently suffer. The latest of the cretinous Please Explain videos put out on Pauline Hanson’s YouTube feed over the weekend features Lambie in cartoon form, and witlessly mocks her condition. One should avoid hyperbole when discussing extremes in political debate, but the cartoon truly represents a new and imbecilic threshold passed.





“They’re not funny when you attack someone personally, and they incite people. When you’ve got other MPs, to be honest, posting things about other MPs, it doesn’t help.” No line can be drawn from the contemptible vulgarity of the videos to the violence of Monday in Wangaratta. But the two things exist in the same sphere of pernicious influence. Anyone who pretends otherwise, or tells others, butter-wouldn’t-melt-style, that hateful rhetoric is “just a joke”, should be called out. To re-purpose former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull’s saying about disrespect and violence towards women – not all hate speech ends in violence, but all political violence starts with hatred.

World.title: Jockeys cleared over Caulfield Cup horse death as stewards release report
World.content:
SportRacingVictorian racing Jockeys cleared over Caulfield Cup horse death as stewards release report Danny Russell Updated October 20, 2026 — 12:27pm ,first published October 20, 2026 — 9:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Racing Victoria stewards have cleared all jockeys of blame for a fall that caused a horse death in the Caulfield Cup on Saturday, as trainer Chris Waller revealed his staff were taking it “one day at a time” to cope with the loss of stable star Ohope Wins. Stewards released a report on Tuesday morning, saying they “could not attribute the incident to the careless actions of any one particular rider”. Loading They interviewed five jockeys – Rachel King, Jabez Johnstone, Ethan Brown, Mark Zahra and Jye McNeil – in the hours before releasing their finding. Stewards have now closed their investigation, referring the incident to Racing Victoria’s veterinary services department, which does not release public findings.



Related Article Blinkers On

Victorian racing Why all the details of the inquiry into Caulfield Cup horse death must be made public Saturday’s carnage unfolded 300 metres from the Caulfield Racecourse finish post in front of a packed public section. Waller’s dual group 1-winning Ohope Wins and jockey McNeil were brought crashing to the ground after last year’s winner Half Yours (Zahra) stumbled and fell in front of them. While Half Yours emerged with minor lacerations and both jockeys escaped serious injury, this year’s Australian Oaks winner suffered catastrophic injuries and had to be put down behind a green screen. The full details of the horse’s fatal injuries have not yet been released by Racing Victoria.



The two-horse tumble followed a bumping duel between King’s mount Green Spaces and the Johnstone-ridden Kings Valley on the home turn. Half Yours was then tightened for room between Kings Valley and Zahrann (Brown). “Stewards are of the view that the marginal shifts from both Green Spaces, when under pressure, and Kings Valley resulted in both those runners becoming unbalanced and shifting in ultimately resulting in Half Yours being tightened and falling,” their report said. “Further, stewards were satisfied Zahrann and Half Yours had both established a clear run prior to Half Yours meeting with interference.”



They found King and Johnstone had taken “the necessary corrective measures to straighten and relieve any pressure caused by their mounts to Half Yours”. “Furthermore, Ethan Brown rider of Zahrann had not contributed to Half Yours being tightened for room,” their report said. Stewards reported that there had been no issue with Caulfield track surface. Chris Waller watch his Cox Plate horses work at Flemington on Tuesday morning. Getty Images Trainer Tony McEvoy said Half Yours had been treated for lacerations and would be sent for a spell, ruling him out of a Melbourne Cup title defence.



Speaking for the first time about the tragic aftermath of the mid-race fall, Waller said on Tuesday it was never easy for staff to deal with the loss of a galloper. “They’re pretty resilient, the people that look after these horses, they obviously love them dearly, and they’re pets, just like a cat or dog,” a visibly upset Waller said at Flemington on Tuesday morning. “So, yeah, it’s always tough when there’s a missing [horse] in the stable.” Waller watched the race tragedy from Randwick, having stayed in Sydney for The Everest meeting. “I’ve spoken to Jye,” Waller said. “He’s improving with each day, and it’s great to see him out of hospital. He’s come out of it pretty well.”



McNeil was booked to ride Waller’s Valiant King in Wednesday’s Geelong Cup, but the trainer has opted to scratch the horse and run him at Flemington in the MV Gold Cup on Saturday. Despite the severity of the fall, both McNeil and Zahra were not deemed to have concussion – a scenario that would have seen them stood down for 12 days under Racing Victoria protocols. James McDonald puts Cox Plate favourite Aeliana through her paces at Flemington on Tuesday morning. Getty Images But Zahra was to meet with doctors again today before making a decision on his return. Waller was in Melbourne on Tuesday to watch his Cox Plate runners, Aeliana and Birdman, have an early morning hit out at Flemington. The Cox Plate barrier draw will be held Tuesday night.



The trainer acknowledged the support of the Melbourne Racing Club, which runs Caulfield Racecourse, following Saturday’s accident. “I commend them for offering counselling, and they’ve been fantastic because it’s good that people really understand how much people love horses and how much goes into a horse,” Waller said. Trainer Chris Waller. Getty Images “No risks are ever taken, and the first choice is to bring them home safe, regardless of where they finish. But the staff, they’re coping well. “You just take it one day at a time, just deal with it as each day comes.”



Waller has won six of the past 10 Cox Plates, including four with the record-breaking Winx between 2015-2018 and the past two with the Yulong-owned import Via Sistina. Related Article Updated

Victorian racing Risks unavoidable, says Racing Victoria, amid fallout from Caulfield Cup death That mare caused the sensation of the spring in 2024 when she dislodged jockey James McDonald during a Breakfast With The Best gallop at Moonee Valley and bolted away with a loose bandage hanging from her hind leg, and running three laps before being caught. While many feared the champion mare would be unable to take her place in the weight-for-age championship after the scare, she came out and won by eight lengths in record time (2:01.07). Waller said Aeliana and Birdman were set to peak in Saturday’s Cox Plate, being run at Flemington for the first time while Moonee Valley is closed for $250 million renovations.



“Both horses are in great form,” he said. “They’re genuine group 1 horses. Aeliana’s ready to peak after a good semi-final run last start (third in the Turnbull Stakes), and Birdman the same (third in the Might And Power Stakes).” McDonald, who has won the past four Cox Plates, flew in from Sydney to trial Aeliana, while Ben Melham rode Birdman. World.title: China’s export boom is becoming its Achilles heel
World.content:
BusinessMarketsTrade wars Opinion China’s export boom is becoming its Achilles heel Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist October 20, 2026 — 12:16pm

October 20, 2026 — 12:16pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

China is rapidly approaching the point where its strengths are making it vulnerable. Data released this week shows its economy is growing strongly. GDP growth of 4.5 per cent in September and 4.6 per cent for the first nine months of the year are keeping it on track to meet Beijing’s target of between 4.5 per cent and 5 per cent growth this year. The figures were stronger than economists had predicted. Chinese cars and other export goods are flooding global markets. But it’s not all good news for its economy. Bloomberg That might appear to demonstrate Chinese exceptionalism in a global economy spluttering under the weight of debt, wars and trade wars, yet it also highlights the ever-growing imbalances within Asia’s biggest economy. For the past five years – after President Xi Jinping implemented his “three red lines” policy that curbed property developers’ leverage and triggered a crash in the country’s property market that continues today – China’s domestic economy has stagnated.



That has left China increasingly reliant on exports for growth, and that dependence has been steadily increasing. In September, exports grew by 36 per cent – their fastest pace in more than a decade and a half – and generated a trade surplus of $US938 billion ($1.34 trillion). The country is on track to beat last year’s record surplus of $US1.2 trillion. As with Trump, Xi is leading China’s economy into dangerous territory. And that’s where the vulnerability lies. Domestic demand is weak. Retail sales, up only 1.1 per cent in September compared with the same month last year, have been near-stagnant since the start of the property market’s collapse. China has become increasingly dependent on exports to soak up the over-capacity that is now rife in its factories.



Donald Trump’s trade war has crimped exports to the US. China has responded by diversifying the markets it is targeting, with a surge in exports to other economies within Asia, emerging markets in Eastern Europe and South America, and a massive increase in exports to the European Union. The EU, by far the biggest market open to China, now represents the most direct and significant threat. Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Europe raids Trump’s tool box for new ‘trade bazooka’ against China Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist There has been some pushback against the tide of Chinese products elsewhere, but China needs the EU to remain open to its industries to sustain the mercantilist model it is pursuing to offset the absence of domestic growth. Europe, where key manufacturing industries are being overwhelmed by Chinese imports, is running out of tolerance as plant closures and job losses mount. Imports from China are running 36 per cent higher this year than last with more than €1 billion ($1.6 billion) worth of goods a day.



The EU reached an agreement with Beijing this month to cap imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles at roughly half their existing levels, after Germany joined France in seeking greater powers for the European Commission to curb the flood of Chinese cars causing increasing damage to the European auto sector. France and Germany – a late convert to the resistance to Chinese imports because of its extensive investments and markets within the country – are also spearheading a proposal to create new powers for the European Commission. The changes would completely shut off a country’s access to the European market in circumstances where that country (read China, even if it weren’t named) was seen to be damaging the EU economy. The so-called “kill switch” could also be deployed in response to coercive trade measures, such as the threat China wielded against the US – cutting off access to the rare earths essential for most advanced manufactures – to (successfully) force Trump to back down from his most punitive proposed tariffs. The Europeans want to slash China’s trade surplus with the EU, and are also considering whether the caps in hybrid imports can be replicated in other sectors. China’s sensitivity to the threat posed by the EU’s newly assertive stance was demonstrated by the alacrity with which it acceded to the cap on hybrids. A complete shutdown of the EU market for its exports, while so drastic a prospect that it is unlikely, could destroy its economic model.



What the angst within the EU and the measures it is prepared to contemplate say is that China has pushed the export model, fuelled by subsidised loans, direct funding, preferential tax treatments, export rebates and state-directed equity injections, too far. Other countries, and the EU bloc is by far the most important, don’t want their industries wiped out by becoming the safety valve and dumping ground for Chinese over-capacity. It’s not just the potential for trade retaliation and the loss of market access that makes China’s export-led strategy vulnerable. Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, during Xi’s state visit to the White House last month. Bloomberg Increasingly, its export growth is being fuelled by high-tech exports and semiconductors, or chips, in particular.



The boom in artificial intelligence has seen those exports soar to the point where they now account for roughly a third of its export growth. The US-centric AI boom is built on fragile and shifting foundations as its voracious appetite for capital is running up against increasing awareness, and pricing, of the risks involved by those supplying it. The deliberate shift in China’s manufacturing and export strategies towards high-tech and AI means that, along with the US, any material slowdown (or bust) in the deployment of AI would have very destructive consequences. So far, China has done little to try to rebalance its economy away from its over-reliance on exports. There have been very modest attempt to stimulate domestic consumption – cuts to mortgage rates and deposits, and subsidies for trade-ins of old autos and appliances – but nothing meaningful.



China’s urban households have been seen their wealth, much of it exposed to property, ravaged by the collapse in the real estate market. That market is showing some signs of stabilising after its hefty price falls – property prices are down about 40 per cent since the three red lines policy was introduced – but property investment continues to tumble, down another 20.6 per cent in the first nine months of this year. What the angst within the EU and the measures it is prepared to contemplate say is that China has pushed the export model too far. That also has implications for local governments and their capacity to spend and generate domestic economic activity, given that they were reliant on property sales and taxes for much of their revenue before the sector imploded. The bright spot in the data released this week – although it is tied into the increased trade vulnerabilities because it highlights how China continues to produce at a rate well above Chinese consumers’ capacity or willingness to buy – was a 5.5 per cent rise in industrial production in September and, within that number, a 14 per cent increase in high-tech manufacturing output.



The gap between the growth rates of flat-lining domestic consumption and increasing exports is blowing out, swelling the imbalances within China’s economy. Related Article Opinion

Trump diplomacy How Trump’s grovelling emboldens China and imperils the Asia Pacific Peter Hartcher Political and international editor China’s exports, and its strategy for moving up the value curve and dominating advanced manufactures, is Xi’s recipe for achieving the country’s global economic and geopolitical leadership. As with Trump, who has presided over blow-outs in America’s debt and deficit to unsustainable levels, and whose war in the Middle East and trade wars are mauling US consumers and companies, Xi is leading China’s economy into dangerous territory. Any significant closure of export markets and subsequent contraction of China’s exports could, given the state of its domestic economy, have over-sized and unpleasant impacts on its economy and stability.



So far, Xi has shown no signs of deviating from the course he set in 2015, when the release of the “Made in China 2025” strategy first broadcast his ambition of dominating global manufacturing. The rest of the world has allowed that to happen, but that tolerance is now being severely tested. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Riders scramble to ‘lock’ e-scooters to speed limits
World.content:
PoliticsQueenslandE-Scooters Riders scramble to ‘lock’ e-scooters to speed limits Felicity Caldwell and Catherine Strohfeldt October 20, 2026 — 1:39pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

A crackdown on e-scooter top speeds has cut the number of kids ending up in Queensland’s hospitals, the state government says, but some riders are struggling to work out how to make their devices legal. E-scooter owners have until the end of February to “lock” their device to a limit of 25km/h, while riders of already legal e-bikes will have to fork out up to $70 for a special check and sticker. Brendan Hemmings, from spare parts company eScootNow, said he took several calls a day from people confused about how to limit the top speed, while some people had difficulty getting help from retailers or manufacturers. Getting your e-scooter locked to a top speed of 25km/h is not as simple as just taking it back to where you bought it, owners say. Dan Peled Police Acting Assistant Commissioner Tim Partridge said new devices would have to be sold locked to 25km/h, and people who already owned an e-scooter could return them to “participating outlets”.



But Hemmings said tens of thousands of e-scooters were sold in south-east Queensland by retailers that had since closed or been liquidated. “There is no [mobility device] industry-wide approach, unlike the [Department of Transport and Main Roads] assurance scheme for e-bikes,” he said. Hemmings said speed limiting was specific to makes and models, but there were several methods. Some advanced models or devices sold into European markets were factory-limited to a top speed, or locked via GPS or upon registration. A speed-limiter wire could be installed under the deck to limit an e-scooter to 25km/h.



Another method was changing the “P-settings”. For example, if the unlimited top speed was 60km/h, users could set this to 41 per cent. Related Article City life Why this family is fighting to get their illegal e-bike back from police Or people could set the mode or gear somewhere between one and five, or change between eco to turbo, to get a top speed close to 25km/h. “For the average e-scooter rider, this is all too complex. It is all too hard, and they talk to different people and get different answers,” Hemmings said. “If you are not the original buyer of a Ninebot, impacting ability to register and log in and make speed changes, you are going to struggle. Often there is no pathway.”



Hemmings argued most higher-class e-scooters could not be set to 25km/h accurately, and speeds would be 22-27km/h due to a simplistic controller. And many e-scooters limited to 25km/h would realise 50 per cent torque, he said, meaning they would struggle to climb hills. Meanwhile, e-bike owners will have to pay up to $70 to get their already compliant ride verified as legal if they do not have an EN15194 sticker, under a statewide assurance scheme starting on November 2. The assurance scheme states higher-powered or higher-speed bikes modified to meet the 25km/h and 250-watt rules will not qualify for the sticker because that would create an “ongoing compliance and enforcement risk, as the modifications may be reversed after verification”. Transport Minister Brent Mickelberg said there was no equivalent compliance labelling for e-scooters “due to the absence of a consistent national or international standard”.



“The Crisafulli government’s nation-leading laws get the balance right between cracking down on those who do the wrong thing while backing those Queenslanders who do the right thing, and delivering sensible exemptions,” he said. On Tuesday, the government said seven children were admitted to the Queensland Children’s Hospital between July and September for more than 24 hours for serious e-scooter or e-bike incidents, compared with 18 between January and March, and 16 from April to June. Queensland Children’s Hospital paediatric surgeon Professor Roy Kimble. Catherine Strohfeldt “We’ve only had three months since the legislation came out, on July 1,” said Professor Roy Kimble, the director of paediatric surgery, burns and trauma at the Queensland Children’s Hospital. “But I’m very pleased to say that there has been a rapid decline in the number of children into this hospital after riding e-scooters and e-bikes.”



This masthead has seen high-powered e-scooters still for sale in Brisbane, including one with peak power of 3600 watts and a maximum speed of up to 60km/h. Police seized 595 non-compliant devices from July 1 to October 9. They would not provide a breakdown between e-scooters and bikes. Road Policing Group Acting Superintendent Gareth Bosley said people who rode illegal or modified e-mobility devices in public, combined with unsafe and reckless behaviour, posed a significant risk to others. “[Queensland police] utilise conventional speed detection equipment to identify devices that may reasonably be suspected to be non-compliant and/or modified, due to the fact they are able to exceed device-specific speed limits,” he said. Three people have died in Queensland while riding “personal mobility devices”, which includes e-scooters, this year.



From 2022 to 2025, 6089 people went to 36 Queensland Injury Surveillance Unit emergency departments at Queensland hospitals as a result of an e-scooter crash. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Melbourne Assembly live: Ex-New York mayor, PM share visions to improve liveability
World.content:
Architect Sarah Lynn Rees is arguing that Melbourne needs to pursue renting as a sustainable housing model, when the historical emphasis has been on home ownership.

We can use legal and regulatory structures to ensure renting is a decent option, says the Jackson Clements Burrows Architects principal.

From left: Steve Bracks, Sarah Lyn Rees and Bill de Blasio. Justin McManus

But former Victorian premier Steve Bracks disagrees, saying: “If you look at what’s happening in Footscray for high-rise developments, they’re all fully let.”

“If you look what’s happening in Box Hill, this is happening already. People are making different choices, particularly young people, and I think you’re going to see more of that in the future as well,” Bracks says.

Rees counters that there remains a need for diverse rentals, beyond one or two-bedroom units that only support the nuclear family.

“It’s not going to support intergenerational living. It’s not going to support families,” she says. “We need to design for how we live now – not how we lived in the industrial era.”

World.title: Look away now Royal Melbourne members, Fox prefers Kingston Heath, too
World.content:
SportGolfAustralian Open Look away now Royal Melbourne members, Fox prefers Kingston Heath, too Peter Ryan October 20, 2026 — 1:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Reigning Open champion Ryan Fox will attempt to become the first Kiwi to win the Australian Open after confirming he will join US Masters champion Rory McIlroy at Kingston Heath in December. It will be the first time the current titleholders of The Open and US Masters have played at the tournament since Gary Player in 1974, while Fox will be aiming to become the first Open champion to win the Australian Open in the same year since Bill Rogers in 1981. New Zealand golfer Ryan Fox holds the Claret Jug as he stands with his wife Anneke Ryff and their two daughters Isabel and Margot during a public reception in Takutai Square. He will get a huge reception at this year’s Australian Open. Getty Images Fox said it was an easy decision to fit the tournament into his schedule, which has become hectic since his dramatic win at Royal Birkdale in July, particularly when the 2026 version is being played at Kingston Heath. Look away now if you are a member at Royal Melbourne. Fox agrees with the controversial view McIlroy expressed ahead of last year’s Australian Open: Kingston Heath is the best sandbelt course.



“My favourite sandbelt course is Kingston Heath,” Fox said from Korea where he is preparing to play this week. Although keen not to upset anyone too much ahead of his return to the country where he learned to play the tough, uncompromising and sometimes brilliant golf which prevailed at The Open, he said rating one course above the other was splitting hairs. View post on X But his preference was clear. “I am definitely in Rory’s boat. I think my favourite is Kingston Heath on the sandbelt, but it is not like they are miles apart. You give me a chance to play either and I am very excited to play,” Fox said.



“It is just a personal thing. I just like the feel of Kingston Heath and the look of some of the shots. I have been lucky enough to play both in tournament conditions. [The chance to play] either of them I am not complaining. “They are some of the best courses anywhere in the world but for me Kingston Heath’s just got it by a hair basically.” Ryan Fox will bring the famous Claret Jug with him to Australia to play at Kingston Heath in December. Warren Little Fox said the automatic admission Australian Open winners were granted into the US Masters and The Open had increased the incentive for the world’s best players to play in the tournament. But he said it was not the only reason the best players in the world were considering making an Australian summer part of their schedule. He said the momentum was real. “If you look at who has won the Stonehaven cup, it’s pretty impressive. It’s the who’s who of golf, [and] it’s an event guys really, really want to play,” Fox said.



Fox finished equal 14th alongside McIlroy in last year’s Open won by Denmark’s Rasmus Neergaard-Petersen after being the joint leader at the end of the opening day. He said his major victory had helped him feel as though he belongs among the sport’s big names and playing in the high-profile groups. On the course, Fox has handled the expectation with comes with his new-found status, but he admitted he was battling to manage his time as effectively as he would like when it came to the increased expectations off the course. One of the most down-to-earth and likeable players on the tour, Fox said he had sought the advice of US Open champion Geoff Ogilvy during the President’s Cup. “He said it does calm down a bit, but the cool thing is it kind of never leaves you as well,” Fox said. “You will always be a major champion. There will always be a bit of extra buzz around.”



Fox said he has to get better at saying no to certain demands now that his downtime was not as free as it once was. He said he was looking forward to going on a fishing trip when the chance arose. Related Article Australian Open ‘One in 72 billion chance’: Sydney golfer does unthinkable with back-to-back albatross and hole in one But he is far from complaining. He will arrive in Australia, knowing he has the claret jug, but also the game and mental resilience to contend in any tournament. “[I know I] can deal with pressure. I can hit some good shots down the stretch when it really matters,” he said. “Playing that well under pressure ... there is just a bit more belief there now.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Friday.

World.title: Dual international says Nawaqanitawase’s NRL stint proves Wallabies aren’t dead
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Dual international says Nawaqanitawase’s NRL stint proves Wallabies aren’t dead Christy Doran October 20, 2026 — 12:36pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Wallabies’ Bledisloe Cup drought might have stretched to 24 years, but dual international Michael O’Connor believes Mark Nawaqanitawase’s extraordinary two-year stint in rugby league proves the 15-a-side game in Australia still produces world-class talent. “You look at his ability and what he’s been able to do; to me, it reflects really well on rugby that we have a player like him come over to rugby league, and there are quite a lot of sceptics in rugby league around rugby union, and to see how he’s dominated the competition, I think it’s a good thing,” O’Connor said. Mark Nawaqanitawase and Robert Toia celebrate grand final glory. Getty Images Nawaqanitawase’s decision to sign with the Roosters following the Wallabies’ dreaded 2023 World Cup campaign caused a stir in Australian rugby. Rugby Australia boss Phil Waugh was shocked the talented back, who had only broken into the Wallabies in late 2022, was jumping codes just 12 months later.



But the athletic winger, who scored twice on his Super Rugby debut in 2020 and also bagged a double in his third Test against Wales in Cardiff, never looked back. Nawaqanitawase made an immediate impression in league, soaring high against the South Sydney Rabbitohs to score on debut. Loading He then topped the tryscorers list in 2025 (with 24) to earn Kangaroos selection for the Ashes in England, before bowing out with an Origin series win and an NRL title, where he scored twice in the Roosters’ 19-18 win, to cap an incredible 26 months. O’Connor, who played 13 Tests for the Wallabies before scoring 87 tries across 10 seasons of rugby league for St George and Manly, said he wasn’t shocked Nawaqanitawase had scaled such heights, having first seen him during his short second stint as a selector with the Wallabies in 2019.



But he added that the player returning to rugby, where he will join Japanese League One club Saitama Panasonic Wild Knights, was better than the one who left rugby in mid-2024 following the Paris Olympics. “The Roosters certainly did their homework when they signed him,” O’Connor said. Michael O’Connor believes Mark Nawaqanitawase’s successful transition bodes well for rugby union in Australia. Rugby AU Media/Stuart Walmsley “He’s a real athlete, and that was apparent even when I was a selector. “He made the Australian under-20 squad that went over to Argentina in 2019. He was scoring tries, he had a great instinct for the game and where the ball was, and his visual awareness was through the roof. But I think he’s just grown into a man, and he’s a far more complete footballer now.



“I think his move to rugby league has been a good thing; it certainly has brushed up some areas of his game … he’ll go back up with a lot of confidence.” Whether the Wallabies bear the fruit of his two years in rugby league remains to be seen. Mark Nawaqanitawase is a better player now than he was when he left rugby union in 2024, according to Michael O’Connor. Chris Hyde Wallabies coach Les Kiss wanted to pick the 26-year-old for next month’s Nations Championship campaign in the United Kingdom, but Nawaqanitawase ruled himself out after seeking time off. The decision means Nawaqanitawase could run out for Fiji or Italy next year, given the outside back would have missed the last three years of international rugby.



O’Connor said Nawaqanitawase’s availability would be critical for the Wallabies if they wanted to go deep at next year’s World Cup. “At a World Cup, it’s just apparent that you need world-class players, and a lot of them,” he said. ‘He’s a far more complete footballer now.’ Michael O’Connor on Mark Nawaqanitawase “Just watching New Zealand on the weekend, just the power of their lineup, there’s just no weaknesses, and that’s where we need to go. We need to get a complement of players who’ve played together and got no weaknesses. “He’s a world-class player, and that’s what we need. When we’ve had success in the past, we’ve had world-class players.”



While Nawaqanitawase might be unavailable for the Wallabies, fellow Origin cross-code star Zac Lomax could get the chance to push for a national call-up on Sunday when Australia A takes on the USA Eagles in Nashville. Lomax will be hoping to link up with another former Origin star, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, who will later this week be named for his third spring tour. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii on the attack against the All Blacks on Saturday. Getty Images O’Connor said he felt Suaalii, who was exposed defensively during the Wallabies’ 43-21 defeat in Sydney on Saturday, had been harshly rated since being catapulted into the Australian team in late 2024. “I feel a bit sorry for him in a way,” O’Connor said.



“He’s not complained once, but he’s played a number of positions, and he seems to be playing one position, and then someone says he’s a fullback or winger, or an outside centre. Related Article Analysis

Wallabies Why Wallabies are a better chance of winning World Cup than Bledisloe “It’s apparent that he has got great attacking skills. He’s very effective at running at the line and breaking through the line, and we need players to do that.” O’Connor, who made his Wallabies debut in 1979, a year before the great Mark Ella first ran out in gold, said today’s generation needed to play flatter at the line. “If you can look at where we can improve, we’re playing a lot behind the advantage line because of the rush defence, particularly from South Africa and also New Zealand,” he said. “But we need players to get through the advantage line and Suaalii can do that. He’s got good feet, he’s got good attacking nous, so there’s a spot for him there somewhere.”

“Not enough politicians are afraid for their lives right now & I think that’s a problem.” The comment had been made into a meme, with the words in fancy font printed on an image of a man pointing a gun. Marija Ercegovac It was posted on the official page of Nichole Overall, a NSW Nationals MP, by an account with a full name and a shadowy profile pic of a man’s back. “I’ve never had anything of this nature, this was quite shocking. I was taken aback,” says Overall of the post, which appeared on Monday, in the hours before the alleged attack on federal independent MP Helen Haines.



Related Article Live

Haines attack Helen Haines attack live updates: Federal Indi MP loses leg after being struck multiple times by car outside Wangaratta office; Brendan Nugent identified as alleged attacker “It’s just not the way, in a civilised society, we should be addressing things,” Overall says, becoming agitated. “It’s too much.” Such social media vitriol is a strange amalgam of public and personalised. It is posted for all to see, but it is deeply silo-ed, which is to say that I don’t know what’s happening in your feed, and you don’t know what’s happening in mine. You will only see the post on Overall’s Facebook page if it pops up in the online bubble that is perfectly tailored to you, courtesy of a tech company’s algorithm, breeding an isolation that is anything but pro-social.



We live in an age of bombardment, with overwhelming amounts of content coming at us all the time – more content than we could ever need or enjoy. But at the same time we are increasingly ignorant of the worlds, lives and viewpoints of those who don’t appear in our over-full feeds. NSW Nationals MP Nichole Overall was targeted in a post on social media hours before the alleged attack on Helen Haines. Alex Ellinghausen This confusion of content has metastasised threats to public safety, which are now splintered along strange fault lines that don’t necessarily follow traditional ideological positions of left/right. As Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said earlier in October of the terrorist threat: “We are getting some weird mixed ideologies, logically inconsistent, all cohering on violence.”



Related Article Haines attack Turn down the temperature: Spy chief’s urgent warning as Helen Haines remains in critical condition But extremists who deal in hostility do tend to share some common denominators – antisemitism being one, and misogyny being the other. These two ancient hatreds are useful bellwethers for talk that might turn violent. It is too early to know if Haines’ gender was a factor in the attack on her. But we are alive to the possibility because we know women politicians cop a degree of sexualised, highly personal abuse unique to their sex.





When asked if she thinks women politicians are singled out for particular abuse, Overall says: “I don’t want to make it a gender thing, but yes, it is most certainly the situation.” “Within the last 12 to 18 months there has absolutely been a heightened level of viciousness and sadly, it is misogyny.” She mentions a recent instance where she was called a “ho”. “It’s things that just simply aren’t said to men.” The political week took a horror turn with Monday’s attack on Haines.



But even before then, the political discourse had already entered a new era of coarseness. Independent senator Jacqui Lambie was mocked in a One Nation Please Explain video. Alex Ellinghausen Independent senator Jacqui Lambie has spoken before about her suffering from vaginal prolapse, in a laudable effort to de-stigmatise the condition from which hundreds of thousands of Australian women silently suffer. The latest of the cretinous Please Explain videos put out on Pauline Hanson’s YouTube feed over the weekend features Lambie in cartoon form, and witlessly mocks her condition. One should avoid hyperbole when discussing extremes in political debate, but the cartoon truly represents a new and imbecilic threshold passed.





“They’re not funny when you attack someone personally, and they incite people. When you’ve got other MPs, to be honest, posting things about other MPs, it doesn’t help.” No line can be drawn from the contemptible vulgarity of the videos to the violence of Monday in Wangaratta. But the two things exist in the same sphere of pernicious influence. Anyone who pretends otherwise, or tells others, butter-wouldn’t-melt-style, that hateful rhetoric is “just a joke”, should be called out. To re-purpose former prime minister Malcolm Turnbull’s saying about disrespect and violence towards women – not all hate speech ends in violence, but all political violence starts with hatred.

World.title: Jockeys cleared over Caulfield Cup horse death as stewards release report
World.content:
SportRacingVictorian racing Jockeys cleared over Caulfield Cup horse death as stewards release report Danny Russell Updated October 20, 2026 — 12:27pm ,first published October 20, 2026 — 9:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Racing Victoria stewards have cleared all jockeys of blame for a fall that caused a horse death in the Caulfield Cup on Saturday, as trainer Chris Waller revealed his staff were taking it “one day at a time” to cope with the loss of stable star Ohope Wins. Stewards released a report on Tuesday morning, saying they “could not attribute the incident to the careless actions of any one particular rider”. Loading They interviewed five jockeys – Rachel King, Jabez Johnstone, Ethan Brown, Mark Zahra and Jye McNeil – in the hours before releasing their finding. Stewards have now closed their investigation, referring the incident to Racing Victoria’s veterinary services department, which does not release public findings.



Related Article Blinkers On

Victorian racing Why all the details of the inquiry into Caulfield Cup horse death must be made public Saturday’s carnage unfolded 300 metres from the Caulfield Racecourse finish post in front of a packed public section. Waller’s dual group 1-winning Ohope Wins and jockey McNeil were brought crashing to the ground after last year’s winner Half Yours (Zahra) stumbled and fell in front of them. While Half Yours emerged with minor lacerations and both jockeys escaped serious injury, this year’s Australian Oaks winner suffered catastrophic injuries and had to be put down behind a green screen. The full details of the horse’s fatal injuries have not yet been released by Racing Victoria.



The two-horse tumble followed a bumping duel between King’s mount Green Spaces and the Johnstone-ridden Kings Valley on the home turn. Half Yours was then tightened for room between Kings Valley and Zahrann (Brown). “Stewards are of the view that the marginal shifts from both Green Spaces, when under pressure, and Kings Valley resulted in both those runners becoming unbalanced and shifting in ultimately resulting in Half Yours being tightened and falling,” their report said. “Further, stewards were satisfied Zahrann and Half Yours had both established a clear run prior to Half Yours meeting with interference.”



They found King and Johnstone had taken “the necessary corrective measures to straighten and relieve any pressure caused by their mounts to Half Yours”. “Furthermore, Ethan Brown rider of Zahrann had not contributed to Half Yours being tightened for room,” their report said. Stewards reported that there had been no issue with Caulfield track surface. Chris Waller watch his Cox Plate horses work at Flemington on Tuesday morning. Getty Images Trainer Tony McEvoy said Half Yours had been treated for lacerations and would be sent for a spell, ruling him out of a Melbourne Cup title defence.



Speaking for the first time about the tragic aftermath of the mid-race fall, Waller said on Tuesday it was never easy for staff to deal with the loss of a galloper. “They’re pretty resilient, the people that look after these horses, they obviously love them dearly, and they’re pets, just like a cat or dog,” a visibly upset Waller said at Flemington on Tuesday morning. “So, yeah, it’s always tough when there’s a missing [horse] in the stable.” Waller watched the race tragedy from Randwick, having stayed in Sydney for The Everest meeting. “I’ve spoken to Jye,” Waller said. “He’s improving with each day, and it’s great to see him out of hospital. He’s come out of it pretty well.”



McNeil was booked to ride Waller’s Valiant King in Wednesday’s Geelong Cup, but the trainer has opted to scratch the horse and run him at Flemington in the MV Gold Cup on Saturday. Despite the severity of the fall, both McNeil and Zahra were not deemed to have concussion – a scenario that would have seen them stood down for 12 days under Racing Victoria protocols. James McDonald puts Cox Plate favourite Aeliana through her paces at Flemington on Tuesday morning. Getty Images But Zahra was to meet with doctors again today before making a decision on his return. Waller was in Melbourne on Tuesday to watch his Cox Plate runners, Aeliana and Birdman, have an early morning hit out at Flemington. The Cox Plate barrier draw will be held Tuesday night.



The trainer acknowledged the support of the Melbourne Racing Club, which runs Caulfield Racecourse, following Saturday’s accident. “I commend them for offering counselling, and they’ve been fantastic because it’s good that people really understand how much people love horses and how much goes into a horse,” Waller said. Trainer Chris Waller. Getty Images “No risks are ever taken, and the first choice is to bring them home safe, regardless of where they finish. But the staff, they’re coping well. “You just take it one day at a time, just deal with it as each day comes.”



Waller has won six of the past 10 Cox Plates, including four with the record-breaking Winx between 2015-2018 and the past two with the Yulong-owned import Via Sistina. Related Article Updated

Victorian racing Risks unavoidable, says Racing Victoria, amid fallout from Caulfield Cup death That mare caused the sensation of the spring in 2024 when she dislodged jockey James McDonald during a Breakfast With The Best gallop at Moonee Valley and bolted away with a loose bandage hanging from her hind leg, and running three laps before being caught. While many feared the champion mare would be unable to take her place in the weight-for-age championship after the scare, she came out and won by eight lengths in record time (2:01.07). Waller said Aeliana and Birdman were set to peak in Saturday’s Cox Plate, being run at Flemington for the first time while Moonee Valley is closed for $250 million renovations.



“Both horses are in great form,” he said. “They’re genuine group 1 horses. Aeliana’s ready to peak after a good semi-final run last start (third in the Turnbull Stakes), and Birdman the same (third in the Might And Power Stakes).” McDonald, who has won the past four Cox Plates, flew in from Sydney to trial Aeliana, while Ben Melham rode Birdman. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport are sent every Monday.
